News.title: Hundreds of tourists rescued by boats fleeing resorts in Greece as ‘wall of flame’ wildfire rages & threaten beaches
News.content:
HUNDREDS of terrified tourists have been evacuated from beaches as a “wall of flames” menaced two popular resorts.

Petrifying infernos threatened multiple busy beaches, sparking 500 holidaymakers – some in their swimwear – to urgently flee into the sea via emergency boats in Greece.



Water-bombing planes, helicopters and more than 200 firefighters battled for hours to stop the flames spreading across the Halkidiki peninsula, south of the city of Thessaloniki.

Local media say a 3km “wall of flames” that roared up to 30 metres high was closing in on the resorts.



Desperate tourists – some with small children in their arms – were taken out to sea while crews tackle the blaze on Thursday.

Wearing protective face masks and holding their pets, residents also boarded the dinghies and small boats in the coastal region of Siviri as flames consumed nearby forests and thick gray smoke filled the clear skies.

Sophia, a homeowner in the region who only gave her first name, said: “We are on the beach and looking for a way to get away,

“From where we are, we can see that flames have reached the town and the houses.”



The region is dominated by flammable pine forests where the blaze is thought to have erupted, with firefighters saying strong winds made battling the blaze harder.

Within hours of erupting, the fire bore down on homes around the popular resorts of Siviri and Fourka, which were packed with summer travellers.

Dozens queued on a pontoon at Fourka waiting to flee as smoke blotted out the sky over the resorts, according to images broadcast by ERT.



Cars frantically trying to leave Fourka and Siviri caused traffic jams in the area.

Two injured firefighters were rushed to hospital.

Greece’s civil protection agency initially sent evacuation warnings by phone to people in the two resorts.



After extensive action, the blaze was later brought under control, according to the regional civil protection chief.

Crews remain on scene, alert for any potential flare ups.

Prior to the blaze Halkidiki authorities had banned the public from entering the region’s pine forests.

The Greek authorities had also issued a maximum five alert for fires for much of the Greek mainland.

Already this month, two crew from a helicopter helping to battle a forest fire near Athens died when their aircraft collided with another helicopter in mid-air.



The fire destroyed 110 square kilometres (42 square miles) of forest.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Earlier this month wildfires raged across Greece with a large fire tearing through the west of Athens, prompting evacuations.

The fire at the capital city gutted homes and burnt through farmland and pine forest, forcing emergency evacuations by land and sea.

News.title: What Brits remember from their childhood revealed – & it’s not big birthdays or expensive presents
News.content:
BLAST FROM PAST What Brits remember from their childhood revealed – & it’s not big birthdays or expensive presents

THE little things Brits remember most from childhood revealed – and it’s not birthdays or presents.

Brits are more likely to treasure family film nights, dinners around the table and long car journeys than big birthdays or expensive presents, research has found.



A study of 2,000 adults found 85 per cent believe their strongest childhood memories were made during small, unplanned moments rather than major occasions.

Family holidays topped the list at 43 per cent, followed by watching films together (32 per cent), family meals (26 per cent), car journeys (16 per cent) and playing games (14 per cent).



The latest research suggests it is often the ordinary experiences rather than the major milestones that stick with us.

More than three quarters (78 per cent) said who they shared an experience with was more important than where they were or what they were doing.

It comes after previous Samsung research revealed just how much of everyday life Brits are now documenting.

The average adult takes 1,040 photos and 312 videos every year, while 37 per cent capture more pictures and clips than they did five years ago.

Holidays (53 per cent) and family occasions (52 per cent) were the moments people were most likely to photograph or film.

And that growing bank of pictures appears to play an important role in keeping memories alive.



More than three quarters (76 per cent) said taking photos and videos helps them appreciate simple experiences more, while 81 per cent said it makes them feel closer to the people who matter most.

More than a quarter (28 per cent) regularly revisit childhood pictures or videos, sparking feelings of nostalgia (48 per cent), happiness (39 per cent), connection (33 per cent) and comfort (29 per cent).

The latest research was commissioned by Samsung to mark the launch of the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Series, including the Galaxy Z Fold8 and Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra.

Annika Bizon, Mobile Experience VP of Product and Marketing for Samsung UK and Ireland, said: “Our research is a reminder that it’s often the everyday moments that matter most.

“From daily routines and family film nights to holidays and unplanned moments, the new Galaxy Z Fold8 and Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra are designed to adapt to whatever comes your way.”

News.title: Woman, 75, dies following burglary at home as man, 81, hospitalised with cops launching urgent appeal for information
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

BURGLARY DEATH Woman, 75, dies following burglary at home as man, 81, hospitalised with cops launching urgent appeal for information

A 75-YEAR-OLD woman has died after a suspected violent burglary as an 81-year-old man was hospitalised.

Police have launched an urgent appeal, urging the public to come forward with information that could help their investigation.

Cops rushed to a home in Tollington Park, Finsbury Park at 9.20pm on Tuesday night, responding to reports of an aggravated burglary.

Paramedics from the London ambulance service also attended.





A 75-year-old woman and an 81-year-old were treated at the scene before being rushed to hospital.

The man was discharged the next day, but the woman died in hospital on Wednesday.

A post mortem is set to take place.

The crime scene on Evershot Road remains secured as cops gather evidence.



Detective Chief Inspector Ben Massink said: “We’re at an early stage of this investigation and awaiting a post-mortem examination to determine how the woman died, with my team working hard to pursue all lines of enquiry.”

He stressed that “no detail is too small” to present to police.

Massink added: “We thank those who have already come forward to provide witness accounts, and appeal for anyone with information or doorbell footage to come forward.

“We believe a number of residents in the area will have key information that could help inform our investigation.”



Superintendent Mark Hambleton said: “Our thoughts remain with the woman’s family and friends at this unimaginably difficult time.

“We recognise the concern this will cause locally and can reassure the community that officers are working tirelessly to determine what happened.

“There will be an increased police presence in place while enquiries continue and we thank the public for their understanding at this time.”

Anyone with information is asked to call police on 101, quoting CAD7757/12AUG, or contact Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.

News.title: Huge £20,000 reward issued for information to locate man who disappeared 18 years ago aged 16 from his home
News.content:
FIND HIM Huge £20,000 reward issued for information to locate man who disappeared 18 years ago aged 16 from his home

A HUGE £20,000 reward has been offered by detectives searching for a man who vanished from his home 18 years ago as a teenager.

Alex Sloley was just 16 years old when he was reported missing from Islington in August 2008.



Alex’s disappearance sparked an extensive Metropolitan Police investigation that continues to be regularly reviewed for fresh leads despite it occurring nearly two decades ago.

Cops have disclosed that Alex was a victim of exploitation who was being coerced into criminality by local gangs at the time he went missing.



Investigating officers now want to hear from anyone who was similarly exploited by gangs in North London around 2008 and may hold crucial information.

Police have released two potential e-fits of Alex that could show what he looks like aged 34.



Detective Chief Inspector Sarb Kaur said: “We are continuing our efforts to find Alex and support his family who have spent the past 18 years desperately wanting answers.

“We are aware that at the time he went missing, Alex was a victim of exploitation and was being coerced into criminality by gangs in the area.

“We are looking to speak with anyone who believes they were exploited by gangs in North London around 2008 and may have seen Alex or have information to contact us.

“You will not be in trouble, but you may hold key information which could help us piece the jigsaw together.



“A £20,000 reward is on offer to anyone who provides information which could lead us to Alex.

“Over time allegiances can change and we hope that the offer of this substantial reward could help someone with information to come forward.”

The Met Police first received a report from Alex’s family on 8 August 2008 after they had not seen or heard from him.



An investigation was immediately launched, with officers gathering statements from Alex’s family and friends while reviewing CCTV from the surrounding area.

At the time he disappeared, Alex was described as being around 5ft 5ins tall, of medium build, and with striking blue eyes.

Repeated public appeals made over the years have yielded multiple reported sightings, but detectives hope the substantial reward will finally provide the breakthrough needed to locate him.



Cops urged anyone with information to come forward immediately and “do the right thing” despite the age of the case.

DCI Kaur added: “Over the years following the appeals we have made, our officers have reviewed hundreds of reports from people who believe they’ve seen Alex in London.

“Unfortunately, this information is yet to provide investigating officers with the information needed to find him.

“Alongside this appeal, we are continuing to put Alex’s image out there, both at the time he went missing and how he may look now at the age of 34, in case anyone has seen him and can contact us.

“We remain committed to this investigation which I believe can be solved.”



Anyone who has any information can contact the investigation team directly, via phone or text message on 07860 369 603.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Alternatively, information can be provided via 101 or submitted online.

Information can also be provided anonymously to independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

News.title: Burnham came to power promising radical change – the signs are that it won’t be for the better
News.content:
Growing pains

ONE of Andy Burnham’s key slogans since becoming Prime Minister is “growth in every postcode”.

Whatever that means.



Yesterday’s quarterly GDP figures show there is still a very long way to go.

Despite the promises, growth has basically flat-lined for over two years.



Tax rises have squeezed incomes and businesses, while giant welfare bills have become a massive drag on the economy.

That has left the construction industry in ruins, shattering any hopes that the Government can build the 1.5million new homes it pledged.

More than one million young people are not in work, training or education as a result of Labour’s National Insurance and minimum wage increases.

What do Burnham and his Chancellor John Healey plan to do about either?

The signs are not good.

More taxes ALWAYS mean less growth. Yet Burnham is planning a wealth whack on individuals and property that will drive away entrepreneurs.



Closer ties with the dying EU won’t deliver growth either.

The ongoing Iran War also threatens to blow a huge hole in Healey’s plans at a time when he MUST ramp up defence spending.

The autumn, with no heatwaves or World Cup to boost spending, could see a painful economic slowdown ahead of Healey’s first Budget.

Burnham came to power promising radical change. The signs are that it won’t be for the better.

Hard Labour

YVETTE Cooper finally admits what most of the country may have decided a long time ago: Labour hasn’t been very good at being in government.



Turning on the man who made her Foreign Secretary, Cooper says Sir Keir Starmer’s hands-off style of management meant their first two years in power were wasted.

Certainly, there have been precious few upsides and plenty of disasters. Welfare up, taxes, spending and debt all up, inflation and unemployment both up and defence spending down.

The Chagos Islands giveaway, the endless U-turns. The Peter Mandelson scandal.

The only question is: Will Burnham prove to be any better?

Dawn of the dud

LABOUR truly is the party of the sneering metropolitan elite.



In response to a post on the struggles of the betting industry — which employs thousands and supports dozens of charities — Dawn Butler MP posted: “lol.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Laughing in the faces of ordinary punters who choose to spend hard-earned money on a harmless flutter is typical of a party that has lost all connection to its working-class roots.

Butler’s attitude reflects many within Labour’s ranks for whom the first instinct is always that Nanny Knows Best.

News.title: When Andy Burnham promised Brits growth in every postcode, did he really mean more illegal migrants?
News.content:
ARE you playing your part? Are you doing your fair share? The Prime Minister wants to know.

It turns out that going to work every day to put a roof over your own family’s head isn’t enough any more. And neither is paying thousands in taxes to fund other people’s families, too.



No, according to Andy Burnham, we all need to do more for the country by accepting our “fair share” of illegal migrants into our local neighbourhoods.

Mr Burnham says middle-class families need to “play their part” when it comes to asylum seeker accommodation, instead of leaving the burden to fall on poorer parts of the country.



He told the country this week: “We cannot have a situation where it’s only the poorest communities in the country that receive all of the dispersal of refugees and asylum seekers.

“I do believe all parts of the country need to work to play their part.”

No10 then doubled down, with a staffer insisting that the PM “feels the current system is unfair, and as a point of principle, he wants to see a redress of the distribution.

“He acknowledges that it would cost more money to do it more fairly, but that is what we need to do”.

Sorry, Prime Minister, but we don’t all have to play our part. We never asked for these people to come here and we don’t want them here.

And it’s not a “point of principle” for us all to have to endure the arrival of thousands of undocumented fighting-age men from far-flung places into our local hotels and residential roads to hang around on street corners, take illegal work and sexually harass teenage girls.



What the PM said is wrong on so many levels.

First, Mr Burnham appears to think that better-off people need to follow poor people who have “accepted” these illegal migrants into their areas.

They absolutely have not.

Illegal migrants have been imposed against their very clearly expressed wishes, and often in the face of opposition from local councils, too.

Apparently Mr Devolution doesn’t like local people power when it comes to asylum seeker accommodation.



Or has he somehow managed to miss all the protests outside asylum hotels in Epping, Crowborough, Canary Wharf, Bristol, Liverpool and Manchester, to name but a few?

The PM also assumes that the middle classes aren’t playing their part already when it’s their taxes which foot the bill for the many billions of pounds spent on migrant accommodation.

Many better-off areas are already sharing the burden, including my own local high street, where the only hotel now only houses asylum seekers.

Only 17 local authorities out of 361 have so far been spared the arrival of illegal migrants in their areas, which hardly suggests most Britons have dodged that particular bullet.

When Andy Burnham promised us “growth in every postcode” on his first day in No10, I don’t think most of us thought he meant that sort of growth.



What was most illuminating from Andy Burnham’s comments, however, was his inadvertent admission that having illegal migrants in your area isn’t necessarily a good thing.

Apparently it’s a burden that we all need to share rather than a blessing.

Who would’ve guessed that all these young men paying people smugglers are not in fact fine, upstanding engineers and doctors desperate to pick up litter and help little old ladies across the road to show their gratitude to us for giving them refuge?



And let’s face it, by calling on us all to share the burden, Andy Burnham was also admitting that he can’t and won’t solve the boats crisis. And he’s not even going to bother to pretend that he will.

Fewer than 300 migrants crossed the Channel on dinghies in December 2018 when the boats crisis first emerged.

It was such a big story at the time that then Home Secretary Sajid Javid had to cut short his family’s Christmas holiday to come home to deal with it.

Eight years later, we see 230 migrants arriving on just one boat in one day and the PM decides to hold an emergency Cobra meeting to discuss . . . the weather and whether to ban disposable barbecues.

Perhaps the only answer is for us all to follow in the footsteps of the Oxfordshire village of Piddington, where the 400 local residents have voted to hold a referendum on seceding from the United Kingdom to prevent 1,250 illegal migrant men from being housed just a few hundred yards away in Bicester barracks.



Meanwhile, all the MPs, charity workers, civil servants, human rights lawyers, BBC and Guardian staff who insist every arrival is a desperate refugee deserving of our sympathy can happily take all these young men into their local communities.

Or, better still, into their own homes.

We’ve seen one illegal immigrant landing on Britain’s shores every 14 minutes since Labour came to power two years ago.

And even though numbers have fallen since last year, most of the illegal boat migrant arrivals — largely fighting-age men from countries with alien cultures — are still here years later.

Indeed, some 200,000 illegal migrants have arrived here since 2018.



And we are still paying for most of them to the tune of some £4billion a year.

It’s not only better-off folk who don’t want illegal migrants in their streets. NO ONE wants them.

We don’t want them in four-star hotels or two-star hotels. We don’t want them in flats, barges or former Army barracks. We don’t want them, full stop.

Spreading asylum seekers around a few more postcodes, shuffling them from inner city sink estates to leafy villages, isn’t the solution to this problem.

The solution is to stop allowing more illegal boat arrivals into our country and to detain and deport the ones who are already here.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The one thing Andy Burnham is right about is that the current system is unfair — but it’s unfair to all British people.

The only “point of principle” he should be caring about when it comes to illegal migrants isn’t which postcode they live in but that people who have no right to live in Britain should not be here at all.

News.title: Crazed Scots dad and son dragged cop along road at 50mph as he clung to car in sickening murder bid
News.content:
'YOU'RE GOING TO KILL ME'

'YOU'RE GOING TO KILL ME' Crazed Scots dad and son dragged cop along road at 50mph as he clung to car in sickening murder bid

A CRAZED dad and son who dragged a cop along the road at 50mph as he clung to their motor were both caged.

Douglas Mills, 58, and Douglas Jr, 32, threw PC Mark Smith from their speeding Audi, inflicting horror injuries. Both fiends were convicted of attempting to murder him in Hamilton in August 2024.



PC Smith told Glasgow’s High Court: “I thought I’d never see my family again.”

The terrified cop yelled “you are going to kill me” while dangling from a motor as a maniac father and son raced off at 50mph, a court heard.



PC Smith, 35, told how he tried desperately to cling on as Douglas Mills, 58, and his namesake son, 32, fled before being shoved into the road and left for dead.

The hero officer’s ordeal unfolded when he approached the Audi after witnessing a suspected drug deal while the duo were parked up in Hamilton.



Suddenly he was yanked inside the vehicle where one of the thugs gripped him and rained blows on his head during a struggle.

He then tumbled out as the motor accelerated and was left in a heap in the road badly injured.

The father-and-son pair denied attempted murder at the High Court in Glasgow and claimed they thought they were being ambushed by a mystery assailant but a jury saw through their story.

They now face lengthy prison sentences after the trial heard PC Smith was left scarred for life and has still not been able to return to duty following the attack. Recalling the kill bid in August 2024, he told jurors: “I thought I was never going to see my family again.”



He testified how he and fellow plain-clothed officer Colin Harris had spotted the car and identified Mills Jnr as the driver.

Jurors heard how the cops watched a man cross the road apparently clutching cash and go up to the passenger-side window before making off.

PC Smith said he believed the male was exchanging the cash “for drugs or some other item”.



He got out of their unmarked car clutching his warrant card and radio and shouted “loudly” that he was police.

As he approached Mills Jnr appeared “irritated”.

Describing what happened next, PC Smith said: “It was all very instantaneous. I felt myself being pulled off my feet.

“The car began to move off at speed.”

Asked who was “pulling” him inside, he told prosecutor Michelle Brannagan: “It all happened so quickly. It took me completely by surprise. I was off my feet before I knew what was happening.”



Then his legs were left hanging outside the car while he was being thumped on the head, the jury was told.

The cop went on: “I was off my feet before I knew what was happening. I had no opportunity to balance myself.

“My legs were outside the car. All I remember was blows to my head and, to be honest, panicking.”

The motor’s speedometer was spotted racing to 50mph “in a matter of seconds”.

PC Smith said he could not tell who was hitting him as things were “blurry”.



The court heard: “They were strong enough to make me feel afraid that I would lose consciousness if I did not protect myself.

“I was shouting that they were going to kill me.”

He then told how his assailant appeared to release his grip on him leaving him at risk of falling out. And the court heard he reckoned he was then shoved out.

PC Smith recalled: “I thought, there is no chance I am surviving here if I hit the road at this speed.”

Then came the “truly terrifying” feeling of “air blowing around” him.



He testified from behind a screen to spare him having to watch footage. But he recalled the last thing he saw before things went “black” was of the driver “almost looking happy”. His next memory was of being rushed to A&E in an ambulance.

Mills Jnr claimed he had earlier been for Botox treatment and visited a bakery to pick up cakes.

The fiend claimed to have stopped to send a text when he saw a man “on top” of his dad. He then drove off as he was “scared for my life”.

When he found out later it was an officer he arranged to hand himself in.

PC Smith refuted claims he failed to indicate he was a cop or that he “launched” himself into the Audi stop it at any cost.



Jurors heard he suffered a fractured skull and blood clot while a chunk of skin came off his back in the fall.

And he remains on a waiting list for ankle ligament reconstruction.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Asked about his injuries, PC Smith — who has seven years’ service with the force — added: “Every time I look in the mirror makes me think of this every single day.”

Judge William Gallacher remanded both men in custody as sentencing was deferred.

News.title: Bizarre moment boar tries to steal food from sunbather’s bag as swine scavenge on beach at Brit hols hotspot
News.content:
THIS is the moment a group of greedy pigs attempt to pillage food from punters at a ritzy beach.

Eye-raising video shows the brazen boar and its piglets snuffling around an unattended bag in front of a stunned audience on the French Riviera.



The hungry family was captured scouting out the beach before something startled them, sending them scuttling before they could rob the beachgoers, in a now-viral clip.

This summer, hordes of the hungry animals have made quite the impression on France’s holiday beaches.



Wild boars are very common across the Côte d’Azur and rural France but as their population grows, human and pig interactions are becoming far more common.

Their stock is currently growing faster than the authorities can control.

In search of food, they are often fed by humans or help themselves directly from garbage cans.

Growing encounters have caused alarm as some fear the animals are losing their fear of humans.



When wild animals lose their fear of humans – known as habituation – it triggers a destructive cycle of human-wildlife conflict.

This loss of fear typically happens when urban expansion encroaches on their territory, or when humans intentionally or unintentionally provide food via overflowing trash bins, pet bowls, or handouts.

The best known example of this is the urban pigeon – which have learned over generations that people are a reliable source of food rather than a dangerous predator.



In reaction to the viral clip, Liz Webster, a British farming advocate, said: “Wild boar populations are booming across Europe and on the French Riviera they’ve discovered beaches, tourists, restaurants and bins provide easy pickings.

“Nature needs management.

“In densely populated Europe, bringing back boar, wolves, beavers and potentially bears doesn’t mean humans can simply withdraw and let nature take over.

“Wildlife, farming and people have to coexist and that requires active land and population management.”

It comes as a wild boar went on a dramatic rampage across a Turkish street in May, sending one man flying and two in hospital.



The savage beast is caught on camera tearing through the middle of a Turkish street, running full pelt towards pedestrians.

One man was seen flipping in the air before crashing face-first onto the road as the crazed creature continues on without care.

News.title: Multiple fires destroy homes and cause devastation in West Midlands
News.content:
A child and three firefighters were among those taken to hospital as several fires raged across the West Midlands, destroying homes and forcing dozens of residents to evacuate.

As the UK recorded its hottest day of the year, fire services in the region said they experienced extreme levels of demand on Thursday.

A huge blaze near Stourbridge Golf Course saw about 100 firefighters battling the fire which spread rapidly through dry grass and woodland, setting alight six homes.

Elsewhere in the region four homes were destroyed by fire in Stoke-on-Trent, a woman was seriously injured in a blaze in Castle Vale, Birmingham, and a major incident was declared because of a fire in Warwickshire.

The region's fire chief Simon Tuhill said there was extensive devastation while Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it was "awful" to see the impact on homes and communities and thanked firefighters tackling the blazes.

Burnham added: "My thoughts are with everyone affected, particularly those who have been injured or forced from their homes, and with the firefighters who have been taken to hospital.

"I'm in touch with local leaders like [West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker] and will be speaking to emergency services on the ground as they continue their response."

Parker described the large number of fires on Thursday as an "extremely worrying and fast-moving situation".

The fire in Stourbridge - which covered about 40 acres of land, including woodland - had "several points of origin", West Midlands Fire Service said.

Tuhill said the service's fire control team had dealt with thousands of 999 calls through the day, and added the fires were "one of the most significant" incidents the service had ever dealt with.

News.title: Two seriously hurt as passenger train derails in East Sussex
News.content:
Twenty people have been injured, two seriously, after a train derailed in East Sussex and a major incident was declared.

Network Rail said the 14:24 BST Southern service from London Victoria to Eastbourne came off the tracks close to Lewes railway station, shortly before 16:00 BST.

Photographs from the scene showed people standing on top of overturned carriages, with passengers describing "pandemonium" on board and screaming.

British Transport Police said three carriages derailed, leaving several people trapped. All 150 on board have now been evacuated.

Several rail routes in the area were closed, as emergency teams rushed to the scene and people were advised to avoid the area.

Patients were assessed and treated at the scene, with some sent to local hospitals.

British Transport Police Chief Superintendent Dominique Ioannou said in a press briefing on Thursday night that a number of passengers were initially trapped but were all safely evacuated from the train.

She said while two people sustained serious injuries, a further 18 suffered less serious injuries.

"The train started rocking violently and then I remember clocking eyes with this guy and then there was a lot of screaming," passenger Rachel Heath said.

"It felt like we flew in the air and the carriage landed on its side and it slid. I felt like it was going to completely flip over.

"There was a mum who was bleeding from her mouth and a dad and his son who had cuts. It was like a movie."

News.title: Final day of heatwave for many before weekend cooldown
News.content:
Kew Gardens in London reached 38.1C on Thursday, making it the UK's hottest day of 2026 so far, and the fifth hottest UK day on record.

It is also the second time this year that the temperature has reached 38C, after Lingwood, Norfolk recorded 38.0C on 26 June.

This is only the second time that 38C has been reached twice in the same year - the previous occasion being 2022.

Though the Met Office amber warning for extreme heat that covered large swathes of England on Thursday expired at midnight, high temperatures will linger in central and eastern parts of England on Friday.

Long spells of sunshine will lift temperatures to 29-34C (84-93F) across large parts of the Midlands, Lincolnshire, East Anglia and the south-east.

For many places it will mark a third consecutive day above official heatwave thresholds.

The heat will ease elsewhere.

Somewhat cooler conditions will begin to move into northern and western parts of the UK, although temperatures will generally remain above the norm for the time of year - widely reaching the low to mid-20s Celsius.

Many places will be dry with a mix of cloud and sunny spells although a few showers are possible, and these could be heavy and thundery in some places.

News.title: 'Two out of four, baby' - Hunt wins 200m as she eyes historic quadruple
News.content:
Britain's Amy Hunt charged to 200m glory to secure her second gold medal of the European Championships - but the sprinter has her sights set on a historic quadruple in Birmingham.

The 24-year-old wants to "be iconic" and become the first athlete to win four European gold medals in the same tournament.

And after triumphing in the 100m on Monday, she added another gold to her collection with a season's best time of 22.19 seconds in the 200m final on Thursday.

Hunt reeled in rival and compatriot Asher-Smith down the back straight to cross the line first.

"Two out of four, baby!" Hunt told BBC TV.

"This is becoming a magical week and one I will remember for the rest of my life."

Hunt is set to compete in the women's and mixed 4x100m relay events later and says there will be "no celebrations and no champagne until Sunday night".

"I have got a debt to the ladies," she said.

"We have got to come out here and make sure we show them who the best sprinting nation is in Europe."

Asher-Smith was beaten to silver by just 0.01 seconds by Ireland's Rhasidat Adeleke, who set a new national record.

"It unfolded exactly how I thought it would," two-time European 200m silver medallist Nethaneel Mitchell-Blake said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"I knew Dina would run a blistering bend and then say 'Amy, come and catch me'. And that's what Amy has done."

News.title: Son of 102-year-old says father died after being 'pushed off stage'
News.content:
Robert said: "He just asked them to turn the music down."

He said his father turned around to come back down off the stage when he was pushed, and that resulted in a broken hip.

"[That's] the most upsetting part. He wasn't going to live forever but it's not a nice way, obviously in pain," he said.

"We want to see justice, of course.

"They must have known he was an old man. It makes you wonder what the world is coming to.

"It has obviously made it difficult. It would've been nice if he'd gone quietly in his sleep.

"He was in hospital, suffering, for a week-and-a-half. It's not nice.

"I feel sad - even though he could be difficult because of his age and dementia, still, you get used to him being around," he said.

Robert, a retired civil engineer, said his father used to visit the Crow's Nest.

"What happened is not nice. The pub has changed a lot over the years. It has become a youngsters' pub," he said.

Robert said he grew up in the home in the the Llanyrafon neighbourhood where his father had lived since 1960.

He said his dad had a career as a design draughtsman and had lived alone since his wife died 40 years ago.

"Me and my brother would visit our father regularly, and clean the house and buy him food.

"His eyesight had deteriorated and he had been diagnosed with dementia two or three years ago."

Robert said: "He's well-known around here, although a lot of his generation are gone," he added.

He said his father would visit the pub two or three times a week, where he would drink beers, and described how he became a familiar face to some locals.

"I suppose he became a pub character," he added.

News.title: BBC Verify speaks to woman who filmed ICE agent pointing gun at her
News.content:
A video showing a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent pointing his gun at a woman has been viewed by millions after she shared the moment on Instagram.

Carolina Molina says she was out delivering business cards in Falls Church, Virginia, when she saw ICE agents, who then surrounded her car.

The US Department of Homeland Security said she "attempted to harm officers by weaponising her vehicle". Molina denies this.

BBC Verify assesses the dashcam footage shared by Molina. Jake Horton reports.

Produced by Tom Joyner. Graphics by Mark Edwards.

News.title: Why heatwaves hit women harder
News.content:
Overwhelmed, irritable, dizzy, bloated, exhausted.

These are the words coming up frequently in comments sent to the BBC by women who, having barely recovered from the record-breaking heat in June, are bracing for more hot weather.

Extreme heat can affect anyone. But heatwaves are a "stress-test" for women's cardiovascular systems, and hit them harder than men, Dr Nighat Arif, an NHS GP who specialises in women's health, told the BBC.

Women may also be marginally more vulnerable to heatwave-related death than men, though more evidence is needed, said Dr Cat Pinho-Gomes, an academic public health consultant at UCL's Institute for Global Health.

So as climate change drives increasingly intense and frequent heatwaves to the UK, experts are calling for better awareness of the risks to women and more targeted efforts to protect them.

News.title: Six ways to keep your home and yourself cool in hot weather
News.content:
Tepid showers can help to cool your body temperature, saving both money and energy. But Prof Tipton warns not to go too cold: "The trick is to try and get the skin as cool as possible whilst maintaining maximum blood flow to it.

"Too cold and the body will shut down blood to the skin and trap the heat in the body making it harder to get out."

Putting an ice pack or cold-water bottle on your body can achieve an instant feeling of relief. You may want to wrap it in a towel to avoid direct contact with your skin.

Your clothes can also really affect your body temperature.

Natural fibres like cotton and linen help to regulate body temperature and loose-fitting clothing allows room for the breeze to cool you down.

This is also why cotton bed sheets can help you sleep when hot air fills a room.

News.title: Ice cream man hit with noise complaint over van's music
News.content:
An ice cream man has been hit with a noise complaint by someone who did not like the loud chimes from his van.

Mark Edwards was contacted by the council after a Tonyrefail resident complained about the van's music being played in the evening.

He said he had been serving the area for more than 20 years without a complaint and was determined "not to let one individual spoil it for everybody else" and has agreed with customers to beep his horn in each street so they know he is there.

Rhondda Cynon Taf council said it received a noise complaint in June relating to music being played after 20:00 BST, which it investigated and found to be valid.

Edwards, from Trebanog, said he was taken aback when he found a letter from the council on the van's dashboard: "Twenty-odd years and I have never had anything like this at all. It's unbelievable."

He said his employer told him to stop operating in the area because continuing to use the chimes could result in a fine, but he did not want to stop serving customers, so came up with the alternative plan.

"I thought 'I'm not going to let one individual to spoil it for everybody else', so have come to an arrangement with my customers in the area.

"They know roughly what time I'm there and I toot the horn in each street, and they all come out and enjoy it. They're not going to beat me."

The council said the law required a 19:00 cut-off time for ice cream van operators to use their chimes, but it did not "prevent them from trading after this time".

It added that Edwards had been sent a letter reminding him of these requirements and that it considered the matter closed.

News.title: Top grades rise again as students get A-level, T-level and BTec results
News.content:
Hundreds of thousands of students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland have opened their A-level, T-level and BTec results on Thursday morning.

The percentage of top A-level grades edged up again, and a record number of students found out they had secured a place at university.

The cost of going to university has been in the spotlight this year, with mounting pressure on the government to reform student loan repayments, and there has been a renewed focus on technical education under Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

But the chief executive of Universities UK, which represents more than 140 vice-chancellors, urged students to not "let politicians make your decision for you".

The percentage of A* and A grades at A-level increased to 28.5% across England, Wales and Northern Ireland this year, up from 28.3% last year.

About 40% of 18-year-olds in England receive A-levels every summer.

Around 250,000 grades for vocational and technical qualifications were also released to students in England.

These include BTec National, Cambridge Technical, Cambridge Advanced National and T-level results.

Almost 20,000 students completed a T-level in 2026, with a pass rate of over 90%.

Launched in 2020, T-levels are two-year technical courses that are taken after GCSEs. They focus more on practical subjects than academic ones, but are an equivalent qualification to three A-levels.

AS-levels, which will count towards students' final A-level results next summer in Wales and Northern Ireland, have also been released.

This year, the pass rate for National 5, Higher and Advanced Higher exams in Scotland rose across the board.

News.title: Couple tie the knot on 'magical' solar eclipse day
News.content:
Wednesday's full eclipse may be something many of us remember for a long time: the special glasses, the colanders, and the eerie shadowing of the sun.

And for one couple, it was especially unforgettable as they got married during the once-in-a-generation event.

Jerry and Jamie Bone, from Gosfield, Essex, planned their big day around the astronomical phenomenon - the first total solar eclipse visible over mainland Europe since 1999 - and tied the knot in Alpheton, near Sudbury, Suffolk.

Jamie said they had realised a few years ago the eclipse would take place in 2026, and decided it would be the "perfect" day to get married.

News.title: Bonnie Tyler's classic hit spiked in streams during solar eclipse
News.content:
Born Gaynor Hopkins in a council house in Neath, Tyler grew up with a love for music before she was discovered by talent scout Roger Bell in a Swansea club.

Tyler released her first single, Lost in France in 1977, but it was the release of Total Eclipse of the Heart five years later which changed her life.

The ballad spent two weeks at UK number one and four weeks in the US.

The iconic love song's music video surpassed 1.2 billion views on YouTube and has had over a billion streams on Spotify.

Spotify previously said it had paid out more than $1.4 million for streams of Tyler's catalogue in 2025.

The music platform said Total Eclipse of the Heart was one of a few "celestial" songs that saw a streaming spike in the UK on 12 August.

According to Spotify, the biggest increases in UK streams during the eclipse were:

Evolfo, Moon Eclipsed the Sun (+12,817%)

Chris Staples, Dark Side of the Moon (+2,805%)

Pink Floyd, Eclipse (+594%)

Delta Goodrem, Eclipse (+104%)

Bonnie Tyler, Total Eclipse of the Heart (+94%)

Bill Withers, Ain't No Sunshine (+17%)

Shannon Carragher, senior editor at Spotify, said: "It is always fascinating to see how major cultural events instantly reflect in what the UK is listening to.

"Cultural phenomena like the solar eclipse naturally bring people together and we instinctively look for the perfect soundtrack to share that moment."

Ahead of the solar eclipse, Tyler's McVitie's Jaffa Cakes TV advert also resurfaced - it was originally broadcast in 2023 when there was a partial lunar eclipse.

The nostalgic advert came after research revealed almost half (49%) of Brits did not understand how eclipses occurred.

In the video, Tyler uses a Jaffa Cake as a prop to describe the different types of eclipse.

She said: "There are three types of eclipse. You've got the lunar eclipse, the solar eclipse, and then there's the total eclipse of the heart.

"When the earth is situated between the moon and the sun it creates a shadow, and when it looks like someone has just taken a bite out of the moon. That's a partial lunar eclipse."

The grammy-nominated star had a string of other hits, including Holding out for a Hero and also represented the UK at the Eurovision Song Contest in 2013.

She was named in the Queen's last Birthday Honours list in 2022 and was awarded an MBE for her services to music by Prince William the following year.

Tyler died "unexpectedly" on 8 July, aged 75, at a Portugal hospital, "as a result of the illness that she was being treated for", her family said in a statement released on the star's official website, external.

At the time, tributes poured in from a host of friends and stars including Catherine Zeta-Jones, Bryan Adams and Rod Stewart.

Tyler's funeral service will take place on 17 August at 12:00 BST at St Mary's Church in Swansea.

It has since been confirmed that her coffin will be brought to her Mumbles home on 15 August at 15:30 BST.

People are invited to "pay their respects" by lining Newton Road at 15:15 BST.

News.title: Honeytrap thieves jailed for killing men they had drugged
News.content:
A couple who drugged men seeking sexual services in order to steal from them have been jailed for killing two men and poisoning others.

Adina Mihai and Madalin Dumitru admitted the manslaughter of Gary Mouat, 37, from Oxfordshire, and Malcolm King, 80, from Gloucestershire, in 2025 and 2024 respectively.

On the first day of their trial in June, the pair also each admitted two further counts of administering poison to surviving victims.

Mihai, 31, and Dumitru, 30, were both sentenced to 17 years in prison at Oxford Crown Court.

Mihai, who posed as a sex worker, and her partner Dumitru, arranged to meet men paying for services she had advertised online at their homes.

The court heard four had their alcoholic drinks spiked with the powerful sedative gamma-butyrolactone (GBL) so the pair could steal from them.

Two men died as a result, while two others - who cannot be named due to reporting restrictions - survived.

News.title: Big Issue says vendors struggling as sales hit by heatwaves
News.content:
Big Issue vendors are struggling to sell magazines in the UK's extreme heat, which is having an "immediate" impact on their earnings, Big Issue's managing director says.

Sales of the British news and entertainment magazine are down on average 20% year on year in weeks where heatwaves have been declared, Catherine Parsons said.

During June's record-breaking temperatures, the worst-hit West Midlands and Wales saw 34% and 33% fewer sales respectively.

George Anderson, who sells the Big Issue near the BBC's Broadcasting House in London, says it is a struggle when footfall is lower and people would rather be near the aircon.

"People are uncomfortable, they don't want to hang around in the heat and chat," he told the BBC on the hottest day of the year.

"I manage it as best I can, and so far so good, but my sales are definitely down which can be quite tough."

Big Issue is sold by people experiencing homelessness or financial instability.

But Parsons said sellers are losing out on vital income due to the heatwaves.

"For most of us, extreme heat is an inconvenience. For Big Issue vendors, it means earning significantly less and making difficult decisions about rent, food and other essentials," she said.

In the week of 22 June, when the UK's June temperature record was broken and temperatures hit 37.7C (99.9F), Big Issue sales fell by an average of 22% compared to the same week the previous year, their figures show.

The latest spell of extreme heat marks the UK's fifth heatwave this year, with the Met Office warning this summer is on course to be the UK's hottest since records began.

Parsons said Big Issue teams were working to support vendors and had been handing out sunscreen, caps and water bottles.

"But in the most extreme temperatures, it's simply unsafe for vendors to be out and selling, and when the heat forces them to cut their working day short, the financial impact is immediate."

News.title: Second attempted murder arrest after cycle path attack
News.content:
A second suspect has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after a man was attacked on the Bristol to Bath Railway Path.

The victim, aged in his 30s, was taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries believed to have been caused by a "bladed weapon" following the incident near Bitton at about 20:00 BST on Tuesday.

One teenager was arrested on the night of the attack and a second was arrested on Wednesday afternoon.

Both have been released on conditional bail while enquiries continue.

Insp Barny Mabbett, from Avon and Somerset Police, said: "Uniformed officers are conducting patrols along the railway path to provide reassurance because we recognise an incident like this does inevitably causes concern.

"Our investigation into what happened is ongoing, but we are also working with other organisations around making sure the railway path is a safe place for people to enjoy and use both in the short-term and long-term."

News.title: Did the eclipse damage your eyes?
News.content:
An eye surgeon says that fewer people have been seeking treatment for eye damage than after the UK's last total solar eclipse in 1999.

Millions across the UK on Wednesday witnessed the most significant solar eclipse in 27 years - which saw more than 90% of the Sun covered by the Moon.

Speaking to the BBC, Mr Alexander Ionides from Moorfield Eye Hospital said hospitals were "inundated" with worried patients in 1999, but said it seemed warnings about looking directly at the sun with the naked eye were "getting through".

He added that symptoms of eye damage can include a spot in the centre of your vision, which may appear grey or yellow. Symptoms can develop within hours, but sometimes take days to develop.

Federal agents launched a sweeping undercover surveillance operation earlier this year targeting progressive organizations, labor unions and other groups protesting the immigration crackdown then raging through Minneapolis, according to court documents filed Thursday.

The program, dubbed Operation Puppet Master, was aimed at what officials called a network of conspirators helping “violent opportunists and agitators.” The documents were filed in a case involving 15 people charged by federal prosecutors in June with impeding the crackdown, accusing them of conspiring against the federal government through a range of actions, from throwing ice chunks to setting up blockades.

The government documents were released Thursday in connection with a motion from a defense lawyer in the case, Kevin Riach, who requested that officials disclose more material collected during the investigations.

The reality, according to government documents revealed in court motions, was Department of Homeland Security officers infiltrating meetings in churches, schools and parks that were often simply discussions of constitutionally protected protests.

A statement from the department said Homeland Security Investigations doesn’t comment on the existence or status of on-going investigations or investigative methods. The statement referred questions to the U.S. attorney’s office in Minnesota, which didn’t immediately respond to an after-hours email from The Associated Press.

Puppet Master, and a later operation called Project Whipple Shield, were a “broad and irrational investigation” driven by politics and not criminal conduct, Riach said in a motion filed Thursday.

Take, for example, a Jan. 31 meeting in a Minneapolis library, when a Homeland Security report says an undercover officer identified as “UCA 9833” listened as supporters of a progressive climate group, the Sunrise Movement, discussed sit-ins, de-escalation tactics and “having a police liaison and safety marshal present during events.”

“During the Action meeting, it was made clear that the Sunrise Movement organization focused on ‘peaceful’ protests,” the agent reported.

Dozens of pages of documents describe agents secretly infiltrating meetings, monitoring activist chat groups and using license plate numbers to compile names of people who attended gatherings.

A slide created by Homeland Security’s investigative branch titled “The Conspiracy” shows 18 organizations, from a small Minneapolis bicycle repair collective to the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of labor groups in the U.S.

The government also obtained years of certain financial records for groups ranging from the Sunrise Movement to major unions, including the Service Employees International Union and the Communications Workers of America.

“You are requested not to disclose the existence of this summons for an indefinite period of time,” warned a DHS request to FedWire, a money transfer system operated by the U.S. Federal Reserve.

“It's very disturbing,” said Ahilan Arulanantham, a professor at the University of California, Los Angeles School of Law. Over time, it could deter people from expressing their beliefs, he said.

Many people don’t want to live in a world where expressing their beliefs gives federal agencies the right to investigate them, he said.

“It’s that fear of that creeping police state,” he said.

Groups that the government investigated were furious at the news.

“Our union has become the latest target of a corrupt administration that weaponizes the legal process against law-abiding Americans exercising our Constitutional rights,” CWA President Claude Cummings Jr. said in a statement. “We will not be intimidated, and we will not be silenced.”

The AP News Guild, the union that represents many Associated Press employees, is part of the CWA.

On Thursday, a coalition of Minneapolis-area civil society groups defended the protests and criticized the investigations.

The government is “lashing out desperately in hopes of intimidating people and organizations that have shown the power of communities acting together," said a statement distributed by Unidos MN, a local human rights group.

DHS deployed about 3,000 federal officers to the Minneapolis-St. Paul area for roughly three months starting late last year in what the department called its “ largest immigration enforcement operation ever.” It led to thousands of arrests, angry mass protests and the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens.

Minnesota U.S. Attorney Daniel N. Rosen said the 15 were part of two groups that he characterized as “antifa,” an umbrella term for a diffuse movement of militant left-wing activists.

Defense attorney Riach said at the time that his client, Isaac Sant, had no affiliation with antifa, which he called “a boogeyman invented by the far-right.”

___

Kelleher reported from Honolulu.

Iga Swiatek claimed her first title of the season with a dominant 6-2 6-3 win over Elena Rybakina in the final of the National Bank Open in Toronto.

The Polish seventh seed gained an early advantage in the first set when the world number two gave up a break point on back-to-back double faults.

That was all the room Swiatek needed as she continued her stellar form from earlier in the tournament to race away with the opening set.

Unforced errors continued to cost Rybakina into the second set, as two missed backhands gifted Swiatek another break.

Rybakina was able to stave off one championship point, but Swiatek converted on her second opportunity to clinch her first title since last September.

Speaking at the post-match awards ceremony, Swiatek dedicated her victory to “everyone who is dealing with unfair judgement and hate”.

She said: “Just keep pushing, keep growing, keep focusing on yourself because you know what’s best for you.

“Always remember what’s ahead and what might be possible.”

In the men’s draw, American Ben Shelton retained his crown by eclipsing compatriot Brandon Nakashima 6-3 7-6 (4) in Montreal.

Shelton did not drop a set throughout the tournament and is just the fourth man this century to go back-to-back at the event, joining Andy Murray, Novak Djokovic and Rafael Nadal.

He told atptour.com: “For me to play the way that I played this week to go through this draw speaks to the work I have been putting in.

“It also speaks to my mental toughness, my ability to focus through everything that was going on this week.”

Cook Islands Prime Minister Mark Brown is expected to lead the South Pacific nation’s government for a second term after his party won more seats than any other group in this week’s election.

Voting continued for one of 24 Parliamentary seats in the country of 17,000 people, which is made up of 15 islands. Bad weather prevented electoral officers from reaching the island of Nassau earlier in the week and results there were expected late Friday New Zealand time.

However, Brown’s Cook Islands Party, a nationalist group that has governed since 2010, was already celebrating victory after winning 12 seats which promised a fifth term in power. A 13-seat majority is required to form a government, but Brown’s party has joined with independent lawmakers to pass laws before.

“Today my heart is full of gratitude,” Brown wrote on Facebook. “Thank you to everyone who came out and voted, for taking part and making your voice heard. This is what makes our country strong.”

In the seat yet to be decided, the incumbent, a member of Brown’s party, is competing with an independent candidate.

Voters worried about cost of living

Ahead of the ballot held Wednesday in the islands, local news outlets reported that inflation and the cost of living were voters’ chief preoccupations. The war in Iran has prompted economic anxiety throughout the South Pacific, where tiny and remote nations are heavily dependent on imported products, including diesel for power generation.

Brown’s opponents hoped dissatisfaction about the price of goods, water, electricity and transport would prompt a closer election. However, preliminary results released by a government agency showed the Cook Islands United Party, which split from Brown’s group in 2018, had won just four seats, up from three in 2022.

The socially liberal Democratic Party, which held five seats and led the opposition before, fell out of Parliament altogether. In an upset, party leader Tina Pupuke-Browne lost her seat by three votes, ending eight years in office.

Result signals minimal fallout from dispute with New Zealand

It will be a second term as prime minister for Brown, 63, who entered Parliament in 2010 after a career as a public servant and property developer. He won his seat of Takuvaine with a large majority in this week’s vote.

The result indicated Brown had survived unscathed a saga that began in 2025, when he quarreled with New Zealand’s government over a suite of deals he signed with Beijing, without first consulting Wellington, Cook Islands’ biggest funder.

Cook Islands is a self-governing country with a 60-year free association relationship to New Zealand, which means it’s defended by New Zealand’s military, and its citizens hold New Zealand passports. The close ties require Cook Islands leaders to speak with Wellington before making pacts with other countries that might affect New Zealand.

When Brown signed a series of cooperation deals with Beijing in February 2025, he defended his decision not to consult Wellington about them. New Zealand disagreed and an escalating standoff led Wellington to freeze millions of dollars in funding to Cook Islands last June, citing security concerns about the range and contents of the Beijing deals.

Frosty relations eased in April when the two countries signed a defense pact clarifying their ties and pledging that New Zealand would be Cook Islands’ “partner of choice regarding defense and security matters.” Wellington feared the prospect of China occupying that role.

In recent years, Beijing has vied with Western powers for influence and closer ties with Pacific Island leaders whose tiny and often aid-reliant countries lie in a vast, lucrative and strategically important ocean.

Ousted opposition leader protested China deals

When relations broke down last year, some Cook Islanders, including then opposition leader Pupuke-Brown, protested the prime minister’s actions. Pupuke-Brown accused Brown of jeopardizing ties with New Zealand, where thousands of Cook Islanders live, work and study.

However, the resumption of aid from Wellington this year appeared to have quashed the outcry.

Brown is also a proponent of Cook Islands developing a deep sea mining industry in its large and possibly rich exclusive economic zone. The matter has divided leaders throughout the Pacific, with detractors warning the practice could harm fragile ocean ecosystems.

More than 60% of adults have not bought sunscreen so far this year despite the run of heatwaves, a survey suggests.

Just 56% of adults in England, Scotland and Wales bought sunscreen in the last two years, the poll by Worldpanel by Numerator for Nivea Sun found.

The survey of 30,000 people across England, Scotland and Wales showed 8.5% more people bought sunscreen this year compared to the previous year, the equivalent of 1.6 million people and the highest in five years.

Nearly 30% bought SPF50, more than double the proportion buying any other SPF level.

However, despite the increase in sales, Cancer Research UK warned that too few adults are buying and using sunscreen.

It warned that using sunscreen from previous years can reduce its effectiveness.

It comes as the charity revealed that the annual number of new melanoma skin cancer cases in the UK passed 20,000 for the first time in 2022, and is projected to reach over 26,000 a year by 2040.

Cancer information nurse at Cancer Research UK, Caroline Geraghty, said: “With temperatures skyrocketing across the UK this summer, it’s easy to focus on the heat and forget about UV.

“But it’s UV radiation, not temperature, that causes sun damage.

“Sunscreen isn’t a suit of armour. Seeking shade and covering up with clothing are some of the most effective and affordable ways to protect yourself from the sun’s harmful rays.

“Checking the UV index on your weather app can help you plan ahead and know when it’s time to take extra precautions.”

Melanoma skin cancer is the fifth most common cancer in the UK, with almost nine in 10 melanoma skin cancer cases caused by excess ultraviolet (UV) exposure.

UV radiation from the sun, rather than heat, causes sunburn and skin cancer and the sun can be strong enough to burn from mid-March to mid-October in the UK, whether there is a heatwave or not, the charity said.

Consumers can look for the open-lid symbol featuring the letter M and a number, which shows how many months the sunscreen will last once open.

Cancer Research UK also advises that people seek shade in the heat, especially between 11am and 3pm in the UK, cover up with with clothes, a wide-brimmed hat and UV protection sunglasses, and apply sunscreen with at least SPF 30 and four or five stars.

Sunscreen should be reapplied regularly and generously, especially after swimming, sweating, or towelling.

News.title: ‘More pain’ to come after economic slowdown
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. The economy grew at a slower pace in the second quarter of the year, official figures show, under pressure from the Iran war.

The UK’s gross domestic product (GDP) expanded by 0.4pc between April and June, down from 0.6pc in the first three months of the year, according to the Office for National Statistics.

The figures underline the challenge that the conflict poses for Andy Burnham, who has pledged to deliver “growth in every postcode”.

The Prime Minister has already been warned that the economy will slow further next year if Donald Trump continues his war in the Middle East.

News.title: H5N1 sparks a very Australian epidemic
News.content:
H5N1 bird flu has reached Australia’s shores and is threatening to infect some of the country’s most unique wildlife.

Australasia is the last continent to be hit by the highly infectious avian influenza H5N1, a new strain of which has been circulating worldwide since 2020.

Since recording its first case in June, more than 200 wild seabirds in Australia have been infected, with fears that the highly infectious flu could quickly ‘jump’ to other species.

While H5N1 has infected animals from foxes to sea lions in other parts of the world in recent years, the epidemic now threatens some of Australia’s most iconic wildlife – many of which are found nowhere else on earth.

An Australian government assessment of more than 2,000 native species warned that nearly one in five faces a high risk from the deadly H5N1 bird flu, with hundreds of unique birds and mammals vulnerable to severe population reductions or even extinction.

Those animals include iconic species like the Tasmanian devils, quolls, and dingoes.

Other aquatic mammals, including the platypus, which is only found in Australia, are at risk of infection through contact with bird droppings in shared wetlands and coastal environments.

News.title: Selfie-seekers bring Man Utd vs Leeds match to premature end
News.content:
Aren’t friendlies supposed to be non-events? Manchester United against Leeds United in Dublin always had the capacity to be lively, but try explaining the half hour that Bruno Fernandes experienced in one breath. It would be impossible.

There was only one player the vast majority of the crowd wanted to see in the grandiosely named Boyle Sports Cup and, in chronological order from his 60th minute introduction, he received a standing ovation, hit the bar, had a goal disallowed, missed a penalty in a shoot-out and lifted a trophy.

Most remarkably – and, certainly, worryingly – of all, he was central to the game being ended early as five young boys, one after the other, breached security and ran to him in the middle of pitch, all of them successfully posing for photos with the Portuguese.

You could say it was harmless fun but it should not have happened and the flummoxed faces that were pulled on the Manchester United bench, as an army in high-visibility jackets stood and watched it all unfold, suggested they took a dim view.

News.title: Brian Madjo, 17, electrifies Villa despite Super Cup defeat by PSG
News.content:
His team played with all the resilience and bravery that has become a trademark, epitomised by the powerful Madjo and another teenager in midfielder George Hemmings.

Emery said: “Brian has scored goals for us in pre-season and has shown his capacity to work in our idea. I am so happy because the young players were involved in our work and not playing last season.

“Of course there is still work to do but they showed they can play with us. They have responded fantastically and will then feel the confidence. With a loss you can never be happy but overall I am proud of all the players and everything we’ve done. Some changes will be needed but we’re confident.”

This was a fine Villa performance to silence the doom merchants who have been fearing a troubled season. After the painful sales of Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne, Villa are clearly a team in transition. They are operating under restrictions to comply with Uefa’s financial rules and there is still the possibility of another important player leaving before the transfer deadline day.

England centre-back Ezri Konsa remains a priority target for Premier League champions Arsenal, and was absent here. Konsa, Emiliano Martínez and Ollie Watkins were all granted extended leave after their participation in the World Cup, which has done little to ease the fears of supporters over more departures. The trio will return to training this weekend.

While some outsiders are predicting a difficult season for Villa, do not bother telling Emery. He has turned putting noses out of joint into an art form since sweeping into Villa Park and with him around anything feels possible.

The Basque remains optimistic about the future and those hopes will only have been underlined by the performance of Madjo. He bullied PSG centre-back Willian Pacho for much of the evening and even managed to steal the limelight from PSG’s magician Khvicha Kvaratskhelia.

When it comes to sending a child or grandchild off to university, it can be tempting to fill their room with every conceivable gadget.

So to help, we asked the Telegraph Recommended Community for their best gift recommendations and their suggestions ranged from desk lamps to cookery books and supermarket gift cards.

Here are the essentials worth buying.

Kitchen basics

From cupboard essentials to electrical appliances and cookbooks, most readers say they’d gift kitchen equipment.

Thinking back to his university days, reader TJ, 43, from London, says “the main essentials are around kitchen items and good long lasting food”.

“It’s nice to have some bits to cook for others as well and to make friends quickly,” he adds.

Susan, 54, from the West Midlands, agrees, recommending “basic cooking equipment” as a key staple and “distinctive cutlery, plates and cups that are easily identified”, which are particularly useful for shared accommodation.

“A box of store cupboard ingredients such as olive oil, soy, stock cubes and spices to use when cooking,” is also well-received, she says.

News.title: Everton dispatch Newcastle to give Matthias Jaissle a reality check
News.content:
Newcastle United manager ​Matthias Jaissle is ‌refusing to dwell on the departure of key players that has left his club in turmoil going into the new season, as they step up their preparations against Everton at Murrayfield this evening.

Jaissle was recruited from Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli after Eddie Howe left last month, with the German coach joining a club who have lost Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and captain Bruno Guimaraes in quick succession.

“It’s a challenge, a big challenge, always when there’s a transitional period. ‌But it’s ‌not time to ⁠complain, it doesn’t make sense to see the negative things,” Jaissle said.

“We want to see the chance in that situation and that’s our approach from day one. We are here to do our ⁠best job. We want to support the players, the current squad.

“There will be adjustments to see in the coming days, weeks. But for now it’s only focused on the daily work, the work we can influence. That’s all that ​matters now.”

The 38-year-old coach arrived in Newcastle ‌having won two Austrian Bundesliga titles with Red Bull Salzburg before leading Al-Ahli to back-to-back AFC Champions League crowns.

He remained tight-lipped about new signings.

“Obviously, in that transition phase, the players who left the club were ‌great ​players, great characters, experienced ⁠players. This is now a vacuum,” he said.

“Either we adjust something in the squad, by signing these players, these profiles, or other players ⁠need to step up and fill ​these positions, these leadership roles. I’m quite optimistic, we can work in both scenarios.”

Jaissle said he had a ​clear vision of how he wants his team to play.

“The phrase how Newcastle ‌should play like is front-footed, intense, ​aggressive and of course also successful. ​In the end, it’s all about what ⁠I can ⁠say and it’s also why I’m sitting here,” he said.

“The approach we have as a coaching team and the identity of Newcastle is famed for, it’s so linked so close together - which is a perfect fit in my eyes and ​that’s going to be exciting.”

Team news on the way shortly.

News.title: Ebola outbreak ‘doubling every 20 days’, warns UN chief
News.content:
Congo’s runaway Ebola outbreak is doubling in size every 20 days, according to the United Nations humanitarian chief, putting it on track to soon be the largest ever seen.

Three months after the outbreak was officially declared, the case load is expanding exponentially and many believe the true toll is far higher than recorded.

If cases continue to double at the same rate, the flare-up in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) will surpass the record West African outbreak sometime around the end of September.

Modelling by one health analytics firm already predicts there is a more than 90 per cent chance that the DRC will become the largest on record.

The two-year West African outbreak grew to more than 28,600 cases and 11,325 deaths across Sierra Leone, Liberia and Guinea from late 2013 to 2016.

This year’s outbreak centred on the DRC province of Ituri has already seen 4,449 cases and 2,061 deaths in only a few months.

News.title: Madagascar forced to divide and share mpox vaccine as epidemic takes off
News.content:
Authorities in Madagascar are being forced to split single vaccines into fifths to try to protect as many people as possible during an ongoing mpox outbreak.

The method, known as “fractional dosing”, is authorised by the World Health Organization (WHO) in emergencies when there are critical vaccine shortages, but is not routinely recommended and carries a level of risk.

Madagascar, the African island with a population of roughly 33 million people, is currently battling its largest-ever outbreak of the virus formerly known as monkeypox, with at least 4,000 cases recorded so far.

Another one million people are thought to be at risk of contracting clade 1b mpox, a fast-spreading strain of the virus that emerged from the Democratic Republic of the Congo in late 2023.

High risk groups include sex workers, young children, and people living with HIV/Aids. Medical workers are also at risk.

“Public health authorities in Madagascar have been given too few doses to protect the at-risk population; they were initially given 30,000 doses in May, and a subsequent 30,000 have just arrived at the end of July,” said Akhil Bansal, a doctor of internal medicine working on the mpox response in Madagascar and a policy fellow at the Centre for Global Development.

“However, we need to vaccinate more than one million people, so we have been “fractionally dosing”, or splitting vaccines, into fifths, to stretch the supply as far as we can.

“This is a somewhat established approach for vaccines, but even then, the number of doses we have is insufficient,” said Dr Bansal.

Sports.title: Opening day clash postponed as pitch left ‘unsuitable for playing football’ following heatwave
Sports.content:
CELTA VIGO’s opening-day LaLiga clash with Osasuna has been postponed due to FUNGUS ravaging the pitch.

The Galician side were scheduled to host the match at Balaidos Stadium this Sunday.



Celta ground staff had been working their fingers to the bone trying to rectify the outbreak that had ruined the playing surface.

And although they had made good progress, hot and dry weather conditions caused the pitch to deteriorate again.



Celta, Osasuna and the Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) all agreed to postpone the match following a LaLiga inspection.

It has now been rescheduled as a Thursday night game on August 27.

Celta said: “LaLiga agreed this morning, in coordination with the clubs and the RFEF, to postpone or find that it had to face Celta and CA Osasuna this Sunday in Abanca Balaídos due to an illness that affected the stadium’s grass, which at this time is not suitable for soccer practice.

“Last week, a technical visit was carried out by LaLiga to validate the work carried out to eradicate the disease that affected the grass and certify that the field met the quality and safety parameters set for sports practice.

“The climatic conditions of the last two days produced an adverse effect on the evolution that was close to the game and led to the decision to suspend or terminate.

“The tickets issued for this match against Osasuna remain fully valid for the new schedule, so it will not be necessary to carry out any additional processing.

Sports.title: West Ham bans much mocked half-and-half scarves from stadium for new season as fans are warned they will be confiscated
Sports.content:
WEST Ham bosses have banned much mocked half-and-half scarves for good.

The divisive neckwear — bearing the names of both home and away teams — are sold outside grounds across the country and are popular with tourists.

But die-hard fans despise them, and they are sometimes outlawed for one-off games against rivals as displaying away colours at the home end poses safety risks.



The Hammers, newly relegated to the Championship, have posted warning signs at their City of ­London Stadium.



They state: “West Ham United would like to remind supporters that half-and-half scarves and any items displaying the colours or crests of both clubs are permanently banned inside London Stadium.

“This policy applies at all fixtures.

“Supporters arriving with half-and-half scarves purchased from unofficial sellers will be required to hand them over to security staff at the security checkpoints and these scarves will not be returned.



“Fans wishing to purchase a scarf for the game are encouraged to visit the official West Ham United Stadium Store where a full range of official merchandise is available ahead of kick-off.”

The rule was brought in for the Hammers’ 3-1 League Cup win over Portsmouth last weekend.

The move divided fans. West Ham nut John Hayes told The Sun: “The scarves are for the tourists who take away from the match atmosphere created by die-hard fans, who are often priced out of attending by the rubberneckers.

“Having a rival club’s crest on view in the home end sparks all sorts of problems.



“These scarves deserve going into the bin — with hydration breaks.”

But Arsenal fan Frank DuPont hit back: “Football is meant to be for everyone.

Tourists spend the most in the club shops, and picking up a half-and-half scarf from a street vendor is not going to damage the match experience for fussy season ticket holders.”

Previous West Ham games where the scarves have been banned include last season’s home match against Tottenham Hotspur.

During these talks, it is reported that a move for Osimhen to Arsenal was proposed. The 27-year-old Nigeria international has been one of Europe's most prolific goalscorers in recent years and has consistently been linked with a move to the Premier League, including to Tottenham this summer.

He only joined Galatasaray permanently from Napoli last summer for €75m (£64m) following a successful loan spell. Osimhen has 59 goals and 16 assists in 74 appearances for the club and is under contract until June 2029.

Martinelli appears poised to leave Arsenal after seven years, 62 goals and 278 appearances at the club. He has entered the final year of his contract and has been made available for a transfer alongside Gabriel Jesus, who is of interest to Napoli.

‌



View 2 Images Arsenal are ready to sell Gabriel Martinelli (Image: PA Wire)

Leandro Trossard (Besiktas), Jakub Kiwior (Porto), Karl Hein (Werder Bremen) and Christian Norgaard (Everton) are the only players have left the defending Premier League champions for transfer fees this summer. And Arteta knows the importance of sales to help free up funds and space in the squad for new additions.

“There is more that we want to do, because every time we have an opportunity to improve the squad and bring more quality and depth, we need to do that,” Arteta said after the 1-1 draw with Como on Wednesday. “We’re actively trying to do so – the thing is, in the market, it doesn’t just depend on you, and we’re very clear on that.

‌



“The will and the desire of the club is unquestionable, but we cannot promise that we’re going to do it because it doesn’t only depend on us.”

He added: “For the margins to improve, there are very few players in the market that are available to do that and bring more quality to the club,. But again, we’re actively looking to improve that and we’re going to try.”
