His words, “Those activities are pushing the erosion directly toward the area where they are dredging. If those activities weren’t taking place, the erosion would have already passed that area by now.”



A Crisis, Decade in the Making

Bayelsa State, with its delicate deltaic geography, has endured decades of coastal erosion, flooding, and land loss. Rising sea levels, tidal surges, and the absence of critical protective infrastructure have left communities like Obogoro and others increasingly vulnerable. Many settlements have lost not just homes, but entire livelihoods. Farmlands have disappeared, access to clean water has been compromised, and families have been forced to scatter inland, fracturing the social fabric that once held communities together.

“The situation is very bad,” Nnamdi lamented..

In 2023, the Bayelsa State government intervened, awarding a contract to a local firm to address the crisis. But residents said the situation has only worsened as work stalled.

Frank Ovie paints a stark picture of what needs to happen to savage the situation. He said: “What should be done is to divert the river current either by excavating an alternate channel or building a wall at the point where the current is incident on the community. Either way, it will reduce the force of the current.” He urged stakeholders in the community not relent in crying out to the relevant authorities. “They should ensure that the issue continues to dominate public discourse,” he added.

Govt Assures

The government, on its part, had assured that the erosion control project in the community has not been abandoned. Governor Douye Diri, had years back in a statement by his Chief Press Secretary, Daniel Alabrah, explained that the government was committed to finding a lasting solution to the erosion menace.

While empathising with the community over the negative effects of the coastal erosion, including the loss of lives, land, property and sources of livelihood, Diri urged the community to keep faith with the government to rescue the situation.

The government, it was further learned, had received a detailed report from the state Ministry of Environment on the Obogoro erosion project and had given directives on how to address the menace permanently.

Coastal Erosion, a Major Problem

Speaking on the erosion menace confronting the state, Alagoa Morris, Chief Operating Officer, Environmental Conservation, Agriculture and Rural Development (ECARD) and Technical Adviser to the Governor on Environment 1, said besides oil industry induced pollution, coastal and river bank erosion is the the most pervasive environmental and ecological menace faced by communities in the state. Morris listed the communities to include Obogoro, Odi, Northern Kaiama, Anibeze, Sampou, Abobiri, Peremabiri, Olugbobiri, Okpotuwari, Lasukgbene, Odioama, Sangana, Kongho, Twon Brass, Okpoama, Koluama, Foropa, Ekeni, Ezetu, Bilabiri and Amatu among others. Morris, however, described Obogoro as the fastest battered erosion troubled site he had witnessed, making available pictures of the school premises before it was swallowed by the rampaging Ekole River.

“We met this school building during our first visit in 2018 or so… next visit in 2019 it became a victim and the community lost it completely to the erosion. Obogoro is the fastest erosion site I have witnessed. See the school building before it was eventually washed away,” ECARD Chief Operating Officer said pointing at the pictures, he once took.

A Model Worth Replicating

For environmental advocates, the solution lies in aggressive intervention. They point to the Emadike shoreline and land reclamation project in Ogbia Local Government Area carried out by the Federal Government through the Ecological office as a success story worth replicating.

“What we have seen at Emadike community is a clear testament that embarking on shoreline protection is quite beneficial to our communities suffering from flooding and coastal erosion,” Morris said.

The Emadike project, he noted, has significantly reduced tidal surges and land degradation, offering long-term environmental and economic benefits.

“We want to call on the Federal Government and the Ecological Fund Office to replicate the same project in our coastal communities where the locals are constantly threatened by erosion,” Morris noted.



A Call to Action

Collins Diepreye, a concerned Bayelsan, warned that without urgent government action, more communities along the Ekoli River face total submersion.

“Whole communities risk being displaced, leading to heightened socio-economic hardship,” he said.

For families like Ayi’s, Madam Eunice’s and others, this is not a mere threat. It is the daily reality of watching your world dissolve into the water.

The government has spoken of a redesigned project and plans for permanent solutions. But for residents watching the river inch closer with each passing day, words are not enough.

As one resident put it simply: “We are still calling on the government to look into our situation.”

For the people of Obogoro, the river that once sustained them now threatens to consume everything they have built. And as the waters continue their advance, they wait not just for intervention, but for hope.

World.title: STREET HAWKING: Why we defy FCTA to sell on Abuja streets
World.content:
*Traders speak out amid crackdown

*Say hunger and poverty leave them with no choice

By John Alechenu

ABUJA- It is 1:45pm on Herbert Macaulay Way, one of the busiest roads in the Federal Capital Territory of Nigeria. Top ranging vehicles ply here as a routine because of the presence of the National Oil company on this road. On this particular day a black colour Sports Utility Vehicle idles outside the popular NNPC Towers. Men in suits pace around them, shouting into phones.

Across the road, cars crawl into a Total filling station. Horns blare ceaselessly in a bid to draw attention. But that causes more distraction of its own. However, beside the station, nylon sheets are spread on the ground. Sachet drinks, groundnuts, cucumber, roasted yam, boiled cassava and roasted corn are arranged in rows. Umbrellas and old campaign posters with faded faces provide shade for traders and customers. This is like a full market in session but it is not. It is actually the mini-market that hawkers have unwittingly created to make a living amid the soaring sun.

“This sun can fry an egg,” Paul, a regular at the roadside eatery, says as he fans himself with a file. He shops here as a means of avoiding the high stakes supermarkets that dot the length and breadth of the city.

Less than a metre away, Mama Ada, 52, arranges boiled corn and coconut in a plastic basin. Her customers are bankers, drivers and dispatch riders from offices in the old NITEL building. She is calling out prices when two white Abuja Environmental Protection Board, AEPB, vans screech to a stop nearby.

Fifteen-year-old Hauwa is coming from the other direction with a plastic bowl on her head. Inside the container are various goods for her customers – Water, Gala, chewing gum and sweets inside. Men in a black car jump down and Hauwa drops everything and flees with the speed of light to avoid being taken away. She disappears between taxis in seconds, leaving her tray and her goods behind. Sachets of water and other items scatter on the road. A driver menacingly swerves to avoid brushing them.

Other traders who see the task force in time also took off. Mama Ada drags her basin behind an SUV. A young man with phone chargers tucks his wares into a backpack and disappears into the crowd. In less than two minutes, the stretch is almost empty. This has become the daily routine of hawkers, who had since been barred by the FCTA and the Abuja Environmental Protection Board, AEPB. But they have refused to leave the road irrespective of measures churned out by the authorities.

They flog the busy areas such as Wuse, Garki, Area 1, Berger, Area 3, Jabi. Hawkers defy government bans to sell in traffic, at bus stops and around government buildings.

‘How Do We Feed?’

For Hauwa, life as a teenager has been difficult and requires struggling to survive. She shares a single room with her two siblings and three cousins in a slum outside Mpape. The room has no running water. They fetch from a borehole 10 minutes away. At night, they sleep on mats on the floor. Her parents are farmers in Niger State. Two years ago, bandits attacked their village. They took food, money and two goats. Months later, drought destroyed the rest of the harvest. “School finish for JSS2,” Hauwa says quietly. “No money again.”

She followed her aunt to Abuja. The aunt sells vegetables in Garki Market and sleeps in a shop. “People say money dey for Abuja. Nobody go tell you say e hard for poor person to get am,” she says, switching between broken English and Hausa as she sets up another tray 30 minutes after the raid. She borrowed the tray from another hawker.

She admits that on a good day she makes between N3,500 and N6,000. Every Friday she sends N10,000 to N15,000 home through a bus driver to her aged parents.

“My capital na N8,000,” she says, wiping sweat with the back of her hand. If they break my tray today, na two weeks food gone.”

She knows the risks. Last month, a friend was hit by a motorcycle while running from AEPB in Wuse. The girl spent four days in hospital. No one paid the bill. The friend now hawks with a limp.

Yet Hauwa is back on the same spot. “If I no come, how we go chop?” she asks.

Her story is not different from that of Felicia who hails from Nasarawa State. “I am a secondary school student. I am selling this groundnut to help my family.” According to her, she has been “lucky enough” to evade the several raids by AEPB enforcement officers because, “I only sell cooked groundnuts and I don’t go near areas where they patrol.”

‘Task Force Collect My Okada’

At Berger roundabout, Musa, 28, moves between cars selling phone chargers, screen guards, earphones and car perfumes. He is fast. He knows which window will open and which driver will wave him off.

Before the okada ban in 2023, Musa was a commercial motorcyclist in Mabushi. On a good day, he makes about N10,000. Then the FCTA banned commercial motorcycles from the city centre and he quickly moved away into hawking, which appears as a fast-moving business in the FCT.

“Colleagues say Area 1 dey move. I follow them,” he says. Now he averages N3,000 to N4,000 daily. On days when task force raids are serious, he returns home with less than N1,000.

“Now if I see N4,000 I thank God. Government say no okada. Wetin I go do? I get wife and three children for Nyanya,” he says. He finished primary school in Kankiya, Katsina State. He also studied Arabic under his late father, an imam.

“I go school. Now I dey run from task force like thief. But hunger no dey hear grammar,” he says. He considered returning to farming during dry season. But his village is close to a forest where bandits operate. Two of his cousins were kidnapped last year. Ransom was paid before they were reluctantly freed and that memory still haunts him even after relocating from his state to Abuja. He rents a room in Nyanya for N200,000 a year. He wakes at 4:30am to catch the first bus. He returns after 9pm.

“They seized my phone once, and I paid N7,000 to collect it. That week, my children no chop well.” Musa says he has applied to several driving jobs. “They ask for experience, license, and money for ‘processing’. I no get.”

Mama Blessing, 45, is a familiar face at a traffic light in Wuse II. She sells roasted yam, plantain, peppered beef, dried fish and sachet drinks. She has a small charcoal stove and a cooler strapped to a trolley. This year, AEPB has seized her wares severally but she is determined to keep the business running no matter how hard they push her.

“Sometimes they say pay N10,000 before you collect am. If you no get, them go scatter everything. You go lucky if them no carry you go office,” she says.

She lives in Gwagwalada and manages to pay the annual rent of N350,000. She leaves home at 5am and returns after 10pm. Transport alone costs N1,500 daily.

“Na here better market dey,” she says when asked why she travels from the outskirts to come and sell in the city. “For Gwagwalada, people no dey buy like this.”

Her husband died in 2021 after a brief illness. They have three children, who are all in secondary school. The eldest wants to study nursing.

“I dey manage. Sometimes I borrow money to buy yam and plantain. If they seize am, na wahala,” she says.

She tried selling in Gwagwalada market. “Sales no dey. People dey wait till month end. Here, even civil servant go buy N500 yam when traffic hold am.”

On days AEPB task force does not come, she makes N8,000 to N12,000. After food, transport and savings for rent, she has little left.

BUYERS KEEP THEM ALIVE

In Abuja’s daily gridlock, hawkers are part of the system. In 40-minute traffic jams, N50 sachet water, N100 Gala, N200 plantain chips and N500 roasted corn sell fast.“It’s easier,” says Mr. Emmanuel, a civil servant from Lugbe. “And you pity them too. These children suppose dey school. But wetin you go do? If you buy, you help somebody.”

A banker who works on Herbert Macaulay Way says she buys from Mama Ada twice a week. “Corn and coconut is what I buy for my lunch. It’s cheaper than the canteen and it’s fresh.” For many drivers, buying is also about time. “If I enter market, I go waste one hour. Here, they bring it to me,” says Danjuma, a taxi driver.

The trade thrives on convenience and compassion. But it also thrives on desperation.

FCTA: ‘ABUJA IS NOT A MARKET’

Over the years, the Federal Capital Territory Administration has tried to enforce the ban on street hawking. Officials say there is no place for it in a modern capital. They argue that hawking blocks drains, causes traffic, litters the streets and attracts crime. To streamline its work, the Board maintains outposts in key areas across the city centre backed by mobile teams that conduct periodic raids.

A former Director of AEPB, Dr. Baba Lawal, who has since retired was quoted as saying, “Abuja was not designed for this. We have markets in every district. We have skills centres. We are not fighting the poor. But we cannot allow the city to turn to a motor park.”

“Every week we seize goods and we talk to them. We even counsel them. Two hours later they are back. Until people stop buying in traffic, this will continue.”

The AEPB impounds hundreds of trays, coolers and goods monthly. Offenders pay fines ranging from N5,000 to N20,000 before retrieving seized items. Repeat offenders are taken to court. Successive administrations have built markets in Kubwa, Gwagwalada, Kado, Wuse and Garki. The FCTA also runs skills acquisition centres in some parts of the city where physically-challenged persons taken off the streets are given life skills. Many of the hawkers argue that the markets are either “too far or the rent is high.” A lock-up shop in Garki can go for N150,000 to N300,000 annually, plus agreement fees.

THE OTHER SIDE

For all the talk about city planning, the human cost is clear. At an FCT shelter in Bwari, a welfare officer who asked not to be named says most of the children picked up by AEPB are not from Abuja.

“They come because of insecurity, hunger or to meet relatives. Parents think Abuja has money. Abuja is expensive,” she says.

The shelter houses boys and girls between ages 10 and 17 rescued from the streets. Some are reunited with families. Others stay for months.

“It’s not clean,” she says. “Girls get harassed. Boys get into fights. Some get knocked down by vehicles.”

Not too long ago, a thirteen-year-old boy was hit by a car at Area 3 while trying to run away from the task force. He spent two weeks in hospital with a broken leg. A church group paid the bill.

The officer says the cycle continues because there is no alternative. “We counsel them. We tell them to go to school. But when they go home, there is no food for them and they return to the street to struggle for survival,” the official maintains.

‘TELL US WHERE TO GO AND WHAT TO EAT’

Although government officials keep mentioning that there are alternatives areas such as Kubwa, Gwagwalada and Area 10 skills centres, Wuse, Garki and Kado markets with lock-up shops, which street traders can patronize for their business, the traders complain that they have no idea on how to access those places and what it costs to do so.

“Government say make we no hawk. Government never tell us wetin we go chop,” Mama Blessing, a roadside corn seller, says, turning her items of trade on fire as she spoke.

But Musa is tired of the talk and he does not believe the government is serious about addressing their needs. “Give us loan. Give us shop. Then talk. You no fit tell person wey dey hungry to wait,” the hustler says

Many others like Musa have tried to survive the hassles on Abuja roads but for how long can they continue without any serious and practical intervention by the relevant authorities? they ask.

For instance, Hauwa’s aunt registered for an empowerment programme being promoted by a local politician last year. She was told to pay N5,000 for forms but nothing came out of it at the end of the day. She is still lamenting how she lost her money to something she now believes was scam dressed like empowerment.

Similarly, Mama Ada, who applied for a space in Garki Market as far back as 2023, said she was put off when the officials demanded for a compulsory N150,000 payment for the “processing” of her application and she lost out because she could not afford the cash.These antics by those who are supposed to help sort out things, have tended to kill initiatives and dampen the creativity of innocent persons.

The Executive Director of the Civil Society Legislative and Advocacy Centre, CISLAC, says banning hawking without addressing unemployment will not work.

“You cannot criminalise poverty,” he says. “Abuja’s economy is built on government and you must understand that when government jobs are few and the cost of living is high, people will certainly find a way to survive.”

He suggests designated vending zones, micro-credit and linkage to markets, adding, “You don’t chase people away; you organise them.”

Economists note that Abuja’s informal sector employs thousands. A 2024 NBS report puts informal employment in the FCT at over 60%. For many, hawking is the only entry point.

A CITY OF TWO WORLDS

By day, Abuja projects order. New flyovers in Wuye and Jahi. Glass buildings in the Central Business District. Police vans patrol major roads. Diplomats and ministers move in convoys. But, in the evening, another Abuja emerges.

At 7pm, the AEPB vans leave. Traffic eases. Hauwa is back at Area 1 with a borrowed tray. She needs N2,000 before going home. Mama Ada made N3,200 today. She will use N1,000 for transport, N1,000 for food, and save the rest.

Musa counted N3,800. He will send N2,000 home and keep the rest for food and bus fare. Mama Blessing covers her stove as the night business ends but she will undoubtedly return at 6am to continue the daily routine of hustling to survive just like others in her group, who see Abuja as the only place where people buy well on the street.

Irrespective of what the FCT and its numerous agencies do to deter them, the hustlers remain under the sun, in the rain, and under streetlights. But, while they run between cars and trucks to avoid being crushed, they are quick to escape before the task force men can pick them or their wares.

In a city designed to be a model capital, they represent a reality officials detest and try to eradicate but with serious headache.

Street vendors interviewed for this report said they are aware of the law but have no alternative than to use available public space for survival.

“If government give us place where people go pass and rent no too much, we go leave road,” Mama Ada said.

Until the economy changes, until there are jobs and affordable markets, Abuja’s last hawkers will keep running. Because for them, the choice is simple: obey the ban and go hungry, or risk arrest and feed their families.

World.title: ‘My chairman sir’: How begging, extortion have become new normal at airports
World.content:
By Dickson Omobola

Imagine arriving at an airport with your backpack on, and your luggage in tow, without anyone trailing you and saying: “My chairman sir, you no go drop something?”

Imagine pushing a trolley through the terminal without being approached by unsolicited helpers expecting a tip before they have even offered a service.

Imagine making your way through the arrival hall without anyone stopping you to ask what you have to declare.

Now, return to reality. Welcome to the Nigerian airport, where the ideal traveller’s experience remains just that.

At most of the country’s airports, touting, begging and subtle forms of extortion are among the first experiences many passengers encounter.

Despite repeated efforts by the authorities to change the situation, especially at the international terminals, these sharp practices persist, leaving even international visitors with an unfavourable first impression of Nigeria.

Impression

One such traveller was American travel vlogger, Tommy El Forastero, better known as Sabbatical Tommy, who complained bitterly about his experience of visiting Nigeria for the first time in 2021.

Tommy, who lamented that personnel at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport, MMIA, Lagos, demanded money at different points, told his more than 500,000 followers that MMIA was “extremely corrupt.”

In a video posted on his YouTube channel, the travel blogger, who tours the world and shares his experiences with his followers, said his encounters with some individuals at the facility made him conclude: “I have been around the world and I have never seen anything like this. I mean, it is extremely corrupt. Picture corruption. The Nigerian airport, the Lagos airport, is that very definition of corruption that would pop up in a dictionary. Literally everywhere.”

No change

Four years later, many travellers say little has changed.

About 16 months ago, specifically on the evening of March 26, 2025, this reporter visited the international wing of the MMA in Lagos to obtain the views of arriving passengers on their airport experience. Harassment and corruption topped the list of complaints.

One of them, a fair-complexioned young man who declined to have his name published, had just arrived from the United Kingdom. As he walked towards the taxi park after exiting the terminal, this reporter approached him for his impressions of the airport.

He said: “Honestly, my experience at the MMIA upon arrival is terrible. It is obviously poor. In fact, I just saw a man harassing a woman. The man was calling himself the woman’s boss, saying he could do anything to her and nothing would happen. There was no respect for the woman’s dignity. He acted as though there was no official channel to report the woman if she did anything wrong.”

Another traveller, who gave his name simply as Chuwkunalu, said: “Some of the immigration staff are corrupt. They treat people differently based on class. I saw them giving white people preferential treatment while we stood in a long queue. All they want from you is money. They keep asking: ‘oga, wetin you bring come for us?’”

Airline operator’s perspective

Travellers are not alone in thinking this way. At the third edition of Naija7Wonders Conference, titled: ‘Detty December: The Lessons and Impact,’ acting Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Akwa Ibom state-owned airline, Ibom Air, George Uriesi, lamented that despite recent investment in airport infrastructure at MMIA, the experience is still disappointing.

Speaking virtually at the event, he said although an airport ought to give an excellent first impression about a country, it is not the case in Nigeria.

He said: “I am in a conference now, the Aircraft Financing Symposium. Everybody is talking about their airport experience coming into the country the last couple of days. Why is it like that? We should stop this.

“We built a new terminal with all its flaws and we carried all the dirty behaviour from the old terminal into the new terminal. You have green and red, which is something to declare and nothing to declare. The nothing to declare is where they go and mount checkpoints. You can’t go through nothing to declare. You must declare something.”

Bad image

In June 2024, Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Mr Festus Keyamo, also acknowledged the problem after receiving complaints from prominent Nigerians.

In a post he made on X, formerly Twitter, Keyamo stated that he had received several complaints about the “menace of begging and extortion at our international airports by a few unscrupulous persons who give all of us a bad image.

“My phones are beeping every minute with messages about this from well-meaning Nigerians. Just to set the records straight, most of the agencies involved in this menace are not under the control of the Aviation Ministry, though they are stationed at our airports.”

He, however, said he was working with other ministers, arms of government and agencies to tackle the problem.

He said: “We are all working under the coordination of the National Security Adviser who called a meeting a few days ago on this issue.”

Two days earlier, the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria, FAAN, had announced the establishment of a dedicated task force to tackle touts and extortionists at the country’s airports.

Managing Director of FAAN, Mrs Olubunmi Kuku, said the Director of Special Duties at FAAN, Mr Henry Agbebire, now Director of Public Affairs, was appointed as the chairman of the task force.

At the time, Kuku said the authority had adopted a zero-tolerance policy towards misconduct and warned that anyone found engaging in illicit practices would face disciplinary action.

Two years later, however, the challenge remains.

Progressive measures

Speaking on FAAN in Focus recently, Kuku disclosed that investigations showed many of those involved in illicit activities at the airport are not strangers to the environment.

She fingered trolley service providers, bureau de change operators and shop as some of those whose staff are involved in the act to earn extra income.

She said FAAN had intensified engagement with the affected organisations while working with security agencies to strengthen monitoring through staff rosters and attendance registers.

While appealing to passengers not to encourage the practice by patronising unauthorised persons, she said: “We found out that these illicit activities are actually internal. We found that some of them (those involved) actually work for concessionaires within the airports. For example, people who work for trolley providers, shops and BDCs within the airport.

“Also, we found out that these illicit activities are actually being encouraged by passengers. If you don’t give them money because you want them to carry a bag for you or do something for you, they will stop being there.”

She, however, added that FAAN had engaged “all of the various security agencies again, what we have done in collaboration with some of the security agencies is to ensure that we now enforce rosters at the airport.

“One of the things we intend to do is to make sure that we get clarity on the rosters of the people who are being posted to the airport so that we have a time and attendance register for when they need to be there.

“And then for those who are found to be culpable, whether they are concessionaires, whether they are staff of other agencies, there are consequences to those businesses as well. The businesses, for example, if you have a two-time offender who is your staff, who has been caught there and has not gone to their homes or not at their place of business, we will withdraw the operating licences of those businesses as well.”

Peep into the future

It is March 5, 2028. Chuwkunalu, who last visited Nigeria in 2025, lands once again at the MMIA. The old terminal has been fully rehabilitated. MMIA wears an entirely new look.

As he exits the arrival hall, this reporter approaches him with the same question asked three years earlier.

“How was your experience?”

This time, he smiles, saying: “Everything was seamless. Nobody asked me for money. Nobody offered to help with my luggage. I simply walked through and nobody called out ‘my chairman sir.'”

While Chuwkunalu’s response exists only in the imagination, it is one many passengers, airline operators and airport authorities hope will one day become reality in the country.

That would, however, be dependent on whether FAAN and other relevant agencies will be able to sustain these reforms.

But as at the time of filing this report, arriving passengers are still being assaulted with the phrase ‘My Chairman, Sir.’

World.title: Iniside Nigeria’s correction centres: Feeding crisis rocks prisons
World.content:
***Inmates face hunger, starvation

***Prison authorities deny claims, defend feeding system

By Henry Ojelu

For three years inside the Kirikiri Correctional Centre in Lagos, survival for Mike Okoroafor came down to a daily calculation: find alternative food or go hungry. Convicted for fraud and later discharged by the Court of Appeal, Okoroafor said that while his legal ordeal eventually ended, the struggle to stay nourished in custody remains the most haunting part of his experience.

He recalled: “The first week I relied on prison food, my body began to weaken. By the second week, I made up my mind never to depend on it again. That was when I realised that if you don’t find alternatives, you can’t survive.”

Okoroafor’s account is not isolated. Interviews with former and current inmates, as well as independent findings by Vanguard, point to a deeply strained feeding system across Nigeria’s correctional centres – one undermined by chronic overcrowding, inadequate funding, weak oversight, and allegations of diversion of food supplies.

A system stretched beyond limits

Nigeria’s correctional facilities are currently operating far beyond their designed capacity. According to data from the Nigerian Bureau of Statistics, NBS, the inmate population has climbed above 80,000, with about 65 per cent classified as awaiting trial.

This imbalance has invariably placed enormous pressure on basic services, particularly feeding. Facilities originally built to house far fewer inmates now struggle to cater to swelling populations. Kitchens designed for hundreds must now feed thousands, often with limited infrastructure and outdated equipment.

The result, according to multiple accounts, is a system where both the quality and quantity of meals are compromised.

What inmates are fed

Across custodial centres, feeding follows a predictable pattern. Breakfast typically consists of pap, beans, or tea and bread. Lunch may include rice and stew, or yam or eba served with soup. Dinner is often a repetition or variation of what was served earlier in the day.

Food items are supplied by government contractors and prepared within the prisons, largely by selected inmates using large pots and gas cookers.

On paper, the arrangement appears functional. In reality, inmates describe a vastly different picture.

“The food is just routine, not nutrition. It is cooked to fill space, not to sustain health,” said Tunde Oyedele, a former inmate of Kirikiri Correctional Centre.

His most vivid recollection is the condition of the food itself.

“Eating beans there is like chewing stones. They don’t sort it properly. Sometimes the stones are almost half of what you’re given. You spend more time removing stones than eating,” he said.

He added that rice served within the facility is often poorly processed and inadequately cooked.

“The rice can be worse. Some inmates take their portion, wash it again, and recook it. That is if they can afford to buy pepper or oil. That’s how people manage,” he noted.

Another ex-inmate, Adam Aboh, who was released a few months ago, corroborated this but pointed more directly to preparation methods.

He said: “The problem is not just quantity, it’s how the food is made. Beans are cooked overnight, and by morning they just add small oil, pepper and seasoning. Then they keep adding water depending on how many people want to eat. It becomes watery and tasteless.”

He described meals that, in his words, “even a hungry man would struggle to swallow.”

Health consequences

For many inmates, the effects of poor feeding go beyond discomfort, they translate into real health challenges.

Joyce Edeh, who was held at the Kirikiri Female Correctional Centre, said her time in custody was marked by recurring illness linked to food quality.

She said: “I was constantly going to the clinic for stomach pain, weakness and sometimes diarrhoea. The food was not balanced, and sometimes it was outright bad.”

She added that cases of malnutrition were not uncommon, particularly among inmates who lacked external support from family or friends.

“When you don’t have anyone bringing you food or money, you are forced to depend on what is available. And what is available is not enough to keep you healthy,” she said.

Government intervention

In response to mounting criticism over prison conditions, the Federal Government, about two years ago, increased the daily feeding allowance per inmate from less than N700 to N1,500.

The move was widely seen as a necessary adjustment in light of rising food prices.

However, some inmates told Vanguard that the increment has not translated into meaningful improvement.

“The amount may have increased on paper, but in reality, it doesn’t go far,” an inmate who did not want his name mentioned said.

Beyond quality concerns, the inmate insisted that the quantity of food provided is equally problematic.

He also alleged that less than half a bag of beans is sometimes used to prepare breakfast for over 2,000 inmates.

“You can imagine the result. Everybody just gets a small portion that cannot satisfy hunger,” he said.

Another inmate who simply identified himself as Adegbite disclosed that while quantity is an issue, many inmates deliberately avoid official meals due to their poor state.

“Not many people rely on prison food. Those who do are mostly people who have no other option. You can’t eat that kind of food and survive,” he said.

Allegations of diversion

A recurring theme in inmate testimonies is the alleged diversion of food supplies.

One inmate told Vanguard that the volume of food delivered to prisons often does not match what is eventually cooked.

“When supplies come in, they are usually much. But when it’s time to cook, only small portions are released. The rest is taken away and sometimes sold,” she said.

She alleged that diverted food items are occasionally resold within the prison system, forcing inmates to buy what should have been freely provided.

“Sometimes when we give prison officials money to help us buy food items and within a few minutes they are back, we know that they didn’t actually buy the food items from the market. They most probably took it from the store and sold it to us. It’s a common practice and they can’t deny it,” she narrated.

Survival strategies

Faced with these challenges, inmates have developed informal systems to cope.

Vanguard findings indicate three broad categories of inmates when it comes to feeding: Those who depend entirely on prison meals and occasional donations from NGOs; those who buy and cook their own food; and a privileged minority who can afford better options through canteens or external vendors.

For many, survival depends on the second category.

Despite official restrictions, makeshift cooking arrangements are widespread. Small stoves, pots, and utensils are often found within cell corridors, allowing inmates to prepare their own meals when they can access raw ingredients.

“I cook whenever I have money. That is the only way to eat something decent,” said one awaiting-trial inmate.

He added that prison authorities are aware of these practices and, in some cases, tacitly tolerate them.

“If they stop us from cooking, there will be serious problems. People cannot survive on official food alone,” he said.

NGOs, family support

For inmates without the means to cook, support from outside becomes critical.

Non-governmental organisations occasionally visit correctional centres, distributing food packs and relief materials. Families and friends also provide assistance through food deliveries or financial support.

However, such interventions are irregular and insufficient to meet the needs of the entire inmate population.

Inequality behind bars

Vanguard findings also revealed that feeding conditions have also exposed a clear divide within the prison system.

So-called “VIP inmates”, typically those with financial resources or influence, are able to access better food through the staff canteen or external suppliers.

“There is a staff canteen inside. But only a few inmates can afford to buy from there. For the majority, particularly those in overcrowded cells, such options are out of reach,” said one awaiting-trial inmate.

Staged inspections

Concerns about prison feeding are further complicated by allegations that official inspections do not reflect everyday realities.

A female inmate told Vanguard that whenever high-ranking officials are scheduled to visit, the quality of food improves noticeably.

She said: “They cook special meals when they know visitors are coming. The food looks good, the environment is clean, everything is arranged.”

According to her, such preparations create a misleading impression.

“What they see during inspections is not what we eat everyday. If they come unannounced, they will see the truth,” she added.

It’s a systemic failure – Human rights groups

Reacting to the feeding conditions in the correctional centres, human rights groups called for urgent reforms to the prison feeding system, warning that the situation reflects deep structural and accountability failures.

Executive Director of the Rule of Law and Accountability Advocacy Centre (RULAAC), Okechukwu Nwaguma, said the Federal Government must introduce strict, real-time monitoring of feeding processes within the Nigerian Correctional Service.

According to him, oversight should be driven directly by the Federal Ministry of Interior and include independent verification of both the quality and quantity of meals served to inmates.

World.title: Osun election: Factors that’ll decide Adeleke, Oyebamiji, Salaam, others’ fate tomorrow
World.content:
***Tinubu assures indigenes of adequate security

***15 candidates battle for 1.9m votes

By Clifford Ndujihe, Dapo Akinrefon, Henry Umoru & Shina Abubakar

OSOGBO — AFTER rounding off their campaigns, yesterday, 15 standard bearers are primed for tomorrow’s governorship election in Osun State.

Amid a cloud of tension unfurled by violence and killings that heralded the campaigns, President Bola Tinubu, yesterday, assured people of the state adequate security during and after polls and urged them to troop out en masse to exercise their franchise.

No fewer than 1.9m of 2,339,233 registered voters who collected PVCs across 30 local government areas, 323 wards, and 3,763 polling units are expected to decide the fate of candidates led by Governor Ademola Adeleke of the Accord seeking re-election, Bola Oyebamiji of the All Progressives Congress, APC; and Najeem Salaam of the African Democratic Congress, ADC.

Factors such as influence of critical stakeholders and leaders, popularity, performance, incumbency, federal might and track record among others are expected to shape the outcome of the balloting.

Meanwhile, fresh violence erupted in Ijesaland, yesterday, as some suspected political hoodlums stormed Esa-Oke, and shot two members of the APC. The victims are Oladele Ayegbo and Taiwo Oluwatobi.

They however, said that the attack happened on Wednesday as security agencies embarked on show force in the state in readiness for the election. Already15,000 policemen, 31 Commissioners of Police, helicopters, and drones have been deployed.

Disturbed by the circle of violence, the Amnesty International Nigeria has vowed to make Senator Francis Fadahunsi an example in its campaign against impunity and inflammatory rhetoric by politicians, following remarks attributed to him in a viral video ahead of the poll.

Also, former Chief of Defence Staff, General Lucky Irabor (retd), has called for decisive action, including arrest against politicians and other prominent Nigerians who make inciting statements capable of triggering violence and disrupting the peace of the country.

Tinubu’s assurance

Ahead of the poll, President Tinubu has assured the people of adequate security during and after the exercise.

Tinubu gave the promise during the grand finale of the governorship campaign of the APC held in Osogbo, the Osun State capital yesterday to formally present its candidate, Munirudeen Bola Oyebamiji, for the Saturday election.

Represented by President of the Senate, Godswill Akpabio, Tinubu said: “Let me assure all Osun indigenes that adequate security has been provided all over the state to ensure people come out to cast their votes for the candidate of their choice without any fear or intimidation. Feel very free to cast your votes for the candidate of your choice.”

The candidates, their strengths, weaknesses

With less than two days to the governorship election in Osun State and the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, confirming that 2,339, 233 residents registered to participate in the polls, candidates and political parties are rounding up campaigns and intensifying moves to warm themselves into the hearts of the people with a view to winning their support to emerge as the next governor of the state.

Of the 15 political parties and their candidates listed by INEC for the August 15 governorship polls, the most visible candidates have presented their manifestoes, gone beyond consultation and round up campaigns across the local government areas.

Candidates and their parties

Candidates in the race include Governor Ademola Adeleke (Accord party), Farinloye Olanrewaju (Action Alliance), Esan Olajide (African Action Congress, AAC); Najeem Salaam (ADC); Adeagbo Opawoye (African Democratic Party, ADP), Mustapha Adeniyi, Social Democratic Party, (SDP) and Bola Oyebamiji ( APC).

Others are Adesina Aseyemi-Doro (All Progressives Grand Alliance, APGA); Adewale Adebayo (Allied People Movement, APM); Clement Adesuyi (Action Peoples Party, APP); Masilo Adeleke (Boot Party); Taofeek Adeleke (New Nigeria Peoples Party, NNPP); Saliu Oyelami (Peoples Redemption Party, PRP), Ogunsakin Olalekan (Young Progressives Party, YPP) and Adefemi Adesuyi (Zenith Labour Party, ZLP).

Out of the 15 candidates, three have emerged as front-runners of which Governor Adeleke hinged his re-election campaign on his five-point agenda reloaded. Mr Bola Oyebamiji of APC, tagged his manifesto as ‘Prosperity agenda’ and Najeem Salaam of the ADC launched a 10-point agenda.

Adeleke’s prospects

Apart from being the incumbent governor, he also enjoys acceptability among the majority of civil servants and the leadership of the labour unions. The NLC, TUC and JNC are all on his side and appeared in the Accord party campaigns soliciting support for the governor.

The governor is also banking on his achievements in the area of infrastructure across the three senatorial districts.

In addition, the Ede-born politician seems to be enjoying the backing of some traditional rulers in the state, led by the Ataoja of Osogbo, who on different occasions publicly declared support for the governor and Accord party despite resistance from his subjects.

Also, Adeleke is said to enjoy the support of his former party, the Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, through which he won the governorship poll about four years ago.and a section of the Labour Party, LP

The PDP’s failure to field a candidate for the 2026 polls in the state is more of an advantage for the governor’s re-election bid as the party’s structure, apart from a few strong men, still works for Accord.

Omisore’s loyalists’ defection

Another major advantage the governor has is the defection of Senator Iyiola Omisore’s loyalists to Accord Party due to the fallout of the APC primaries.

Although, Omisore did not leave the APC, many of his associates who served in the Gboyega Oyetola administration, including three commissioners and special advisers, left the party and joined Accord. He is a strong factor in the Ife axis.

It is also believed that Governor Adeleke has an advantage in Osun-West Senatorial District, where he won massively in 2022.

Interestingly, the APC candidate is also from the district, which is expected to deepen the battle for votes in Osun West.

Ede federal constituency, which the Governor hails from, consisting of Ede-North, Ede-South, Egbedore and Ejigbo local governments, has a total of 319,489 registered voters. This is a major advantage for the governor who still retains a hold on the area.

Besides, some bigwigs like Ibukun Fadipe, Sunday Bisi, Disu Babatunde among others may swing votes in Adeleke’s favour in Ijesaland.

In Osun Central, the governor enjoy the support of the Ataoja of Osogbo, Secretary to the State Government, Teslim Igbalaye, Mr Gani Ola-Oluwa and the House of Representatives member, Mr Morufu Adewale, who are likely to help the governor’s cause in Osogbo and Olorunda local government.

Challenges

The governor’s major problems stem from policy decisions early in his administration.

The opposition cites the sacking of teachers and health workers without replacements; sacking of media workers at the state-owned broadcast stations and the administration’s failure to recruit civil servants as a minus for his re-election bid.

The administration is facing allegation of nepotism, with outcry over recent employment into the teaching service and the University of Ilesa favouring Ede indigenes and shutting out other towns.

Also, the governor’s performance in major sectors like agriculture, health, commerce, industry and education form major issues for his opponents’ campaign strategies.

Another factor that may affect the fortunes of the governor is that a major PDP bloc loyal to former governor, Olagunsoye Oyinlola has publicly dumped the governor for the candidate of the APM, Mr Adewale Adebayo.

Oyebamiji’s prospects

The APC candidate, whose personality and philanthropy have endeared him to the people, is believed to enjoy the support of President Tinubu and APC governors.

Apart from being endorsed by the President, Oyebamiji’s election bid received a major boost with the defection of all the federal lawmakers from Osun-East senatorial district, who are also major political gladiators from the towns.

They include Senator Francis Fadahunsi, Mr Wole Oke (Ijesa-North federal constituency), Sanya Omirin (Ijesa-South federal constituency) and Mr Taofeek Ajilesoro (Ife federal constituency).

Besides, some of Omisore’s point men in Ife have also pledged loyalty to the party and its candidate.

While Adeleke got massive votes from Osun-West in 2022, the candidature of Oyebamiji may change the narrative, with the total registered votes from Ikire federal constituency amounting to 222,786 votes for Irewole, Ayedaade and Isokan local governments, likely reducing the influence of the governor in the district.

While Governor Adeleke seems to enjoy endorsement of royal fathers from Ife, Oyebamiji’s major endorsement has been coming from markets and traders.

In most of his engagements, the APC candidate took advantage of the allegation of nepotism against the incumbent to sell himself as a man for all and inaugurated 30 vote canvassers for each of the 3,763 polling units across the state.

Oyebamiji is likely to win in Osun-East due to the presence of Senator Francis Fadahunsi, a major political gladiator from Ijesaland, Hon Sanya Omirin and Wole Oke from Ijesa-South and North respectively.

Although, Senator Iyiola Omisore is still a member of the APC, some of his loyalists are still within the party. Also Engr. Kayode Adereti, the deputy governorship candidate of the party, is influential, having contested against incumbent member of the House of Representatives in 2022 – Taofeek Ajilesoro, who is now also in the APC.

In Osun-Central, whoever wins in Osogbo and Olorunda local government is likely to win the senatorial district. Oyebamiji has the likes of the party’s national secretary, Senator Ajibola Basiru who is from core Osogbo supported by Executive Director, Marine and Blue Economy, Olalekan Badmus and many elites in the Olorunda and Osogbo, supporting the APC.

Challenges

Oyebamiji’s major issue is the policy decision of the Oyetola administration under whom he served.

The modulated salary under Governor Rauf Aregbesola and the inability of Governor Gboyega Oyetola to pay part of it has been a major issue confronting his candidature.

His critics, especially from the Accord party, believe he is responsible for the modulated salary under Aregbesola’s administration and should not be trusted with the governorship seat.

Najeem Salaam’s prospects

Since unveiling his 10 point agenda, anchored on workers’ welfare and sustainable electricity for industrialisation of the state, Salaam, a former Speaker of the House of Assembly, has continuously engaged with the electorate on the need to abandon the traditional political parties.

Salaam’s advantage is Aregbesola’s grassroots appeal when he was governor in the state and the candidate’s humble nature that attracts him to a section of supporters across the state, especially from Osun-West Senatorial District where he hails from.

Many grassroots politicians, who left the APC along with Aregbesola, are with Salaam.

His Osun-West senatorial district roots can harm both Adeleke and Oyebamiji, and could be an advantage should he decide to go into an alliance work with either of the two.

He has, however, vowed to reach the finish line as he claims to be better qualified to govern the state than any of the candidates.

Ogbeni Aregbesola’s influence in Osogbo and Ilesa East local government may also work for Salaam’s ambition.

His challenges

Salaam’s major challenge is his affiliation with Rauf Aregbesola, who is National Secretary of the ADC. Civil servants are yet to forgive the former governor, who had bitter experiences with the modulated salary and pension issues during Aregbesola’s tenure.

Observers of political events in the state posit that the ADC does not have the necessary state-wide structure needed to prosecute an election, and the needed resources to run a successful governorship project. The three major candidates are from Osun-West Senatorial District, hence the district is going to be a battleground with Adeleke coming from Ede-North and Ede-South; Oyebamij from Irewole local government and Salaam is from Ejigbo local government area of the state.

LG crisis

Another important factor is control of the grassroots, local government administration is said to be the closest to the local people and the Accord and APC battled extensively for control which is yet to be resolved as the matter is still a subject of litigation. However, in the meantime the APC is still “controversially” in control of Local Government in the state.

Infrastructure development

A major factor is the infrastructure drive in the state in the last three and half years, the Governor Adeleke-led administration said it has completed over 300 km of road network across the State, including many first, such as the first dualised roads in Ilesa, Iwo, Ede and Ila-Orangun. The people applauded the governor for the feat achieved.

Elite conspiracy

One of the issues going into the polls is the elite conspiracy against the governor’s immediate family members. The governor may not really have problems with the Osun elite, but the way his immediate family, especially his elder sister, allegedly runs the affairs of government behind the scenes does not go well with them.

Many classified the administration as the Adeleke dynasty government rather than one run by party or state stakeholders. This formed part of the reason many political gladiators like Senator Francis Fadahunsi, Mr Wole Oke, Prince Olagunsoye Oyinlola, Alhaji Shuaib Oyedokun among others parted ways with the governor.

Single-term syndrome

Since the creation of Osun State, those elected as governor, apart from Aregbesola, served only one term in office. It is to be seen if Adeleke will get a second term like Aregbesola.

Traditional rulers

This election has divided traditional rulers along party lines.

While others simply chose to support their subject, the Timi of Ede, Oba Adesola Lawal, openly campaigned for the Accord and the governor.

He publicly disclosed that Ede indigenes should vote for Accord to retain power in the town.

Also, the Akire and other traditional rulers in Irewole federal constituency have endorsed Oyebamiji, saying the constituency will prefer to have their son on the seat of power as means to guarantee their growth and development.

While the Ataoja of Osogbo, Oba Jimoh Oyetunji has thrown his weight behind Governor Adeleke over what Adeleke has done in the town, the Oluwo of Iwo, Oba Abdurosheed Akanbi is backing the APC. The Oluwo has openly told monarchs from Iwoland not to go the wrong way during the election on Saturday.

However, the Ooni of Ife, Oba Adeyeye Ogunwusi has retained his status of father to all, separating the palace from party politics.

Oyinlola backing Oyebamiji

Former Osun State governor, Prince Olagunsoye Oyinlola has pitched his tent with Oyebamiji and has promised to mobilize for the victory of the APC candidate. Oyinlola, a chieftain of the PDP, who announced his support for Oyebamiji, said Osun requires a different direction.

Several political leaders from the PDP and other political structures had also thrown their weight behind Oyebamiji, including former senator Olasunkanmi Akinlabi, former secretary to the Osun state government Fatai Akinbade and former PDP national vice-chairman Tajudeen Oladipo.

Omisore’s support

In the 2018 governorship election, Senator Iyiola Omisore, who was also contesting the governorship race, supported Oyetola during the supplementary elections to defeat Adeleke.

Omisore’s looming image helped Oyetola get 28,000 votes to beat Adeleke.

In the Ile-Ife axis, Omisore is seen as a power bloc, whose support base is capable of swinging the votes in favour of Oyebamiji.

Though during the electioneering campaigns, Omisore was conspicuously absent due to his being allegedly sidelined, however, a meeting with President Tinubu a fortnight ago made him change his mind to support Oyebamiji.

APC’s campaign DG killed 2days to election

Meanwhile, few hours to the election, fresh violence has erupted in Ijesaland as some suspected political hoodlums stormed Esa-Oke, and shot two APC members – Oladele Ayegbo and Taiwo Oluwatobi.

Oladele Ayegbo, a nephew of the APC campaign council Director-General, Mr Wole Oke, was reported to have died on the spot while the second victim, Oluwatobi is recuperating at the hospital.

The APC campaign council Media Committee Chairman, Remi Omowaye while addressing newsmen yesterday, said three other persons were attacked in Ilesa same day while one of its House of Representatives candidates, Francis Eniade was attacked inside police station at Okuku by hoodlums working for a governorship candidate.

“The APC was not accusing the police of complicity but urged the security agency to act swiftly and decisively in line with its constitutional responsibility to protect lives and property as the state prepares for Saturday’s governorship election,” he said.

In a statement issued on Thursday, Osun APC spokesperson Kola Olabisi revealed that Ayegbo was killed on Wednesday night near his residence in the Idofin area of Esa-Oke, located in the Obokun Local Government Area.

According to the party, suspected hoodlums operating from a vehicle carried out the attack.

“The Osun State chapter of the APC has condemned the killing of the party’s governorship campaign Director-General, Wole Oke’s nephew, Dele Ayegbo, in Esa-Oke, Obokun Local Government Area of the state on Wednesday night by the hit squad of the Accord party who have been terrorising the members and supporters of the opposition APC across the state,” the statement reads.

“Information has it that Ayegbo was gunned down at the road junction close to his house at the Idofin quarters area of the ancient town by the Accord Party hoodlums who were riding in a car.”

Olabisi stated that two party members were targeted in the shooting. While Ayegbo died instantly at the scene, the second victim sustained gunshot wounds and was rushed to an undisclosed local hospital for medical treatment.

Attack happened on Wednesday —Police

When contacted, Police Public Relations Officer, Osun Command, DSP Abiodun Ojelabi confirmed the incident, saying the attack was carried out on Wednesday night around 11pm.

Ojelabi said: “One Oladele Ayegbo has passed away while the other victim is receiving treatment at the hospital. More police unit have been deployed to the area to assist the Division to secure the town more appropriately,” he said.

15,000 policemen, 31 CPs deployed

To police the poll, the Force Public Relations Officer, Anietie Iniedu said the Police have deployed 15,000 policemen and 31 Commissioners of Police to oversee each local government during the exercise.

He added that police helicopter and drone unit have also been deployed to conduct aerial surveillance before, during and immediately after the election on Saturday.

His words: “We have 15,000 police officers on the ground, drawn from several combat and tactical units; the PMF, the TAPU, the Bomb Squad and the Special Protection Unit. We also have men from our tactical units on the ground. We have men on patrol, and we have men stationed at strategic locations.

“As I speak to you, we have deployed one unit of armed mobile police officers to every local government area. So, we have 30 units across the local government areas. A unit is actually about 60 police officers, including 50 armed police officers. So, we have a unit for each local government area.

“The men posted to the local government areas are being coordinated by a Commissioner of Police. There is a Commissioner of Police in each local government area. We also have a Deputy Commissioner of Police in each local government area, as well as a Mobile Police Commander and a PMF Commander in each local government area”, he said.

INEC office

CSP Iniedu further disclosed that two units of armed mobile policemen were attached to the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, headquarters in the state to ensure adequate security

“We also have two units of armed mobile police officers attached to the Independent National Electoral Commission headquarters in Osogbo. We have two units of armed police officers posted there.

Helicopters, drones deployed

“As of today, our helicopter and drone units have arrived in Osogbo, and they will be conducting area surveillance from now, during and immediately after the election”, he added.

Security agencies embark on show of force

The security agencies, including Police, DSS, Army, Air Force, NSCDC personnel among others have been going round for show of force to deter criminal-minded people from engaging in activities that may disrupt the peace and harmony of the state ahead of the poll.

He also disclosed that the state will be locked down from 12am on Saturday till after the election and only essential workers, and voters will be allowed to move around throughout election period.

“The Army is cordoning all border roads leading into Osun State. And so, by 12 a.m. on Saturday, we will be locking down the state. We will not be allowing any vehicular movement apart from those on essential duty, security duties and those going to cast their franchise”.

‘We’ll use Fadahunsi as example’ – Amnesty vows

Amnesty International Nigeria has vowed to make Senator Francis Fadahunsi an example in its campaign against impunity and inflammatory rhetoric by politicians, following remarks attributed to him in a viral video ahead of Saturday’s governorship election in Osun State.

In the video, Fadahunsi, who represents Osun East Senatorial District, was alleged to have directed his supporters to “kill” members of the Accord Party, which has incumbent Governor Adeleke as its governorship candidate.

The senator has, however, denied making any call for physical attacks, insisting that the viral video was edited to distort the meaning of his comment.

Speaking on Channels Television’s Sunrise Daily on Thursday, Country Director of Amnesty International Nigeria, Isa Sanusi, condemned the remarks attributed to Fadahunsi and said the organisation would use the case to challenge what he described as impunity among Nigerian politicians.

“We are going to use him as an example because this is the first time. We had so many other terrible politicians say terrible things ahead of elections, but this one is exceptional. A situation whereby somebody came out on record saying ‘kill them wherever you find them’, I believe that that person does not deserve any peace again because advocacy of hatred is a crime under international law as well as Nigerian laws.

“Therefore, we are going to use this man as an example to show that the impunity by Nigerian politicians cannot continue and we cannot tolerate it again; the people have to hold them to account if the government could not do that,” Sanusi said.

People who make inciting statements should be arrested – Ex-CDS Irabor

In like manner, former Chief of Defence Staff, General LEO Irabor(retd), has called for decisive action, including arrest, against politicians and other prominent Nigerians who make inciting statements capable of triggering violence and disrupting the peace of the country.

Speaking on Channels Television’s The Morning Brief on Thursday, Irabor condemned Senator Fadahunsi’s statement and commended the police for questioning him.

“For me as a person, any time we hear individuals who make inciting comments, I think that such people should be picked up immediately, and that is why I am glad that even though the statement made by Senator Fadahunsi is a political one, but I think that it also borders on incitement to violence. I think the police have done the right thing by inviting him, and he should be questioned even beyond that,” General Irabor said.

The former Defence chief also called for the arrest of Islamic clerics Sani Jingir and Ahmad Gumi over what he described as inciting statements they had made at different times.

“Added to that is of course the Sheik in Kano, Sheik Jingir, who also made some comments which of course I believe is also inciting that could also add to the bouquet of threats that we have, he also should be arrested and I also believe that the various comments that someone like Gumi has been making also demands that he be called not just to order but of course invited and arrested in other to let the populace know that there is nobody who is above the law and then when you say things that are not right you should be called in to answer,” the former service chief said.

Let people choose, peace must

prevail — Obi

Also, Presidential candidate of the National Democratic Congress, NDC, Mr. Peter Obi has called on all stakeholders in Saturday’s Osun State governorship election to ensure that voters are allowed to exercise their franchise freely and without intimidation.

Obi made the call in a statement posted on his X platform, yesterday, urging the INEC, security agencies, political parties, candidates and other stakeholders to maintain neutrality, professionalism and restraint before, during and after the election.

The former Anambra State governor said the people of Osun State must be allowed to determine their leaders through a transparent and credible electoral process.

He urged INEC to ensure that votes were properly counted, protected and announced in accordance with the wishes of the electorate.

“Osun belongs to its people. Therefore, I call on the Independent National Electoral Commission, security agencies, political parties, candidates, government institutions, civil society organisations, religious and traditional leaders, the media, and every stakeholder to act with the highest degree of neutrality, professionalism, and restraint,” Obi said.

He appealed to residents of Osun to reject violence and resist attempts by politicians to create divisions within communities for electoral advantage.

“To those within Osun State, I appeal for peace. Do not allow politicians to turn your neighbours, friends, and communities against each other. Do not destroy your state in the name of winning an election,” he said.

Obi also called on politicians, supporters, influencers and financiers outside the state to avoid actions that could fuel violence or intimidation during the poll.

He specifically urged security agencies to remain loyal to the Constitution and the Nigerian state rather than political parties or individuals.

Obi appealed to the international community, diplomatic missions and election observers to closely monitor the election, saying their presence could strengthen public confidence in Nigeria’s democratic process.

Sensitive materials arrive Osogbo

Meanwhile, INEC sensitive materials arrived Osogba, late yesterday, ahead of tomorrow’s poll.

Osun AG sues IGP, seeks order compelling police to probe Fadahunsi

The Osun State Government has approached a state high sitting in Osogbo, seeking an order compelling the police to investigate Senator Francis Fadahunsi over alleged inflammatory remarks and threats against members and supporters of the Accord Party ahead of Saturday’s governorship election.

The suit, filed by the state Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice, Oluwole Jimi-Bada, SAN, seeks an Order of Mandamus against the Inspector-General of Police and Commissioner of Police, Osun State Command.

Fadahunsi, who represents Osun East senatorial district, was joined in the suit as the person affected or interested party.

The government said the action followed a video circulating on social media, allegedly showing Fadahunsi addressing a political gathering in front of the Owa Obokun’s Palace, Ilesha, on August 11, 2026.

According to court documents, the senator allegedly made remarks interpreted as calls for violence against Accord party members, including directing supporters to attack them wherever they were found.

The government alleged that Fadahunsi also threatened their families, directed supporters to chase Accord members from hotels and made derogatory comments about the party’s yellow caps.

It further alleged that the senator threatened that the election would not hold if Accord members resisted the alleged actions of APC supporters.

The state is asking the court to compel the police to investigate the video and determine whether the alleged statements constitute criminal offences.

It also wants the police to preserve, authenticate and conduct forensic examination of the complete video to establish whether it had been altered or edited.

Other reliefs sought include an order directing the police to take preventive measures to protect Accord candidates, members and voters from intimidation and harassment before, during and after the election.

In a supporting affidavit, Nurudeen Kareem, Special Adviser to Governor Ademola Adeleke on Legal Matters, said Accord members had expressed “reasonable and legitimate concerns regarding their safety and security before, during, and after the forthcoming election.”

The government argued that the police had a statutory responsibility under the Police Act 2020 and the 1999 Constitution to prevent crime and maintain public order.

It said: “The applicant believes that waiting until actual violence, deaths, or injuries occur before investigating an alleged public instruction to kill political opponents would amount to a dereliction of duty.”

The Attorney-General stressed that the suit was not asking the court to determine Fadahunsi’s guilt, but to compel the police to perform their statutory duties and take appropriate preventive action.

With the election scheduled for Saturday, the government said “time is of the absolute essence,” warning that failure to act on the alleged threat could have serious consequences for public safety and the electoral process.

World.title: I ignored warnings before backing Gbenga Daniel for Senate in 2023 – Abiodun
World.content:
Gov. Abiodun

Ogun State Governor Dapo Abiodun has disclosed that he was advised not to support former governor and current senator representing Ogun East, Gbenga Daniel, for the Senate during the 2023 general election because of fears that the former governor might later oppose him politically.

The governor made the revelation while receiving members of Daniel’s political family and loyalists of the late Senator Buruji Kashamu into the mainstream of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in Abeokuta.

In a statement issued on Thursday by his Special Adviser on Information and Strategy, Kayode Akinmade, Abiodun described the return of the political groups as an important development that would strengthen the APC ahead of the 2027 elections.

Reflecting on the political events of 2023, the governor said he was cautioned against supporting Daniel’s emergence as the APC senatorial candidate because of concerns that the former governor could eventually turn against him.

“Despite the warnings, I supported Daniel because of my respect for him as a former governor and my belief that political disagreements should not diminish the respect accorded former occupants of the office.

“I just decided that we should honour him because one day, I will also become a former governor.”

Abiodun also recalled a political meeting during which, according to him, Daniel expressed uncertainty over who would become the next governor of Ogun State, despite one of the contenders belonging to his political party.

“Now the gloves are off. He is the same person that we heard in an audio saying he had taken someone to court,” Abiodun added.

The governor further expressed concern over what he described as the recent relaunch of Daniel’s foundation, where the Peoples Democratic Party governorship candidate, Hon. Ladi Adebutu, was reportedly a special guest of honour.

According to Abiodun, the development appeared to indicate that Daniel had chosen to operate outside the mainstream of the APC, despite remaining a respected political figure in Ogun State.

He said his relationship with the former governor had always been guided by respect for the office of governor and the status of former office holders.

“You know OGD is my leader because he was governor before me. I joined Ogun State politics way before him. Without a doubt, I was a senator-elect in the state in 1996/1997,” Abiodun said.

The governor also reflected on his political journey and cautioned against the misuse of political power.

“You don’t begin to act as if you are God. You don’t begin to play as if you are an emperor. God gives us power and looks at how we use it. If you utilise it very well, God will leave it with you for a long time to continue to wield it. If you abuse it, God will take it away from you and give it to somebody else,” he said.

At the meeting held at the Presidential Lodge in Abeokuta, Abiodun commended the defectors for aligning with the APC and urged politicians with shared interests to speak with one voice rather than work for different political parties.

In response, Daniel’s media aide, Steve Oliyide, denied that the former governor had relaunched any foundation, insisting that the gathering was merely a reunion of old and new members of the Gateway Front Foundation ahead of its 25th anniversary.

“There was no ‘relaunch’of the Foundation yet, but a reunion of old and new members of the Gateway Front Foundation to plan for its 25th Anniversary. I am not sure if there was ever any need for a Special Guest of Honour at such an event.

“Hon. Ladi Adebutu is also an old member of the Foundation, except the writer is asking that an old member of over 20 years should be excused from an event in which he played a significant role simply because of his political ambition to please some other people.”

Daniel’s media office had earlier distanced the senator from a circulating audio recording, describing it as manipulated and fabricated.

“The OGD Media Office has been inundated with enquiries regarding a purportedly leaked private conversation allegedly involving His Excellency, Otunba Gbenga Daniel, and a respected elder statesman.

“For the records, this Office became aware of the existence of the audio over six weeks ago, following attempts by its purveyors to deploy the maliciously doctored recording as an instrument of political blackmail, coercion, intimidation, and other criminal ends.

“The audio in circulation is a manipulated and deliberately doctored material, calculated to mislead the public, malign the reputation of His Excellency, and advance a premeditated political agenda.

“Accordingly, the appropriate law enforcement agencies have been formally invited to investigate the source of the recording, those responsible for its manipulation and dissemination, and the criminal motives behind its circulation.

“In addition, our legal team has been instructed to pursue all available civil and criminal remedies against every individual or group connected with this orchestrated campaign of calumny, defamation, malicious falsehood, and cybercrime.This shenanigans must stop in our body politics.”

The exchange comes amid growing political tension between Abiodun and Daniel over the 2027 Ogun East senatorial ticket. Daniel is reportedly seeking another term in the Senate, while Abiodun, who will complete his second term as governor next year, is also believed to be interested in the seat.

The APC has since adopted Abiodun as its consensus candidate for the 2027 Ogun East Senate race, and he was subsequently declared winner of the party’s primary election.

World.title: 2 African countries qualify for 2027 Women World Cup playoffs
World.content:
Ghana and South Africa have secured Africa’s two places in the inter-confederation play-offs for the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup after both countries recorded crucial victories in Casablanca on Thursday.

The Black Queens booked their place first after coming from behind to defeat Côte d’Ivoire 2-1.

Inès Konan put the Elephants ahead from the penalty spot in the fourth minute, giving Côte d’Ivoire an early advantage.

Ghana responded strongly after the break, with Princess Marfo restoring parity before Josephine Bonsu completed the comeback with 18 minutes remaining.

The victory sent the Black Queens through to the 10-team inter-confederation play-offs, where they will battle for one of the three remaining World Cup places.

South Africa then joined Ghana after defeating Nigeria 2-1 in the later fixture.

The Super Falcons had been hoping to keep their World Cup qualification record intact, but Banyana Banyana secured the crucial victory to end Nigeria’s hopes of reaching the tournament for the first time in their history.

South Africa’s victory means the two-time WAFCON champions will represent Africa alongside Ghana in the inter-confederation play-offs.

The play-offs will be held across two international windows between November 2026 and February 2027, with the 10 participating teams divided into three mini-tournaments.

The winners of the three mini-tournaments will secure the final three places at next year’s Women’s World Cup in Brazil.

Ghana and South Africa will therefore have another opportunity to secure their places at the global tournament after missing out on direct qualification through the Women’s Africa Cup of Nations route.

Vanguard News

World.title: Police mopped up 34 illegal weapons in Osun ahead poll – Force PRO
World.content:
File image.

By Shina Abubakar, Osogbo

The Nigeria Police Force has disclosed that it has mopped up 34 illegal firearms ahead of the governorship election in Osun State.

This was disclosed by the Force Public Relations Officer, CSP Aniete Iniedu, while fielding questions from stakeholders at the town hall meeting held at the Osun State police command headquarters in Osogbo on Thursday.

He said investigation is ongoing into the sources of the weapons after which the illegal owners will be prosecuted in line with the directives of the Inspector General of Police.

“With regards to illicit weapons, about 34 recovered arms in Osun State ahead of the election. Investigation is ongoing about it, after which there will be prosecution”, he said.

CSP Iniedu further disclosed that illicit weapons were not allowed at the polling units.

“Even the four policemen that were deployed to each unit will not carry weapons. All kind of firearms or any weapon is prohibited at the polling units in line with the Electoral Acts.

“What we will do is that apart from the uniformed officers deployed at the unit, secret police officers and other security agents will be at the polling units to profile voters and the people present at polling units,” he said.

The Force PRO had earlier disclosed that apart from the 15,000 policemen deployed to the state, police helicopter and drone units have also arrived the state to conduct aerial surveillance before, during and immediately after the election.

World.title: Chinonso Lilian Osuofia: Celebrating a Life of Resilience, Enterprise and Humanity
World.content:
In a business environment where success is often measured by commercial achievements, Dr. Chinonso Lilian Osuofia stands out for combining enterprise with a strong commitment to humanity. As Director and Chief Executive Officer of Jigsimur International (Jigsimur Zdex Ltd), she has built a reputation as an entrepreneur and business leader whose journey is defined by resilience, purpose and service. Beyond her achievements in business, her philanthropic engagements continue to reflect a belief that true success is best measured by the lives positively impacted along the way. Precious Ugwuzor writes

Dr. Chinonso Lilian Osuofia, Director and Chief Executive Officer of Jigsimur International (Jigsimur Zdex Ltd), has carved a distinctive path as an entrepreneur, business leader and philanthropist. Her journey reflects the resilience required to build enterprises in a challenging economy, while her commitment to humanitarian service has placed people and community at the heart of her success.

Through business, empowerment and philanthropy, Osuofia has demonstrated a philosophy of leadership that extends beyond commercial achievement. Her story is one of enterprise with purpose, showing how success can become a platform for creating opportunities, restoring hope and positively influencing lives.

Building Enterprise Through Resilience

Osuofia’s entrepreneurial journey reflects the courage, determination and adaptability required to build and sustain businesses in Nigeria’s competitive economic environment. Her leadership at Jigsimur International demonstrates her belief in the power of enterprise to create opportunities and contribute to economic empowerment.

Putting Humanity at the Heart of Success
