World.title: Muere el músico y artista Víctor Coyote de manera repentina a los 68 años
World.content:
Víctor Aparicio Abundancia, más conocido como Víctor Coyote, de 68 años, falleció hoy jueves, mientras circulaba en bicicleta por una carretera de Segovia, adonde había acudido la noche anterior para contemplar el eclipse. Tan súbita muerte ha noqueado a sus amigos, que conocían su pasión por mantenerse en buena forma y su gusto por los deportes.

Gallego de Tui, llegó a Madrid para estudiar Bellas Artes en la segunda mitad de los setenta, a tiempo de contagiarse de la fiebre generacional por formar grupos. Fundó un trío de rockabilly, Los Coyotes, que pronto abandonó lo purista para derivar hacia la variedad del psychobilly, por su gusto por lo truculento (no fue casualidad que terminaran grabando para 3 Cipreses, el sello fundado por Eduardo Paralisis Permanente Benavente y sus amigos).

En realidad, el cambio sería la divisa de Víctor. La curiosidad le llevaba a patearse las tiendas de segunda mano, donde localizaba discos raros de portadas feas que a veces ofrecían ventanas a inesperados mundos sonoros; su cultura musical estaba muy por encima de lo habitual entre sus colegas. Y lo mismo podríamos afirmar de la capacidad narrativa de sus canciones, historias fascinantes que no ocurrían en los locales modernos de Berlín o Londres.

Iba por libre: el primer LP de Los Coyotes, Mujer y sentimiento (1985), negaba directamente los parámetros de la escena de la Movida, tan obsesionada por encajar en la modernidad europea. Víctor se situaba en el medio de un hipotético triángulo definido por la Península Ibérica, América y Africa. Una propuesta tricontinental que algunos empezaron a etiquetar como “rock latino”. No debería extrañarnos que fuera uno de los pocos artistas del rock que incorporara a sus preocupaciones el fenómeno de la inmigración.

Víctor Coyote, en una imagen de 2009. ÁLVARO GARCÍA

Por alguna razón, Víctor no cayó en gracia entre el gran público. En letras, fotos promocionales y conciertos alardeaba de masculinidad, con una actitud que muchos confundieron con la arrogancia. Eso suponía menospreciar su humor y su notable capacidad para la metamorfosis (durante un tiempo, compartió escenarios con Alaska, supliendo la ausencia militar de Carlos Berlanga). Creó incluso un cancionero infantil para Xabarin Club, el programa de la TVG.

Pero no hubo manera, a pesar de que su discográfica invirtió millones de pesetas en conseguir que su “Jaguarundi” fuera sintonía de las transmisiones de la Vuelta Ciclista España de 1995. Reflexionando sobre su situación profesional, un ejecutivo discográfico que trabajó con él en aquella época sugiere ahora que sus cambios constantes desconcertaban a medios, oyentes y compañeros de profesión: “no se le concedían la misma libertad que a un Prince, por poner un ejemplo que a él le gustaba”. Victor terminó tomándoselo a broma, imaginándose -en uno de los relatos de su libro Cruce de perras- acogido en un asilo, pero siempre orgulloso, buscando un enfrentamiento con Santiago Auserón, alguien que tuvo mayor suerte con propuestas similares. Conviene mencionar que en esas páginas también aprovechaba para saldar cuentas con los tópicos de los ochenta, desde su posición de culto esteta que no rehuía lo convencionalmente considerado “hortera”. En sus letras, también estaban presentes los condicionantes de clase.

Muy trabajador, organizó con el desaparecido Pepo Fuentes el estudio de diseño Pocateja. Su buen talante le abrió la puerta a todo tipo de aventuras: cómics, carteles de cine, portadas de discos, realización de videos para otros artistas, documentales, la cabecera y el score de la serie “Poquita fe”, literatura. Su modus operandi pasaba por buscarse la vida haciendo esto y aquello, para volver a la música cuando había suficiente material nuevo o la oportunidad para actuar. Que conste que defendía a muerte su legado: este año había editado El propio, otro recopilatorio de su trayectoria. Hacía bien: esas canciones merecían seguir paseando por las calles más castizas, con chulería y determinación.

World.title: La pólvora y la mecha
World.content:
Artículos estrictamente de opinión que responden al estilo propio del autor. Estos textos de opinión han de basarse en datos verificados y ser respetuosos con las personas aunque se critiquen sus actos. Todas las tribunas de opinión de personas ajenas a la Redacción de EL PAÍS llevarán, tras la última línea, un pie de autor —por conocido que éste sea— donde se indique el cargo, título, militancia política (en su caso) u ocupación principal, o la que esté o estuvo relacionada con el tema abordado

Las imágenes de Ceuta han dado la vuelta al mundo. Reflejan dramáticamente los problemas de nuestro tiempo, los desequilibrios sociales y entre territorios y regiones. Han mostrado la acritud del debate político en torno a la emigración. Y han causado otro grave episodio de división europea, con más países dispuestos a explotar para uso interno los problemas de los demás que a ejercer una cooperación leal para proteger una frontera exterior común. Una masa humana en movimiento que ha dejado detrás cerca de 140 muertos, según los cálculos de algunas ONG, y supera en intensidad a los boat people de Vietnam o a los balseros cubanos. Solo es comparable a la huida de una guerra como las de Siria o Ucrania. Pero ese no era el caso de Marruecos.

Las distintas formas de llamar a lo ocurrido —crisis migratoria, invasión, atentado a la soberanía nacional, complot internacional, etcétera— interpretan implícitamente sus causas. Pero, en cualquier caso, 78.000 personas que asaltan en pocas horas una frontera es una verdadera explosión humana. Y toda explosión, accidental o provocada, necesita un detonador para inducir la reacción en cadena de la masa explosiva. Como cuando el fuego de la mecha alcanza la pólvora. O cuando basta una narrativa para provocar una avalancha, porque los seres humanos a diferencia de las partículas de un explosivo, tenemos expectativas y actuamos de acuerdo con ellas

La masa reactiva es fácil de identificar, pero conviene decirlo. La crisis social en Marruecos se complementa con la acumulación de emigrantes subsaharianos que están bloqueados, ni para atrás ni para adelante, esperando una oportunidad para cruzar un brazo de mar o una alambrada en su camino hacia Europa.

Sabemos por propia experiencia que el crecimiento económico sin desarrollo social genera crisis. Y que, a veces, la única salida que se percibe es el exilio. Esa es la situación de muchos jóvenes marroquíes cuya educación —un 70% ya tiene el bachillerato— ha crecido más rápidamente que sus oportunidades. El paro juvenil supera el 35% y afecta especialmente a las mujeres y a los titulados. Y eso genera una frustración que les empuja a buscar oportunidades fuera.

No es que la economía marroquí vaya mal. Al contrario, crece al 5% con una inflación controlada; baja deuda pública; una de las tasas de inversión más altas del mundo (32% del PIB), solo por detrás de China; e inversión extranjera en rápido crecimiento en sectores como el automóvil, la aeronáutica y las energías renovables.

El empleo crece, casi 200.000 empleos netos en 2025. Pero la mitad de los que alcanzaron la edad de trabajar no se incorporaron al mercado laboral, y la tasa de actividad sigue siendo una de las más bajas de las economías emergentes.

La estampida humana de Ceuta muestra cómo un relato basado en parámetros macro no basta si las desigualdades persisten y la creación de riqueza no se corresponde con la percepción social. Que el malestar social sea compatible con una tasa alta de crecimiento del PIB no es un fenómeno exclusivo de Marruecos. Se podría decir lo mismo de nosotros, que con la mayor tasa de desempleo juvenil de Europa no estamos para dar lecciones. Allí y aquí el problema es político e institucional: cómo aumentar la productividad del conjunto de la economía, la verdadera fuente de progreso, en vez de recrearse en el número de puestos de trabajo de baja retribución creados en sectores de baja productividad estructural. Y esa masa reactiva sigue ahí. No va a desaparecer sin profundas transformaciones que escapan a nuestra capacidad, pero que deberían inducirnos a impulsar un nuevo pacto para el desarrollo para contribuir mucho más a combatir las causas profundas de la emigración.

Sé que una cuestión de esta trascendencia no se puede despachar con cuatro frases bien intencionadas. Pero es el gran tema de fondo que quieren ignorar los partidarios de la Europa Fortaleza. Durante demasiado tiempo he visto cómo nuestro discurso sobre democracia y derechos humanos escondía en realidad la preocupación por la estabilidad política y la contención de la emigración. Y creo que una visión exclusivamente securitaria en realidad nos debilita.

Sobre el detonante, parece incuestionable que el más importante ha sido la difusión masiva por las redes sociales de una noticia, cierta: la sentencia del Tribunal Supremo, que no es el momento de comentar sino de acatar, sobre la no devolución en caliente de quien llegue a nado, por no implicar que haya “forzado una barrera física”. Pero deformando su interpretación y acompañándola de otras noticias absolutamente falsas, como que la frontera estaría abierta. Multitud de videos difundían los métodos para cruzar la frontera y la idea de que no habría expulsiones.

Así hemos aprendido que la desinformación puede matar, y que la vigilancia de las fronteras tiene qué ser física pero también y cada vez más digital e informacional.

Como se ha dicho, estamos ante la primera “avalancha algorítmica” de la historia. Hay un precedente de menor cuantía: en septiembre de 2024, vídeos virales en TikTok convocaban una travesía masiva a nado hacia Ceuta. Pero entonces se previó una ola de contagios y hubo muchas detenciones en Fnideq, el municipio más cercano a Ceuta por “difusión de contenidos digitales falsos que incitan a la emigración ilegal”.

Nada de esto ha ocurrido esta vez. Y el proceso de desinformación en las redes parece ser cualquier cosa menos espontáneo. Pero, como dice mi colega el excomisario Thierry Breton, sabemos muy poco sobre las métricas de difusión de estos contenidos: visualizaciones, alcance geolocalizado, curva de propagación, cuentas que lo han impulsado, amplificación algorítmica, los bots y la viralidad real.

Tampoco ha habido ninguna reacción oficial por parte de las plataformas afectadas. Queda pendiente una gran investigación sobre las fuentes y la dirección de esos procesos en los que seguramente habrán intervenido todos los interesados en crearnos problemas —desde luego Rusia— o en celebrarlos, como han hecho los EE UU de Trump y el Israel de Netanyahu.

Desde una perspectiva europea hay que señalar que no ha habido ninguna medida por parte de la Comisión en aplicación del Reglamento sobre los Servicios Digitales (DSA, por sus siglas en inglés), que entró en vigor el 12 de junio pasado, el primer paso para detectar y sancionar las instrumentalizaciones de la información para “fomentar o facilitar el desplazamiento de nacionales de terceros países hacia las fronteras exteriores de la UE para desestabilizar a un Estado miembro”. Como anillo al dedo le viene a lo de Ceuta.

Sobre la desunión europea ya se ha lamentado todo lo lamentable. Italia y Dinamarca no tenían ninguna razón para pedir la suspensión de España de Schengen. Ni siquiera sabían que llegar a Ceuta no es llegar a la Península. Su Gobierno ha jugado al miedo de su electorado, acosado por las perspectivas electorales de otro partido más a la derecha que Meloni. Como aquí le pasa al PP con Vox. España ganó la batalla diplomática en el Consejo de Ministros, donde nadie insistió en sus críticas y proclamaron una tardía solidaridad como la de la Comisión Europea.

La emigración actúa así como el caldo de cultivo de la extrema derecha y también como disolvente de la unidad europea. De la solución que seamos capaces de dar a esta cuestión, y hasta ahora no hemos sido capaces de dársela, depende, más de lo que creemos, nuestro futuro de sociedades libres, solidarias y prósperas.

World.title: Man admits bomb attack on D66 office, calls it protest
World.content:
The man who set off a firework bomb at the D66 headquarters in The Hague in May has admitted the attack, telling a court it was a protest against Dutch asylum policy and what he called the dismantling of the country.

The 37-year-old, identified as Berry van D., appeared at a preliminary hearing at The Hague district court on Thursday. He is accused of causing an explosion with terrorist intent.

About 30 people, most of them members of the party’s youth wing, were inside the building when the firework bomb went off shortly after 9pm. No one was hurt.

Van D. said he had not known anyone was there because he had seen no lights on and that he never intended to hurt anyone.

Prosecutors said he acted alone and told the court he had a political message and wanted to silence people who think differently, ANP reported.

Van D. was arrested about an hour after the blast in the Grote Marktstraat, the city’s main shopping street, carrying two knives. NOS reported that he has a previous conviction for setting fire to city buses in Tilburg, where he had worked as a driver.

He told the court he had turned to violence because voting and peaceful demonstration had achieved nothing.

Psychiatric assessment

Thursday’s hearing was procedural and no trial date has been set yet. Van D. will be transferred to a forensic psychiatric clinic to assess whether he can be held responsible for his actions.

NOS reported that Van D. presents himself on social media as a supporter of the anti-immigration PVV, and described D66 leader Rob Jetten being sworn in as prime minister in February as a black day for the country.

The office on the Lange Houtstraat was also attacked in September last year, when rioters from an anti-immigration demonstration smashed its windows.

One person has been killed and several others injured in an explosion at a site in the Port of Rotterdam, police say.

The blast happened shortly after midday on Thursday at a company on the Moezelweg in Europoort, regional broadcaster Rijnmond reported. Police said they had no further information at this stage.

Multiple people were injured and taken to hospital. Six ambulances, a trauma helicopter and fire crews were sent to the scene.

Rijnmond reported that a hired maintenance crew had been working on pipelines at the site and that something may have gone wrong as those pipes were being disconnected.

Traces of an explosion were visible on a storage tank, the broadcaster said.

Earlier on Thursday, a power cut shut down systems at the Esso refinery on the Botlekweg, sending large flames and black smoke over the port as gas lines were emptied. The Rotterdam-Rijnmond safety authority said it had not established whether the incidents were connected.

World.title: Amsterdam researchers find remedy for fatal child brain disease
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Researchers from the Emma Children’s Hospital at Amsterdam UMC have for the first time found a way to treat a rare genetic brain disease found mostly in children – vanishing white matter, or VWM.

According to The Lancet Neurology, which published the findings, VWM is a neurodegenerative disease “with onset mostly in children aged 1–6 years that causes early death and has no effective therapy.” It’s caused by a genetic defect and occurs in 1 in 100,000 people in the Netherlands.

But now the blood pressure drug guanabenz has been found to inhibit the disease.

In a trial at Amsterdam UMC, 33 children from various countries received guanabenz for four years, while the comparison group included 66 children who did not receive it. Children who received the drug stabilised and ended up needing a wheelchair less often and less quickly.

They also lived – as compared to five patients in the comparison group who died.

“We saw that the disappearance of the white matter in the brain slowed down or even stopped,” chief researcher Marjo van der Knaap told broadcaster NOS.

Moving forward, “the disease-modifying effect of guanabenz should be confirmed in a long-term extension study,” wrote the researchers. The drug also needs the approval of the European Medicines Agency to be used as a treatment for VWM.

World.title: Once-in-a-lifetime solar eclipse has Netherlanders over the moon
World.content:
Eclipse mania took over the Netherlands Wednesday night as people flocked to the coast, roofs and open spaces to watch the largest solar eclipse of the past few decades.

“It looks like a moon giving off light,” a woman on the beach in Petten, a village about 60 kilometers northwest of Amsterdam on the North Sea, told broadcaster NOS. “This is truly very special.”

Indeed traffic jams were rampant on the roads to the sea. But weather conditions were perfect for viewing the eclipse, which was broadcast live on NOS. Some of its broadcasters were clearly moved by the phenomenon.

“This is making me a bit emotional,” NOS weatherman Peter Kuipers Munneke said.

Underwhelmed

But others were less enthusiastic.

College student Sophie joined the crowds to watch the eclipse from the Marineterrein in Amsterdam Oost. Originally planning to make glasses out of old photo negatives, her friend managed to get hold of the hard to come by eye protectors in Amstelveen. But after all the effort, she said they were underwhelmed.

“It wasn’t that special,” she told Dutch News. “The moon didn’t even cover the sun fully. It was like 88% covered and all the sudden, everyone clapped and the sun came back. It wasn’t a total eclipse like in Spain, and it didn’t really become dark. But we had fun.”

A solar eclipse occurs when the moon passes between the sun and earth, blocking all or some of the sun’s light and casting a shadow over the earth.

World.title: Drought means less honey this summer as nectar dries up
World.content:
The persistent drought in the Netherlands has now affected beekeepers, who have noticed that honey production is down this summer. Flowers are blooming for a shorter period, if at all, making it impossible for honeybees to collect the nectar they need to survive.

Professional beekeeper and secretary of the Professional Beekeepers’ Association John Hoogendoorn chalks it up to climate change. “There are increasingly longer periods of drought and higher temperatures, which changes the habitat of the bees,” he told broadcaster NOS. “Nature and the rich biodiversity have deteriorated over the years.”

He said the damage is particularly acute on the dry sandy soils in the east of the country, where the heather honey season has only just begun. Beekeepers report seeing dry shrubs and very little purple, flowering heather there.

Beekeeper Frauke Wessel from Haarlemmermeer has also seen the change. “The bees bring in food to keep their colony alive. But we notice that the honeycomb is no longer filled. The queen bee also lays fewer eggs because she does not get enough food,” she told NOS.

Honeybees need nectar to give them energy for flight and other daily colony tasks. They also convert any excess nectar into stored honey to get them through flowerless winters.

Because the honeybees can’t build up their winter supplies this rainless summer, beekeepers like Hoogendoorn are making up for the lack of honey with dissolved sugar. He told NOS that he needs about 15 kilos of sugar per colony this year to substitute for the honey shortage. “That’s more than in previous years.”

Bees are usually active in the country from the end of February until mid-September. “But due to the high temperatures, the bee season lasts longer and starts earlier,” said beekeeper Joris Knoops.

Flies, wasps, mosquitoes and dragonflies are also suffering from the lack of water.

World.title: Your takeaway habit is feeding Dutch inflation, says DNB
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Dutch households are spending so much on takeaway meals that it is impacting national inflation, the Dutch central bank DNB has reported.

Delivery meals have nearly doubled as a share of the average shopping basket, from around 1.6% in 2015 to just over 3% today, DNB said on Thursday.

Prices have climbed fast. With more people spending, delivery firms have also passed on higher wage, energy and ingredient costs, and between 2020 and 2023 the category went from adding less than 0.1 percentage point to inflation to a full 0.35 point.

It has since eased back to 0.13 point – but only because prices stopped rising so fast, not because anyone is ordering less, DNB said.

The bank traces consumer habits back to the Covid pandemic, when locked-down households began using ordering apps much more, especially while working from home.

Dutch inflation has sat above the European Central Bank’s 2% target for years, driven mainly by rents and food prices. The pizza and sushi deliveries are now also hitting the figures.

World.title: Monument against violence in youth care system vandalised
World.content:
Just two months after it was unveiled, the national youth care monument (Nationaal Monument Jeugdzorg) commemorating violence against young people in the system was vandalised in Apeldoorn.

“This feels like a new attack,” Naomi van Aggelen told broadcaster NOS. She worked for years on the monument and was herself wrongly sent to live at a youth care institution when she was 12 years old.

“It is a very sad sight,” she said of the monument meant to acknowledge the suffering of young people in care homes. “Actually, [it’s] a denial of that recognition.”

Located in Apeldoorn’s Zuiderpark, the wings of the monument – titled De Erkenning (The Recognition) – were broken off and are now missing while scratches and dents are visible on what remains.

“Who does such a thing? We have no idea,” said Van Aggelen. “We don’t know where the wings are.”

The council has filed a police report and is said to be reviewing if additional security measures are needed.

The monument was commissioned after a 2019 report by De Winter Commission that found since WW2, some 20,000 children were the victims of violence in youth care. The organising foundation calls it a place of reparation, remembrance and “of vigilance: all current forms of violence must also stop.”

The future of the monument is still unclear. “I have no idea if we should leave the work for what it is,” said Van Aggelen. “Maybe we should glue it, then it symbolises another broken child in youth care.”

World.title: Barcelona legend Xavi appointed Netherlands head coach
World.content:
Xavi Hernández has been appointed head coach of the Netherlands men’s national team on a contract running to the 2030 World Cup, the Dutch football association KNVB has announced.

The 46-year-old Spaniard succeeds Ronald Koeman, who stepped down after the Netherlands’ last-32 defeat by Morocco at this summer’s World Cup. His appointment ends a long and closely watched search, and comes as a surprise after several higher-profile names fell away.

Former Feyenoord and Liverpool coach Arne Slot, ex-Ajax and Manchester United manager Erik ten Hag and PSV’s Peter Bosz all ruled themselves out, while the KNVB passed over Jong Oranje coach Michael Reiziger and Louis van Gaal. On

Tuesday, Roberto Martínez was reportedly the front-runner, though the KNVB never held direct talks with him.

“A son of Dutch football”

Xavi becomes the first foreign coach of Oranje since the Austrian Ernst Happel, who led the side to the 1978 World Cup final.

“It is a great honour to become head coach of the Netherlands national team,” he said in a statement released by the KNVB. “As someone who was developed at the FC Barcelona academy, with strong influences from, among others, Johan Cruyff and Rinus Michels, I feel a special connection to Dutch football. You could say I am, in a way, a son of Dutch football.”

As a player, Xavi is regarded as one of the best midfielders of his generation, winning four Champions League titles in more than 750 games for Barcelona and lifting the 2010 World Cup with Spain – beating the Netherlands in the final – as well as the European Championship in 2008 and 2012.

He started out as a coach at Al Sadd in Qatar, then took charge of Barcelona in 2021 – also succeeding Koeman – and won the Spanish league title in 2023, but made little impression in Europe before leaving in 2024.

Restoring tactics

The KNVB has handed Xavi an explicit task: restore the attacking, possession-based football long associated with the Dutch game, after a World Cup exit widely seen as a low point in style as much as result.

“As a coach, he has been shaped by years of working with top coaches who share a footballing vision that aligns very well with the way we want the Netherlands national team to play,” said the KNVB’s director Nigel de Jong. He pointed to “taking the initiative, playing dominant and attractive football, combined with the flexibility required in modern football at the highest level.”

Xavi said he shared that ambition. “The Netherlands has a rich football culture and a clear vision that strongly appeals to me: attacking football, based on possession, with creativity, passion and conviction,” he said. “The main objective is always to win, but I prefer to do so in a way that reflects those characteristics and that people can enjoy watching.”

He will be presented at the KNVB’s Zeist headquarters on August 25 and takes charge for the first time on September 24, at home to Germany in the Nations League.

World.title: Polish household assets hit record 4 trillion zloty amid fastest growth in years
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poles are building up wealth at the fastest pace in years, with the combined value of household financial assets surpassing 4 trillion zloty (€930 billion) for the first time, according to new data from the Polish Development Fund (PFR), a state entity. The figure reached 4.1 trillion zloty at the end of the first quarter of this year, up 4.3% from the previous quarter, said PFR. That was the largest quarterly increase in just over six years. On an annual basis, assets rose 15.3%, the fastest pace in five years. After deducting liabilities, household net financial assets stood at 3.2 trillion zloty, also a record. Net assets were up 18.4% from a year earlier and 4.9% from the previous quarter. Ponad 4,1 bln zł – tyle wynoszą już aktywa finansowe polskich gospodarstw domowych. To historyczny rekord. W najnowszej analizie PFR pokazujemy, że w ciągu roku wzrosły o 15,3% – to jedna z najwyższych dynamik w historii. Skala i tempo wzrostu aktywów pokazują też, jak duży jest… pic.twitter.com/fSx1yOZtkn — Mikołaj Raczyński (@MikRaczynski) August 7, 2026 The biggest contribution to the quarterly increase came from what PFR classifies as “other equity holdings”, which include shares in limited liability companies, partnerships, cooperatives and mutual insurance societies. They rose by 61.5 billion zloty. Bank deposits recorded the second-largest increase (44.4 billion zloty). Despite the strong rise in equity holdings, bank deposits and cash remained the largest components of household financial assets, accounting for 26.3% and 11.1% respectively. Pension and disability funds accounted for 10.5% of household financial assets. Meanwhile, shares listed on stock exchanges and regulated over-the-counter markets made up 2.9% of household financial assets. Their value is equivalent to 3% of GDP, one of the lowest shares in the European Union, where the average is 8.2%. Although shares make up only a small share of household assets, the Polish stock market has performed strongly in recent years, with its blue-chip index reaching a record high last week and breaking its previous high set 19 years ago. By contrast, Polish households have a relatively high level of cash holdings. Cash was equivalent to 11.5% of Poland’s GDP in the first quarter, well ahead of the EU average of 4.5% and behind only Slovenia (11.7%) and Germany (11.6%). PFR’s data also show that household liabilities in Poland increased by 5.2% year-on-year to more than 891 billion zloty in the first quarter, well below the rate of asset growth. Long-term loans accounted for 92.2% of liabilities, while short-term loans accounted for 5.1%. Rising household wealth reflects three decades of strong economic growth in Poland, accompanied by a rapid rise in wages and living standards. Earlier this year, state research agency CBOS found that a record 39% of Poles say they are financially comfortable, up from just 3% in the early 1990s. Separate data from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, show that only 2% of the population live in severe deprivation, the lowest level on record. Poland last year rose to its highest-ever level in a measure of household prosperity in European Union member states, overtaking four other countries. That growth has also fuelled a rapid increase in the number of ultra-wealthy people in Poland, whose number has almost doubled since 2019. However, the PFR data show only total combined household assets and liabilities, not how they are distributed across society. The personal data of almost 19 million people, including medical information, has been compromised in a major cyberattack on a company that provides services to thousands of medical facilities in Poland. “We are dealing with one of the largest incidents in Poland’s history,” said digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski on Wednesday. He urged people to use government services to check whether their data is affected and to “lock” their national identity number to prevent potential fraud. (￼🧵 1/2) 💬 Dziś doszło do poważnego wycieku danych w firmie MyDr, który może obejmować blisko 19 milionów osób korzystających z opieki medycznej. W związku z sytuacją krytyczną zostały natychmiast podjęte działania mające zabezpieczyć dane i wyjaśnić okoliczności incydentu –… pic.twitter.com/nIp6EvbKiu — Ministerstwo Cyfryzacji (@CYFRA_GOV_PL) August 12, 2026 The attack targeted MyDr, a company that provides services used by many medical facilities in Poland. Its data includes patients’ personal information, as well as medical details such as diagnoses and prescriptions. It was first reported on Monday by Zaufana Trzecia Strona, an IT security news service, which said that it had been contacted on Saturday by the alleged perpetrators, who claimed to have accessed the data of around 18.8 million people. The hackers, who have not been identified, had also sent a screenshot from the compromised database showing the personal data of “one of the most important politicians in Poland”, added Zaufana Trzecia Strona. Shortly afterwards, MyDr confirmed that it had “become the target of an external, deliberate criminal activity involving some of our data”. In an update on Wednesday, it said that, at the time of writing, there was no evidence that the data had been published anywhere. Największy wyciek danych osobowych w historii Polski i co możemy z nim zrobić – nasza analiza incydentu w MyDr i jego potencjalnych skutków.https://t.co/vXUmVfpPAP Opisujemy aktualny stan wiedzy i możliwe scenariusze rozwoju sytuacji. pic.twitter.com/uqhjz1CjZ1 — ZaufanaTrzeciaStrona @zaufanatrzeciastrona@infosec (@Zaufana3Strona) August 13, 2026 Gawkowski addressed the issue at a press briefing on Wednesday. He noted that “there is no indication we are dealing with an external attack…from Russia or any other country”. Poland has recently regularly been targetted by Russian state-linked hackers. It is “very likely” that cybercriminals are behind the attack on MrDr, said Gawkowski, who pledged that there would be an “uncompromising” response from the Polish security services. The minister advised Poles to check in a secure government database whether their data had been leaked. He also advised citizens to use the state web portal, known as mObywatel, to “lock” their identity number, known as a PESEL, which prevents fraudsters from using it. Around 12,000 medical facilities use MyDr’s services, the digital affairs ministry told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The company claims that it processes three million medical consultations and 2.7 million prescriptions a month, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. A letter sent to a Polish court by Marcin Romanowski, who served as a deputy justice minister in the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government and is now on the run from criminal charges, suggests that he is residing in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links with Russia. The Polish authorities have been trying to locate and extradite Romanowski, whose whereabouts have been unknown since he fled Budapest earlier this year after Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, who had granted him asylum, lost power. Były wiceminister sprawiedliwości ma przebywać w Tyraspolu, stolicy zbuntowanej mołdawskiej prowincji znajdującej się pod patronatem Rosji. Spod tego adresu w Naddniestrzu polityk PiS miał wystąpić o wydanie listu żelaznego.https://t.co/m05dtQv3KV — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) August 12, 2026 On Wednesday, following media reports that Romanowski had sent a letter to the Polish authorities from Transnistria, a spokeswoman for Warsaw’s district court, which is responsible for extradition matters, confirmed to news website Gazeta.pl that this was the case. “The letter and envelope indicate that the package was sent to the court from Tiraspol in Transnistria,” said judge Anna Ptaszek. “It bears his handwritten signature.” Przemysław Nowak, the spokesman for Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office, also confirmed to broadcaster RMF that Romanowski had sent the letter, in which he indicated that he was residing in Tiraspol, the capital of Transnistria, and requested safe passage to Poland. The fugitive politician said that he would be willing to appear in court or before prosecutors, on the condition that he was not placed in detention, said Nowak, who added that prosecutors had not yet taken a position on Romanowski’s request. Transnistria is a region of eastern Moldova, bordering Ukraine, that sought to become a separate state in the early 1990s, even fighting a war between 1990 and 1992. Today, the territory, which has a population of around 360,000, operates as a de facto state but is not recognised by any other country. Transnistria has close ties with Russia, which maintains a military “peacekeeping” force there. The territory’s flag and national emblem feature the Soviet hammer and sickle. Romanowski’s apparent presence in the Russian-linked territory was condemned by figures from Poland’s government. “I would say that Romanowski is now very likely under the influence of Russian intelligence,” said deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk, quoted by broadcaster TVN. Paweł Wojtunik, the former head of Poland’s Central Anticorruption Bureau (CBA), who previously worked in Moldova, wrote that “it is impossible to enter [Transnistria], let alone to live there, without the consent of the local KGB, which is directly managed by the Russian GRU and FSB [intelligence agences]”. – Dzisiaj powiedziałbym, że Romanowski z dużym prawdopodobieństwem jest pod wpływem rosyjskich służb – ocenił wiceszef MON Cezary Tomczyk. Sprawę skomentował też szef MSZ Radosław Sikorski.https://t.co/LuWw0bkh2j — tvn24 (@tvn24) August 12, 2026 Even a deputy leader of Romanowski’s own party, the national-conservative PiS, was unwilling to defend him. In an interview with Polsat News, Przemysław Czarnek noted that it is still not confirmed that Romanowski is in Transnistria. But he agreed, when asked by the host, that it “would be crossing a line” for Romanowski to be in the territory. Romanowski served as a deputy justice minister in the former PiS government between 2019 and 2023. He remains a member of parliament, despite having fled Poland in December 2024 after prosecutors sought to bring charges against him for 11 alleged crimes, including participating in an organised criminal group. Those alleged offences relate to Romanowski’s time at the justice ministry, which was then led by Zbigniew Ziobro, who is also wanted on multiple charges. Both Romanowski and Ziobro obtained asylum in Hungary when the country was led by PiS-ally Orbán. The Polish government says that Hungary has revoked the refugee status and travel documents granted to fugitive ex-justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro by Viktor Orbán. Poland will now seek Ziobro's deportation from the US, where he fled after leaving Hungary https://t.co/TcVw0AiEMX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2026 However, after Orbán lost power earlier this year, Ziobro fled to the United States, where he remains. Last month, Poland requested his extradition, though that is a process that could take years. Romanowski, meanwhile, disappeared completely, leading to months of speculation as to his whereabouts. Both politicians have denied the allegations against them and have claimed to be victims of “political revenge” by the current government, a more liberal coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk that took power in December 2023. They have argued that they would not be able to receive a fair trial in Poland while Tusk remains in power because of the government’s influence over the judicial system. On Wednesday, Romanowski’s lawyer, Bartosz Lewandowski, confirmed that his client had requested safe passage to Poland and that he was “outside the territory of the European Union”. The Polish government has appealed to Starlink, the satellite internet service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, to reverse its decision to exclude Poland from its European roaming area. It says that Polish users, who will now face greater costs when travelling, should not be treated as “second-tier customers”. Starlink, which provides users with portable terminals that act as receivers for internet connections from its network of satellites, offers a “Roam” service that lets customers continue using their connection outside their home country without extra charges as long as they remain within their designated region. One region is Europe, in which Starlink has included 36 countries and territories. However, the firm makes clear that “Poland is not included in the Europe region”, meaning users registered in that country are not included in the Roam system. The company offered no explanation for Poland’s exclusion from the system. Some media reports have suggested that it is because terminals registered in Poland are used in Ukraine. However, Ukraine is itself not included in Starlink’s European “Roam” region. The company’s decision prompted an angry response from Polish government ministers. “I do not agree with a global technology company treating Poles worse than other Europeans,” wrote digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski on X, the social media platform owned by Musk. “If Elon Musk’s SpaceX wants to operate in Poland, benefit from the Polish market, and earn from Polish customers, it must treat them fairly and on equal terms,” he added. “That is why I have appealed to SpaceX for the urgent restoration of equal terms for the company’s Polish customers.” Nie zgadzam się, żeby globalna firma technologiczna traktowała Polki i Polaków gorzej niż innych Europejczyków. Jeżeli @SpaceX @Elon Musk chce działać w Polsce, korzystać z polskiego rynku i zarabiać na polskich klientach, musi ich traktować uczciwie i na równych zasadach. Od… — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) August 12, 2026 Meanwhile, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski revived a dispute he had with Musk last year over the provision of Starlink terminals to Ukraine during its war with Russia. That dispute saw Musk tell Sikorski to “be quiet, small man”. “Hey, Elon Musk, big man,” wrote Sikorski today on X, “stop discriminating [against] Polish users of Starlink or we might re-think paying you $50 million p.a. for your services.” The latter was a reference to the fact that Poland spends around $50 million a year to help provide Starlink services for Ukraine. World.title: Negative views of Polish-Ukrainian relations reach highest level on record in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The proportion of Poles who hold a negative view of Polish-Ukrainian relations has risen to 46%, the highest figure ever recorded by Polish state research agency CBOS. Only 12% think relations are good. By contrast, three years ago, in mid-2023, only 3% had a negative view and 64% a positive one. Meanwhile, CBOS also found that belief among Poles that reconciliation between the two neighbours, who share a difficult history, is possible is at its lowest level on record, 53%, down from 78% three years ago. The findings follow other polls showing worsening attitudes towards Ukraine and Ukrainians in Poland in recent years, and come amid an ongoing diplomatic crisis triggered by President Volodymyr Zelensky naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles in World War Two. Przekonanie o możliwości pojednania między Polakami 🇵🇱 a Ukraińcami 🇺🇦 spadło do najniższego poziomu w historii naszych pomiarów. 📙 Więcej w komunikacie #CBOS "Stosunki polsko-ukraińskie" ⤵️ https://t.co/kw2o4upY3Q#Ukraina #Ukraińcy pic.twitter.com/LItCFC3f2m — CBOS (@CBOS_Info) August 11, 2026 Relations between Poland and Ukraine improved significantly in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, as Poland welcomed millions of Ukrainian refugees and provided Kyiv with extensive military, humanitarian and diplomatic support. However, since 2023, those relations have been hit by a series of controversies over Ukrainian agricultural exports, border blockades by Polish farmers and truckers, and, above all, over the two nations’ difficult World War Two history. Among Poles who now hold a negative view of relations, CBOS also asked them who was responsible for the situation. A large majority, 65%, primarily blamed Ukraine, while only 4% said it was Poland’s fault and 28% placed responsibility on both sides. In its regular surveys since 1997, the agency has also asked Poles if they believe that reconciliation between Poles and Ukrainians is possible or not. In the early 2000s, that figure rose to a record level of 81%, and in 2023 it still stood at 78%. Now, however, it has dropped to an all-time low of 53%. There have long been tensions between Poland and Ukraine over their difficult, intertwined histories, in particular during the first half of the 20th century. In World War Two, Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, in an ethnic-cleansing operation known as the Volhynia massacres. Poland has officially recognised that episode as a genocide. However, Ukraine rejects that label and also points to the persecution of Ukrainians who lived in the interwar Polish state, as well as to massacres of Ukrainians by Polish groups during World War Two. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 Those tensions recently boiled over after Zelensky, in May this year, approved a request to rename a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”, the group that led the Volhynia massacres but is remembered positively in Ukraine for its role in fighting Moscow-imposed Soviet rule. Zelensky’s decision prompted his Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, to strip the Ukrainian president of Poland’s highest honour. While tensions have since calmed somewhat, the dispute remains unresolved. However, even before that diplomatic crisis broke out, polling showed increasingly negative attitudes in Poland towards both Ukraine and Ukrainians, who are by far the country’s largest immigrant group. In its annual survey of attitudes towards various national and ethnic groups, published in February, CBOS found that the proportion of Poles who said they disliked Ukrainians had increased by five percentage points year-on-year, to 43%. Only 29% said they liked Ukrainians. In January, CBOS reported that opposition to accepting Ukrainian refugees in Poland had risen to its highest ever level. In December 2024, a poll in Ukraine found that positive sentiment towards Poles had fallen by half in the space of two years. The proportion of Poles opposed to accepting Ukrainian refugees has reached its highest ever level of 46%, up from 3% in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion. Other recent surveys have also indicated declining sympathy towards Ukrainians among Poles https://t.co/DLPGY2ToZG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 7, 2026 Meanwhile, the number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland rose by 30% in the first half of 2026, including a number of high-profile incidents. Poland’s government has blamed increasing anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from the right-wing and far-right opposition. Last month, Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, called on “Polish politicians to stop inciting hatred against Ukrainians”. CBOS’s new study shows that attitudes towards relations with Ukraine differ significantly depending on political affiliation. Whereas 35% of supporters of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO), Poland’s main ruling party, hold a negative view of relations, that rises to 52% among voters of the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party and 81% for the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja). Among those with a negative view, 49% of KO voters blamed Poland and Ukraine equally for the situation while 10% blamed mainly Poland. By contrast, 86% of Confederation supporters and 82% of PiS supporters placed responsibility on the Ukrainian side. Demonstrations took place in 25 Polish cities on Sunday against the “growing wave of hate and violence” against Ukrainians, who are Poland’s largest immigrant group. Reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland are up 30% this year https://t.co/gGAEc6QZWT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has unveiled its first frigate to enter service in decades at a ceremony in the Baltic Sea port of Gdynia, where the ship was constructed. The development marks a major milestone in a 15 billion zloty (€3.5 billion) programme to modernise the ageing Polish navy and strengthen NATO’s maritime defences. “Poland is becoming a maritime power in the Baltic Sea,” declared Prime Minister Donald Tusk at a ceremony to name the new ship, which he attended alongside opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki in a rare show of unity. Na terenie PGZ Stoczni Wojennej w Gdyni prezydent RP Karol Nawrocki, @PremierRP @donaldtusk oraz wiceministrowie @MON_GOV_PL @magdasobkowiak i @pawelbejda uczestniczą w uroczystości chrztu pierwszej jednostki programu „Miecznik”, fregaty wielozadaniowej – przyszłego ORP Wicher. pic.twitter.com/X2ftjoKTLZ — Ministerstwo Obrony Narodowej 🇵🇱 (@MON_GOV_PL) August 12, 2026 The ORP Wicher, a medium-sized warship designed for escort, air defence and other fleet protection duties, is the first of three multi-role frigates based on Britain’s Arrowhead 140 design being built under Poland’s Miecznik programme, the largest modernisation project in the history of the Polish Navy. It is due to be launched on Thursday in a complex manoeuvre involving its transfer and controlled launch from a semi-submersible barge. Shipyard officials have described the operation as one of the most demanding engineering projects undertaken by Poland’s shipbuilding industry. The three frigates are intended to form the core of Poland’s surface fleet and will replace Poland’s two current Oliver Hazard Perry-class frigates, which were constructed in the 1970s and transferred from the US Navy in the years 2000 and 2002. Ahead of Wicher’s launch, leading Polish officials attended the naming ceremony in Gdynia, including Tusk and Nawrocki, who are normally bitter rivals but have sought to present a more united front when it comes to national defence. “There can be no arguments or disputes when it comes to our country’s security,” said Tusk, who declared that Poland was seeking to play a role in “determining not only its own future, but also the entire region and Europe”. Nawrocki, meanwhile, said that the modernisation of the Polish navy “sends a clear message that we will develop our armed forces in every theatre – on water, on land, and in the air”. Both leaders also hailed the fact that the new frigates are being built in Poland itself, helping bolster the Polish shipbuilding industry. Prezydent RP @NawrockiKn w #Gdynia: Życzę, abyście zawsze szczęśliwie wracali do portu, któremu na imię Polska. pic.twitter.com/hHia2sCZfn — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) August 12, 2026 The contract for the three frigates was signed in 2021 between Poland’s state Armament Agency (AU) and a consortium led by state-owned defence group PGZ, with British defence firm Babcock and other foreign partners also involved. The project was initially valued at about 8 billion zloty but had risen to around 15 billion zloty by the end of 2023 following amendments. Construction of the second frigate in Gdynia’s military shipyard began in May 2025, while work on the third began in April this year. The programme is scheduled to be completed by the end of 2031. Swedish defence giant Saab has signed a strategic collaboration agreement with Polish state defence group PGZ. The firms will cooperate on naval production, servicing and technology, including establishing an underwater technology centre in Poland https://t.co/dykKjMIAzX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026 The ships are more than 140 metres long and are based on Britain’s Arrowhead 140 design, developed by Babcock and adapted to Polish military requirements. The frigates will be equipped with British CAMM and CAMM-ER surface-to-air missiles, naval guns and anti-ship missiles capable of striking targets at ranges of more than 200 km. Their missions will include protecting shipping lanes and critical energy infrastructure and taking part in NATO naval groups. NATO has launched a new military operation in the Baltic Sea, an idea promoted by Poland last year in response to sabotage targeting undersea cables.@donaldtusk said at today's summit that "all signs point to Russia" being responsible for the damage https://t.co/cBPdL1fKkK — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 14, 2025 Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has embarked on a major defence procurement spree. In recent years, Poland has also increasingly oriented itself towards the Baltic region, forming closer economic, energy and military ties with allies around the sea. Last year, Poland and Sweden signed a strategic partnership on defence and economic ties. They subsequently held their first ever bilateral military exercises in the Baltic. As part of its naval modernisation programme, Poland has selected Sweden’s Saab as the supplier for three advanced A26 stealth submarines in a deal worth around €4.5 billion. World.title: Negative views of Poland’s justice system have grown under Tusk government, finds state pollster
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The proportion of Poles who negatively assess their country’s justice system has increased under the current government, despite its promises to restore the rule of law and ensure that courts function more effectively and independently. New polling by state research agency CBOS found that, in June this year, 61% of Poles had a negative view of the functioning of the justice system, up from 55% in 2022 and 51% in 2017, when the former Law and Justice (PiS) government was in power. Only 26% now positively assess the system, down from 28% in 2022 and 36% in 2017. The last time positive views were lower was in 2005 (22%). The findings come two and a half years after the current government, a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, came to power in December 2023, replacing the national-conservative PiS administration. One of Tusk’s main promises was to restore the rule of law after eight years in which PiS had implemented a series of contested judicial reforms that experts, European courts and many Polish judges had condemned as undermining the independence and functioning of the judiciary. However, Tusk’s government has struggled to implement its promised changes. In many cases, its efforts have been blocked by PiS-aligned Presidents Andrzej Duda and Karol Nawrocki or other officials appointed under the former government. But in other cases, such as with a pledge to separate the functions of justice minister and prosecutor general, which were fused by PiS in 2016, the current ruling coalition has simply not followed through on its promises. In its latest polling, CBOS found that supporters of the current opposition are most dissatisfied with the functioning of the justice system: 72% of PiS voters have a negative view, as do 71% of those who support the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja). However, even among voters of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, a majority, 53%, have a negative opinion, with only 38% holding a positive one. Interestingly, public attitudes towards judges themselves have hardly changed. Currently, 19% of Poles have a positive view towards them and 23% a negative one. That is similar to findings in 2017 (22% positive, 24% negative) and 2012 (19% positive, 23% negative). More Poles (35%) think that the rule of law has got worse under Tusk's government than believe it has improved (24%). A further 28% think there has been no change, finds a new poll https://t.co/KkiuY2vDSW — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 5, 2025 When asked to identify the greatest problems with the justice system, Poles instead often point to structural issues – that is, those that are under the control of politicians. The most commonly identified problem (chosen by 38% of respondents, who could select up to three main problems) was “prolonged proceedings” in court cases. The second biggest issue was “politicisation of courts” (18%). Only 4% said that “judges’ neglect of duty, incompetence and impunity” were among the biggest problems. However, 23% of respondents were unable to name a single major issue that the justice system faces. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 CBOS’s findings echo a number of other polls. After the first year of Tusk’s government, a survey by SW Research for the Rzeczpospolita daily found that 35% of Poles thought the rule-of-law situation had got worse, compared to only 24% who thought it had improved. Another poll by the same agency for Onet, a news website, in January this year similarly found that 40% of Poles believe the justice system has not improved under the current government, while only 33% think it has got better. In response to the latter poll, justice minister Waldemar Żurek admitted to Onet that there had been problems in addressing the rule of law. But he blamed the “hurdles [put] in our path” by Presidents Duda and Nawrocki. Opposition-aligned President @NawrockiKn has vetoed a government bill intended to reform a judicial body at the heart of Poland’s rule-of-law crisis. He argued that the measures would simply create even greater “legal chaos” https://t.co/I7FHRKIoP1 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 19, 2026 In 2024, Duda refused to sign government bills overhauling the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), which still contains judges illegitimately appointed under the former PiS administration. As a result, Tusk’s government refuses to recognise rulings issued by the TK. In February this year, Duda’s successor, Nawrocki, vetoed a government bill intended to restore the legitimacy of the National Council of the Judiciary (KRS), the body responsible for nominating judges to positions on courts. In 2017, the KRS was overhauled under PiS in a manner that rendered it illegitimate, according to multiple Polish and European court rulings. That in turn has led to doubts over the legal status of around 3,000 judges appointed by the KRS since 2017 and all the rulings issued by them. Nawrocki has also refused to swear in four new TK judges nominated by parliament this year, despite an order by the European Court of Human Rights that they be allowed to take up their positions. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
