The Armenian side did not want to agree to this. But it did not have many alternatives. If the war had continued, we would of course have suffered losses as well, but Armenia’s losses would have been much greater. Its troops were, so to speak, surrounded, and their destruction had effectively become a possibility,” the president said.

Point 9 of the November [statement], which the leaders of Armenia, Azerbaijan and Russia signed, does not refer only to a road linking Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan. It states: “All economic and transport links in the region shall be unblocked.” Moreover, the document does not contain the term “corridor”.

Aliyev went on to say that Armenia had delayed implementation of the relevant provision of the 9 November statement and had taken no practical steps to create the “Zangezur Corridor”.

According to him, Russia, the third signatory to the statement, either could not ensure its implementation or had other reasons for not doing so.

“Until August last year, this issue remained frozen. The situation changed when the United States became involved, around spring 2025. The implementation of the project known as TRIPP then began successfully,” Aliyev said, linking the Trump Route transit project to the idea of the “Zangezur Corridor”.

For several years, Baku had demanded that Armenia provide a “Zangezur Corridor” to connect Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan. The Armenian authorities repeatedly said they were ready to unblock all transport links, but refused to provide a “corridor”. The issue stemmed from the fact that Azerbaijan used the term “corridor” to refer to an extraterritorial route. Armenia, meanwhile, refused to give up sovereign control over its own territory.

On 8 August 2025, the sides reached an agreement in Washington, with the mediation of the US president, under which Armenia would provide a route while retaining its sovereign rights. The transit project therefore received the name “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” (TRIPP).

Aliyev also said that, as part of TRIPP, Azerbaijan had already prepared a project to build power transmission lines from mainland Azerbaijan to Nakhchivan through Armenian territory:

“As a result of our specialists’ survey of Armenian territory, we identified the points where the supporting pylons should be installed.”

The Azerbaijani president expressed hope that “Armenia will not delay this process”, saying it would also benefit the country.

“There is no infrastructure by that name in Armenia” — MP

Arman Yeghoyan, an MP from Armenia’s ruling Civil Contract party, said that documents signed by Armenia and Azerbaijan, including the peace agreement initialled in Washington, do not contain the term “Zangezur Corridor”.

“At the level of political narratives, you can say many things. But we are saying that there is no such concept or infrastructure with such a name or term on Armenian territory.”

The MP urged people to remember that Armenia is implementing the TRIPP project. The leaders of Armenia, Azerbaijan and the United States signed the declaration launching the project in Washington on 8 August 2025.

Comment

According to political analyst Samvel Meliksetyan, when the Azerbaijani side explains what it means by the “Zangezur Corridor”, it refers to the railway from Horadiz to Nakhchivan and then on to Turkey. He also noted that Aliyev used the name TRIPP in his interview.

The analyst said the meaning attached to the term “Zangezur Corridor” in 2022–2023 differs from what it means today. In his assessment, the project no longer involves an extraterritorial corridor:

“From a legal standpoint, TRIPP cannot become an extraterritorial corridor. But from a propaganda standpoint, Azerbaijan uses and will continue to use the term ‘Zangezur Corridor’, with some modifications.”

Meliksetyan stressed that the “Trump Route” project would proceed according to principles agreed with US mediation.

Commenting on Aliyev’s statement about building power transmission lines through Armenian territory, the political analyst said the sides were assessing the most suitable routes. He said the involvement of Azerbaijani specialists should not be interpreted as “acting on their own”.

“All the work is being carried out within the TRIPP framework. An electricity link will run through Armenian territory and connect the two parts of Azerbaijan. Azerbaijani specialists can only discuss where the link will enter Armenia from Azerbaijani territory and where it will re-enter Azerbaijan,” the expert explained.

Summing up his impressions of Aliyev’s interview, Meliksetyan said the Azerbaijani president had spoken in his characteristic style, seeking to highlight his “political achievements”.

The analyst said it was no coincidence that Aliyev focused on Nakhchivan’s economic and energy development, as well as its transport prospects. The president said Azerbaijan would finance the railway restoration itself, but also expressed interest in attracting international investors.

“Although Azerbaijan has repeatedly said that it has no financial problems, they certainly exist. Baku is trying to attract new investment to Nakhchivan through TRIPP to restore this section of the railway,” Meliksetyan said.

Yerevan reacts to Aliyev’s AzTV interview

World.title: Severe petrol shortages hit Abkhazia amid Russia fuel crisis following Ukrainian attacks — VIDEO
World.content:
Fuel shortages in Abkhazia

Severe fuel shortages continue in Abkhazia in the middle of the tourist season. All petroleum products are supplied exclusively from Russia, leaving one clear explanation: fuel shortages in Russia caused by Ukrainian drone attacks on oil and gas facilities.

The Abkhaz authorities are holding emergency talks with Moscow and say progress has been made. Reports say Russia has already arranged for 1,600 tonnes of AI-92 petrol to be sent to Abkhazia, with the first shipment expected to arrive in the coming days.

For now, petrol is available only at Rosneft and Podorozhnik filling stations.

Meanwhile, reports say petrol was supplied from territory controlled by Tbilisi

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed this:

“Amid the severe fuel shortage, a shipment was made to Abkhazia, but it was not supplied by the state, it was supplied by private businesses. If we continue to have the opportunity to ease the situation for the people living there, both Georgians and Abkhaz, we will continue to do so,” Kobakhidze said.

The Abkhaz news agency Apsnypress asked the Abkhaz government for comment following Kobakhidze’s statement and received the following response:

“Due to the circumstances caused by external factors, there is not enough motor fuel to meet Abkhazia’s needs. The authorities therefore decided to allow fuel supplies from alternative sources. Fuel market participants managed to arrange a shipment of petrol from Georgian territory. As is well known, Abkhazia also supplied fuel to Georgia from its territory in the post-war 1990s.”

Kobakhidze’s statement drew criticism from the opposition in Tbilisi. Opposition politicians said the fuel supplies to Abkhazia “could in fact mean supplies to Russian military bases”.

Economist and opposition politician Roman Gotsiridze said: “It is possible that the fuel could also have been transported to Russian territory. The company that made these deliveries will not escape sanctions.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Fuel shortages in Abkhazia

World.title: Georgian PM confirms “fuel was supplied to occupied Abkhazia from Tbilisi-controlled territory”
World.content:
Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed that petrol had been supplied from Tbilisi-controlled territory amid a severe fuel shortage in occupied Abkhazia. A journalist asked Kobakhidze about the issue.

Occupied Abkhazia has recently faced a severe fuel shortage, leading to significant restrictions on supplies of petrol and other petroleum products.

“We did not introduce this; it was introduced by private businesses,” Kobakhidze said at a briefing. He added that such measures were being taken in line with Georgia’s existing legislation, including the Law on Occupied Territories.

He said the Georgian government was ready to help ease the situation for people living in occupied Abkhazia where possible.

“If we can ease the situation, including for the population living in Abkhazia, we will do so, but we will act within the framework of the Law on Occupied Territories,” Kobakhidze said.

Kobakhidze also referred to the government’s “A Step to a Better Future” programme. According to him, it provides support for people living in the occupied territories, including the Abkhaz population.

Comment

Opposition Coalition for Change leader Nika Gvaramia reacted to Kobakhidze’s statement and called on the government to provide further clarification.

Gvaramia noted that Georgia’s Law on Occupied Territories generally prohibits direct unauthorised economic activity in Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region, although it provides certain exceptions, including for activities carried out for humanitarian purposes.

Gvaramia suggested that the fuel supplies in this case could have been intended for Russia’s “war machine”.

Nika Gvaramia: “We are dealing with an action that was presumably authorised by the government in advance. However, the public has not been told the grounds for such authorisation, or when and why it was issued.

“Given that:

— the Russian military machine is facing a severe fuel shortage, while Russian military bases are located in occupied Abkhazia;

— the Ivanishvili regime has repeatedly and deliberately stressed the need for cooperation with Russia;

— taking into account Georgia’s security and territorial integrity interests, as well as Western sanctions imposed on Russia, fuel supplies to territory controlled by Russia cannot be justified on legitimate humanitarian or socio-economic grounds,

“it becomes clear that the Ivanishvili regime has effectively acknowledged that, with its authorisation — and, in essence, by the regime itself — an action is being carried out that runs counter to Georgia’s sovereign interests. It:

violates Georgia’s Constitution;

violates Western sanctions imposed on Russia;

is aimed at assisting the Russian military machine by supplying strategically important products.”

Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

World.title: PM denies knowing about 'shag, marry, date' podcast game
World.content:
The prime minister has denied he or his office were aware a game of "shag, marry, date" would be played during a controversial podcast, despite its host saying he must have known.

On Friday Anthony Albanese repeatedly denied he or his office had any prior knowledge comedian Nikki Osborne would play the game during the Deep Bush podcast episode in which he said he would "shag" Kylie Minogue.

Mr Albanese unequivocally apologised for those remarks last month.

The prime minister has "unequivocally" apologised to Kylie Minogue for the remarks. (News Video)

On Friday Osborne claimed that not only were Mr Albanese and his staff aware of the nature of the podcast, they knew he would be asked to play "shag, marry, date" during the 20-minute conversation, which was filmed at The Lodge in June.

But Mr Albanese twice denied the claim during a later press conference.

Osborne plays the game with all of her podcast guests.

"He's watched the show, he knows my podcast," she told the Straight Talk with Mark Bouris podcast.

"He knew it was coming."

Osborne also said Mr Albanese had immediately accepted her invitation to appear on the podcast.

PM doesn't do interviews with 'arms crossed'

At an earlier press conference in Canberra on Friday Mr Albanese doubled down on his defence of the hand gestures made on the podcast while referring to a pair of melons given to him by Japan's prime minister.

He also sidestepped questions about why he did not intervene in a joke Osborne made about Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae looking like Pamela Anderson when she was carrying the melons.

Loading...

Mr Albanese did not accept responsibility for the general tone of the conversation.

"I'm responsible for my words and I note that all the words that have been written on this … none of my words have been criticised. None," he said.

Mr Albanese insisted he always gesticulated during interviews.

"There's a bit of footage of me doing interviews sitting on chairs … I don't do them with my arms crossed," he said.

"The interpretation that some have put on this is simply not correct and the Japanese ambassador has made that clear as well."

Anthony Albanese says he has already apologised for "elements" of the podcast. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Mr Albanese also avoided directly answering a question about his reflections on the appropriateness of a prime minister appearing on a podcast full of sexual innuendo.

"You can look at these things in hindsight, but I do a range of interviews," he said.

"In modern media I talk to a range of people, many of whom I don't agree with everything they say."

Apologies for 'elements' of podcast made, Albanese says

The prime minister has been under mounting pressure this week over the podcast chat, with the opposition calling on him to personally apologise to the Japanese prime minister.

Despite parliament returning from the winter break Mr Albanese had not held a press conference in Canberra until Friday and took only one question on the matter at a press conference near Newcastle.

Japan responds to Albanese's 'melon' gesture, playing down concerns Japan's government has broken its silence on Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's hand gestures while describing a gift of two melons from the Japanese prime minister, which its former ambassador claimed were a disrespectful joke about the nation's first female PM.

He stressed he had already apologised "unequivocally" for "elements" of the podcast.

Mr Albanese has not apologised for the melon interaction specifically and maintains the gestures have been misinterpreted.

Japanese officials have mostly avoided weighing into the matter, but got drawn into commenting this week after former ambassador Yamagami Shingo criticised what he considered to be a quip about the female leader's body.

Japan's current ambassador to Australia Suzuki Kazuhiro subsequently said his government was "aware of the reporting in the media".

"We have been informed by the Australian side that Prime Minister Albanese did not make the comments in the way that has been reported," he said in a statement to the ABC.

"In any case, the dinner hosted by Prime Minister Albanese during the prime minister's visit to Australia this May was held in a very relaxed atmosphere.

"We believe it helped build a personal trust relationship between the two leaders."

Mr Yamagami had a fraught relationship with Labor when he was in Canberra and was particularly angry when Penny Wong, then in opposition, urged him to pull back his public criticisms of China.

World.title: Hazard reduction burns fast-tracked as NSW faces higher fire risk
World.content:
The NSW Rural Fire Service says it has been able to "accelerate" hazard reduction burns this year, as the state prepares for a looming season of elevated fire danger.

Authorities have warned this summer is likely to bring challenging fire conditions, with above-average temperatures and below-average rainfall expected.

It comes after the Bureau of Meteorology confirmed El Niño conditions earlier this year.

NSW Rural Fire Service (RFS) Commissioner Trent Curtin said the agency had increased the amount of hazard reduction burning by 21 per cent since July last year due to improved weather conditions.

"Over recent years, we've seen reduced windows for hazard reduction burning," he said.

" We've seen increased rain, that's increased the amount of fuel across our landscapes. "

Trent Curtin says his crews are prepared for summer. (ABC News)

Mr Curtin said he was "pleased" that improved weather conditions had resulted in 124,000 hectares of hazard reduction burning across NSW in the last year.

But he said the elevated fire danger and forecast conditions were a cause for "concern".

'We recognise that this high-risk season involves sometimes storms as well as fires," Mr Curtin said.

The RFS says it has been working to speak with communities ahead of the fire season. (ABC News: Adriane Reardon)

Minister for Emergency Services Jihad Dib said the agencies would seize every opportunity to continue hazard reduction burning before the summer season.

"We've been going hard," he said.

" We can't control the weather, but what we can do is ensure that we're as best prepared as possible. "

Bushfire roundtable

Representatives from more than 15 organisations attended today's roundtable conference, including the NSW Rural Fire Service, Fire & Rescue NSW, the National Parks and Wildlife Service, and the Forestry Corporation.

A bushfire roundtable discussion happened today. (ABC News: Adriane Reardon)

Environment Minister Penny Sharpe said the collaboration between agencies was crucial ahead of a "long, hot summer".

"As we see the fires that are raging across the northern hemisphere, we know that this could be us in the coming months," she said.

"We are alert, we're not alarmed, but we are prepared."

The Australasian Fire Authorities Council (AFAC) is expected to publish its spring bushfire outlook later this month.

NSW urged to prepare early

Residents are being urged to conduct "mechanical hazard reduction" on their properties, including cleaning out gutters, trimming trees and keeping grasses low.

"We want to make sure that people are cleaning up their properties, that they're developing their bushfire survival plans," Mr Curtin said.

A hazard reduction burn in 2024 in NSW. (ABC News: Adriane Reardon)

The bushfire danger period starts on October 1 for the majority of NSW, with some northern areas of the state expected to enter the danger period earlier.

According to the Department of Primary Industries, about 37 per cent of NSW was in drought or was drought-affected at the end of July.

Agriculture Minister Tara Moriarty said her team was working with farmers to ensure they had materials on their properties to assist with firefighting, as well as plans to escape potential blazes.

Jihad Dib is urging people to be make bushfire survival plans and download the Hazards Near Me app. (ABC News)

Mr Dib said people living in urban areas should not be complacent.

"Sometimes people who live in urban areas make the mistake of thinking that bushfire won't come to them because they're living a long way away," he said.

"There's a history of embers just jumping ahead of the fire, in some cases up to 1 kilometre.

"We'd urge people, wherever they may be, to take their precautions."

World.title: SA man charged for alleged threatening messages targeting AFP
World.content:
A South Australian man has been charged for allegedly posting threatening messages online targeting the Australian Federal Police (AFP).

The AFP received information about the alleged messages posted on social media that were directed at the agency earlier this year.

Police linked the alleged posts to a 40-year-old man and executed a search warrant at an Adelaide home on Thursday.

A mobile phone was found and seized during the search, which police alleged contained messages posted over several months from social media accounts linked to the man.

The man has been charged with one count of using a carriage service to menace, harass or cause offence.

He has been granted police bail and is expected to appear in the Adelaide Magistrates Court in September.

World.title: Breathtaking finalists from the Ocean Photographer of the Year awards
World.content:
Oceans cover 71 per cent of Earth spanning 361 million square kilometres of water.

This vast, often unseen expanse is celebrated every year by a worldwide photography competition that also highlights the urgent need to protect the world's oceans.

The finalists for the 2026 Ocean Photographer of the Year competition have been revealed, showcasing the full spectrum of ocean life, from breathtaking encounters to sobering evidence of environmental damage.

Stand-out entries include an image showing a pair of orcas working in tandem to carry away a humpback whale calf, and a photo of a pygmy seahorse that is no larger than a grain of rice.

Will Harrison, the founder and director of the annual contest, said the photographs "don't just capture what's beneath the surface; they surface the stories our planet most needs us to hear".

The winners will be announced on September 11.

Here is a look at some of the finalists in their respective categories.

Wildlife

Arms of Connection captures two octopuses courting on a shallow coral reef at Lady Elliot Island, Great Barrier Reef. (Ocean Photographer of the Year: Josh Blank)

A southern elephant seal pup in the shallow rock pools on Sea Lion Island in the Falkland Islands. (Ocean Photographer of the Year: Matty Smith)

Orcas carry a humpback whale calf they successfully hunted in the Pacific Ocean off Mexico. (Ocean Photographer of the Year: Rafael Fernandez Caballero)

Fine Art

A Hingeback Cleaning Shrimp rests against a pink barrel sponge. (Ocean Photographer of the Year: Ajiex Dharma)

Five spotted eagle rays glide above a sandy seabed in Hawaii. (Ocean Photographer of the Year: John Kowitz)

Two razorbills touch beaks during the breeding season on Skomer Island, Wales. (Ocean Photographer of the Year: Rachel Bigsby)

Adventure

A free diver is surrounded by a school of sardines in the Philippines. (Ocean Photographer of the Year: Ben Yávar)

Dolphins ride the waves alongside surfers at Tamarama Beach, Sydney. (Ocean Photographer of the Year: Gergo Rugli)

Deep inside Yab Yum cave in Mexico, leaves falling from the jungle above have accumulated underwater. (Ocean Photographer of the Year: Leticia Carbajal)

Conservation (Impact)

Gentoo penguins stand beside the rusting remains of the former Hektor whaling station at Deception Island. (Ocean Photographer of the Year: Romain Barats)

A California sea lion with plastic netting around its neck is a stark reminder of the lasting impacts of plastic pollution. (Ocean Photographer of the Year: Celia Kujala)

A whale shark surrounded by divers in the Maldives reveals the overwhelming pressure that crowded wildlife tourism can place on marine animals. (Ocean Photographer of the Year: James Ferrara)

Conservation (Hope)

European lobsters are raised at the National Lobster Hatchery in Padstow, Cornwall, before being released into the wild. (Ocean Photographer of the Year: Francesca Page)

A Hawaiian monk seal rests with its week-old pup on Kaimana Beach. (Ocean Photographer of the Year: Leighton Lum)

Hawaiian green sea turtles rest together inside a sheltered sea cave on Maui at sunset. (Ocean Photographer of the Year: Leighton Lum)

Human Connection

As the tide returns across the mudflats of the Yellow Sea, shellfish collectors make their way home. (Ocean Photographer of the Year: Liu Xuzhong)

A giant oceanic sunfish glides through the clear waters of Mexico's Baja Peninsula. (Ocean Photographer of the Year: Anita Verde)

The Cornish Seal Sanctuary was the first place in the UK to provide permanent care for rescued puffins that could not survive if returned to the wild. (Ocean Photographer of the Year: Lewis Jefferies)

The Ocean: Unseen

A harlequin crab rests at the entrance of a tubular sponge, carefully tending to her cluster of orange eggs. (Ocean Photographer of the Year: Andrea Michelutti)

A pygmy seahorse, no larger than a grain of rice, clings to a delicate hydroid in the reefs of Raja Ampat, Indonesia. (Ocean Photographer of the Year: Iris Uijttewaal)

World.title: Asbestos in 320 tonnes of rubbish allegedly dumped near waterway
World.content:
A skip-bin business owner has been ordered to remove more than 320 tonnes of rubbish it allegedly illegally dumped near a "sensitive waterway" in northern New South Wales.

Officers from the state's Environment Protection Authority (EPA) and NSW Police searched a property at Stockyard Creek, north of Grafton, in May as part of an investigation into pollution.

The EPA said in a statement that laboratory analysis of samples taken from the site showed asbestos and lead contamination in the refuse piles, which also included construction waste, synthetic turf, scrap metal and furniture.

The EPA has issued a clean-up notice. (Supplied: NSW EPA)

It said drone images revealed contaminated waste had allegedly been stockpiled at the site since 2022.

Area of 'high ecological value'

The EPA issued a clean-up notice to Gardners Yamba Skip Bin Hire, which has until November 2 to comply.

"This behaviour shows a complete disregard for the environment and the Clarence Valley community," an EPA spokesperson said in a statement.

"The land is on a tributary of the Clarence River which is used for agriculture, swimming and fishing.

"[It is] an area of high ecological value, and dumping waste so close to a sensitive waterway is unacceptable."

The spokesperson said customers had paid the skip-bin company to responsibly dispose of their waste in a facility legally authorised to receive it.

"People hire skip-bin companies expecting their waste will be taken to the right place — not discarded on private land to avoid disposal costs," the EPA said.

Construction waste was amongst the rubbish the EPA discovered. (Supplied: NSW EPA)

The landowner has been ordered to provide receipts from a lawful receiver for each load of waste taken from the premises and photographs of every stockpile location once the clean-up is complete.

The ABC contacted Gardners Yamba Skip Bin Hire. The proprietor declined to comment.

World.title: Bird flu detected in second spot in Tasmania
World.content:
The H5 strain of bird flu has been detected in a crested tern on King Island, marking the second confirmed case of the virus in Tasmania.

Department of Natural Resources and Environment (NRE) Tasmania staff collected the bird from the coast near Currie on Thursday, with testing overnight confirming the H5 strain.

The bird had been reported through the Emergency Animal Disease hotline.

Late yesterday afternoon, another two crested terns from the same location were also reported. Test results are expected on Saturday.

Crested terns are common around coastal areas in Australia, including Tasmania.

If a member of the public spots a sick or dead bird, they should avoid contact with the animal, record what they see and report it to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888.

To report sick or dead birds or other animals Call the ​ Emergency Animal Disease Hotline 1800 675 888 ( 24 hours)

Emergency Animal Disease Hotline 24 hours) Use the online bird flu reporting form

Do not touch sick or dead birds or other animals. To report sick or dead wildlife (other than birds), please visit the wildlife health in Tasmania webpage.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff thanked the community and NRE staff for their swift response.

"Unfortunately, H5 bird flu's arrival in Tasmania was expected at some point given the spread across the globe and across other Australian states," he said.

"We are responding through surveillance activities across the state, including field monitoring, sample collection and testing, aerial observations and remote surveillance technology.

" We are prepared, we are taking a proactive approach, and we are responding quickly. "

What species are most at risk now that H5 bird flu is in Tasmania? Which of Tasmania's unique animal species is most at risk from H5 bird flu, and what is being done to protect them?

There have been no detections of H5 bird flu in commercial poultry operations in Tasmania.

The state's first case of the virus was confirmed on Thursday in a migratory brown skua found at Burgess Cove at Rocky Cape, on the north-west coast of Tasmania.

A member of the Parks and Wildlife Service found the carcass while undertaking coastal surveillance.

Primary Industries and Water Minister Gavin Pearce yesterday said Tasmania was "prepared to respond" and had enacted its bird flu plan.

World.title: Map finds native water mammal rakali thriving in Melbourne's waterways
World.content:
A native water mammal once dismissed as a "water rat" is quietly thriving in Melbourne's waterways, according to a new University of Melbourne mapping project.

Conservation biologist Kylie Soanes said the rakali was sighted more than 700 times across Greater Melbourne, with hotspots at the St Kilda breakwater, Southbank and Coburg Lake.

The 746 rakali sightings show various hotspots around Melbourne's waterways. (Supplied: Emily Fitzgerald)

Rakali have long been difficult to track as they slipped or chewed their way out of monitoring gear.

The new data shows how well they have adapted to city life.

They have turned up in drains, fountains, ponds and rivers across the state.

Loading...

No average rat

At first glance, a rakali can look remarkably similar to an invasive black or brown rat.

A rakali's white-tipped tail and golden belly are among the easiest ways to tell it apart from invasive rats. (iNaturalist: Snow Dennis, CC BY-NC 4.0)

But it was recognised as Australia's most underrated animal of 2025.

"People just think, 'Ew, get rid of it," Dr Soanes said.

She mentioned the switch from water rat to rakali came out of a push in the 1990s to shed the stigma that lumped native species in with pest rodents.

Australia has more than 50 native species of rats and mice, many of which were trapped as pests by people who mistook them for vermin.

The name rakali, from the language of the Ngarrindjeri people of the Lower Murray, was adopted in 1995 to give the animal a rebrand.

Dr Soanes said the rakali was hardly a pest, and did the city a favour.

"What the rakali have done, which is incredible, is they're able to take down black and brown rats in cities," she said, referencing footage from Sydney of a rakali squaring off against another rat.

" They're good at keeping the nasty rats away. "

Loading...

The footage came from University of Sydney research led by Professor Peter Banks, whose motion-sensing camera captured the first documented evidence of a rakali ambushing a black rat on the foreshore of Sydney Harbour.

Researchers say the native swimmer, which also happens to be the largest of Australia's native rodents, could offer a natural way to control introduced rats.

The rakali has been nicknamed Australia's answer to the otter.

Water-repellent fur and partially webbed hind feet allow it to thrive in water environments, while its streamlined body and long, rudder-like tail make it a strong and graceful swimmer.

Ferocious hunter with table manners

Rakali are known to be opportunistic predators and scavengers.

The native species shares the rocks at the St Kilda breakwater with the famous little penguin colony.

They mostly hunt marine invertebrates and crustaceans, but researchers have set up motion-sensing trail cameras and caught them preying on penguin eggs or chicks.

For all its skill as a predator, the rakali has a surprisingly refined side.

"They're very polite eaters," Dr Soanes said.

"You won't find them raiding your pantry".

When a rakali takes down a fish or a crayfish, it carries the meal to a flat rock or log, dissects it neatly, and leaves behind a tidy pile of bones and shells.

"That's one of the ways you can find them," Dr Soanes said.

"You'll see these really strange piles and collections of bones. And that's actually the rakali's leftovers from the night before".

Rakali thrive near water where fish make up a key part of their diet. (iNaturalist: Ron Greer, CC BY-NC 4.0)

The rakali have become precision surgeons and are one of only a handful of animals that can safely eat a cane toad, which is toxic at all stages of their life.

Rakali know how to carefully cut out the toxic glands and eat only the safe parts.

How to spot one

The mapping project is part of a University of Melbourne series called Map of the Month.

Its first project tracked vital highways of native bee species.

The most recent rakali map is published on the university's Pursuit website.

Water is the place to start for people who want to see one in the wild.

Rakali need to climb in and out to hunt, so can be found on the edges, concrete steps, stepping stones and little islands, especially where urban rivers are hard to exit.

Dr Soanes said the range of places had surprised her, from ponds in the Botanic Gardens to fountains, artificial creeks and floating litter traps.

Rakali were long assumed to be nocturnal, but sightings on the map have come in at all hours.

Dr Soanes said dawn and dusk were still the easiest times to find one when the water was calmer and their movement could be seen through ripples.

The rakali's scientific name translates to "golden-bellied water mouse". (Supplied: Australian Platypus Conservancy/ Carolyn Hall)

In the water, the main giveaway will be a white tip on its long tail.

A shimmer of orange on its tummy has earned the rakali its scientific name, Hydromys chrysogaster, or "golden-bellied water mouse".

Williamstown and Werribee had some of the highest numbers of sightings on the map, but they can be spotted as far out as Ballarat and beyond.

The project focused on Melbourne, but Dr Soanes said the animals were common across most of Australia, thinning out only in arid areas.

Rakali are found across much of Australia, inhabiting rivers, lakes, wetlands and coastal waterways. (ABC News Breakfast)

"What we're trying to do with this mapping project is show people how many amazing native animals live all around us," she said.

"I can guarantee you that if you live near a river or a creek anywhere across Melbourne, there's probably a rakali in it."

People who see a rakali are encouraged to report it to the Australian Platypus Conservancy, which tracks the species due to its shared habitat with platypuses.

Before appearing on News Breakfast, about 50 people had fed sightings into the map.

Among them were fishers who had watched rakali steal their catch and dog walkers along the creeks.

Dr Soanes said many more had been in touch since and they had been able to add an area near St Leonards due to new reports.

She said she was still waiting on her own first sighting.

World.title: Fraser officially enters Carlton coaching race after mid-year turnaround
World.content:
Josh Fraser has presented to the Carlton hierarchy after officially entering the club's process to find its full-time coach.

After a stunning run of 10 wins from 12 matches since becoming interim coach when Michael Voss left the club in May, Fraser has Carlton on the cusp of the most unlikely finals appearance.

Although he has delivered a perfect on-the-job audition, Fraser was still required to pitch to the Blues' coaching panel on Wednesday.

Loading...

Untried assistants Jaymie Graham (Fremantle), Corey Enright (St Kilda) and James Kelly (Geelong) have been through the process, with Fraser only formally putting his hand up this week.

"A fortnight ago, the club came to me and asked me to be a part of this coaching process," Fraser said today.

"Then this week, I was in a position to go back to the club and accept that offer to go through the process.

"I presented to the coaching panel this week."

At his first press conference when taking over from Voss, Fraser was adamant he was not interested in being Carlton's coach beyond this season.

But after a wildly successful 12 weeks in charge, buoyed by enthusiastic fans, Fraser could not turn down the opportunity.

"I have said, previously, that I've been ambitious to be a senior coach," Fraser said.

"I've been fortunate to be able to sit in the chair and consolidate some of my thinking; get some opportunity exposure to the role that otherwise you wouldn't normally get.

"It's been something that's been crystallising in my mind and my thoughts.

"Really confident that I'm ready to assume the responsibility of being a senior coach.

"There are 19 jobs to be a senior (AFL) coach.

"I'm as excited about this group as a lot of our Carlton supporters will be."

Joyous Blues fans were chanting "we want Fraser" as the Blues steamrolled St Kilda on Sunday night to put themselves in the box seat to earn a spot in the wildcard round.

If they defeat the Western Bulldogs, who will be without superstar captain Marcus Bontempelli on Sunday, the Blues will lock in their spot in the top 10.

It has been one of the more remarkable in-season turnarounds in AFL history, with Carlton 1-8 when Fraser took over.

"It can disrupt the club at times, when there's a significant change, like when you lose a coach, and you bring another coach in mid-season," Fraser said.

"That speaks to the culture that's been here, but I'm grateful for all the support I've had around me."

AAP

World.title: Sydney private school put dog collar and lead on student, inquiry hears
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWEducation Sydney private school put dog collar and lead on student, inquiry hears Emily Kowal August 14, 2026 — 1:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A former member of Redeemer Baptist School and Church has told a parliamentary inquiry her sister was placed in a dog collar and pulled by a lead, while another witness described the school as a “criminal gang who uses religion as camouflage”. Speaking on the second day of hearings into the North Parramatta private school and its church – which has been described as a “cult” during the inquiry – Helen Johnstone said her family joined the community in 1976 when she was a child. Helen Johnstone gives evidence at the inquiry on Friday. Sitthixay Ditthavong “Within months of joining the community, [my sisters] and I can remember feelings of discomfort, fear of adults within the community, and a sharp change in our lives,” she said. “It was a change for the worse.” Johnstone told the inquiry her older sister was viewed as a “rebel” and subjected to regular abuse.



“I witnessed her experience some awful treatment, including a dog collar being placed on her neck and being pulled around by a dog lead,” Johnstone told the inquiry. She told the inquiry she witnessed her sister being held underwater and thrown into a “filthy duck pond”, and “shunned, shamed and humiliated routinely”. Johnstone also detailed the abuse of her foster brother, an Indigenous boy she believes may have been part of the Stolen Generation. She recalled her father belting the boy while he lay curled in the fetal position. “He came into a home where learning consisted of punishment,” she recalled. “He was routinely hit and belted for not eating, getting homework answers wrong, soiling his pants or his bed, etcetera.” Witnesses have told the inquiry corporal punishment was common within the church until as late as 2005.



“Sadly, he’s still in the community today and was subsequently adopted into the family. I’d like the circumstances around his arrival investigated,” said Johnstone. The inquiry also heard sweeping allegations of financial misconduct. Graeme Glossop gives evidence at the parliamentary inquiry on Friday. Sitthixay Ditthavong Accountant Graeme Glossop, who previously took on the school in 2004, accused the institution of operating a “scheme of arrangement designed to avoid taxation.” He told the inquiry the school and church were a “criminal gang who uses religion as a camouflage” and were “stealing government money”.



He said the school and church operate a “scheme of arrangement designed to avoid taxation,” and that the school and church were not paying fringe benefits tax. Glossop said the church and school community “had a disease”. “It’s like a cancer going through that whole community, and people are getting affected by it,” he said. Related Investigation

Private schools Redeemer Baptist School investigation Former member Barney Jones testified the institution enjoyed “a series of beneficial loopholes” used to amass wealth, including at least 40 properties valued at a minimum of $140 million. Because volunteers are paid low stipends, Jones said the institution avoids payroll tax, GST, capital gains tax, fringe benefits tax, stamp duty, and HECS repayments. He highlighted what he called “double-dipping” into government funds, claiming members accessed Centrelink benefits to support their lifestyles due to their artificially low incomes.



Holding up a 102-page dossier documenting alleged legislative breaches and employment practices, Jones said he had raised the alarm with the Board of Studies (now the NSW Education Standards Authority) in 2005, but his warnings “fell on deaf ears”. NESA told the inquiry on Monday it was investigating the school under section 83C of the Education Act, which requires non-government schools to operate on a not-for-profit basis to remain eligible for government funding. Redeemer leader and principal Jonathan Cannon was invited to attend the inquiry, but headmaster and elder Russell Bailey declined, citing concerns over procedural fairness. Related Article Updated

Education ‘Fire and brimstone on acid’: Inside a Sydney private school’s control tactics In a written response, Bailey argued the inquiry was unfairly targeting the school, maintaining the school and church were two separate legal entities. Bailey said the school’s 535 students had now been labelled as “members of a cult, despite not even being members of the Church (which is also not a cult)”.



“The inquiry should be ashamed of itself for that baseless aspersion,” Bailey wrote. Both Jones and Johnstone told the inquiry there was “absolutely no difference between school and church.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Complainant ‘C’ felt ‘uncomfortable’ in bedroom at former 2GB broadcaster’s farm, court told
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day eight of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. My colleagues Clare Sibthorpe and Harriet Alexander will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

The NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court building will hear today from complainant “C”, the second of six men who have accused the former 2GB host of unwanted touching and kissing over a 20-year period.

Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Friday. Peter Rae

Jones denies the claims and is entitled to the presumption of innocence.

In the first week of the trial, the court heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted “J”, a young athlete, starting with unwanted kissing and progressing to touching. On the Crown’s case, “J” was aged between 17 and 21 at the time of the nine alleged indecent assaults.

The defence case is that the alleged incidents didn’t happen.

This week, the older brother of “J” and the complainant’s ex-girlfriend gave evidence about what they said he told them about the alleged assaults, and his mother and his former coach gave evidence yesterday.

His mother testified that “J” initially told her that Jones had not touched him, before telling her the following year that he had lied. She said that she was in shock when “J” made the disclosure, and she told her son she should have protected him.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men without their consent between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him.

Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, said during her opening address to the court that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Young Talent Time legend Johnny Young dies aged 79
World.content:
Updated CultureTV & radioVale Young Talent Time legend Johnny Young dies aged 79 Chris Hook Updated August 14, 2026 — 1:15pm ,first published 11:31am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former Young Talent Time host Johnny Young has died aged 79, his family announced on Friday morning. Young’s family said he had died following a “brief battle with pancreatic cancer”. Musician Johnny Young at his home in Perth, Western Australia, in 2018. Tony McDonough Although he was best known for his work on the children’s talent show Young Talent Time, which spawned the careers of stars such as Dannii Minogue, Tina Arena and Debra Byrne, Young was also a singer-songwriter in his own right, penning hits such as The Real Thing for Russell Morris and Smiley for Ronnie Burns. Born Johnny de Jong in The Netherlands in 1947, the youngest of four children, Young migrated with his family to Australia following World War II and settled in Perth, where he grew up in the suburb of Kalamunda.



Loading After working as a trainee disc jockey in his late teens, Young scored a job as the host of Channel 7 Perth’s pop music show Club Seventeen, where he met various pop stars and began writing and performing himself. After a brief period in London, Young returned to Australia and launched Young Talent Time in 1971. The show would become appointment viewing for families across the country and ran until 1988. Young with Dannii Minogue (left) and Lorena Novoa in 1987. The show featured a core group of performers doing well-known pop songs, as well as hopeful youngsters competing in a talent show, and making household names of Minogue (long before Kylie came to fame) and Arena, among others. Each week, Young would sign off by singing The Beatles’ All My Loving, a version of which he had recorded in 1967.



Related Article Obituaries There was more to Johnny Young than Young Talent Time. He also wrote one of Australia’s biggest hit songs Earlier this month, Arena paid tribute to Young’s guidance in comments to this masthead. “He’s very much like a father figure; he wanted me to be as protected as I possibly could,” she said. “There were times when he said, ‘Be careful, I don’t like that person’ – and he was right. He taught me about discernment as a very little girl. I wasn’t able to intellectualise the term back then, but it became much clearer down the track.” In 1990, Young was inducted into the Logies Hall of Fame. In 2010, Arena returned to Australia from her Paris base to induct Young into the ARIA Hall of Fame.



“I don’t think I would ever have had the beauty and the diversity of career that I’ve had without my apprenticeship on TV,” Arena said at the induction. Arena also performed Young’s Here Comes the Star, which was a hit in 1969 in Australia for Ross D Wylie and in Britain for Herman’s Hermits. Following news of his death, Beven Addinsall, who joined Young Talent Time at the age of 11, paid tribute to Young on Instagram, sharing a photo of himself alongside Young on a red carpet. “Rest in peace, my dear friend,” the caption read.

World.title: Panthers close in on massive re-signing but mystery remains over Cleary
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Panthers close in on massive re-signing but mystery remains over Cleary Dan Walsh August 14, 2026 — 1:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Penrith are closing in on the biggest piece of their multi-million dollar retention puzzle yet, with co-captain Isaah Yeo expected to recommit to the club before the finals. While champion halfback Nathan Cleary is still yet to sit down with Panthers officials or his management to discuss his future, extension talks with Yeo progressed positively this week as he rehabilitates his pectoral injury. Loading Multiple sources speaking on the condition of anonymity due to the confidential nature of negotiations expect Yeo’s future to be finalised over the last few rounds of the regular season. The Australian, NSW Origin and four-time premiership-winning Panthers skipper ranks behind only Cleary in Penrith’s roster priorities, and has long been considered the most likely of their out-and-out stars to stay put.



The terms of Penrith’s latest offer to Yeo, 31, are unclear. But the prospect of being a one-club player with a multi-year deal holds obvious appeal to Yeo, who is on track to pass the fabled 300-game milestone next season. In another piece of good news for the Panthers, fellow back-rower Isaiah Papalii has told the club he will take up a new deal beyond 2027. Injured Panthers captain Isaah Yeo. NRL Imagery As reported by this masthead on Wednesday, centre Paul Alamoti is also set to re-sign as he awaits scan results on a hamstring injury suffered late against the Roosters in Thursday night’s enthralling 12-6 loss. Alamoti has already been scratched for next week’s clash against Melbourne. Left centre Izack Tago is expected to switch to the opposite side in Alamoti’s place against the Storm, with Casey McLean pushing to return from a broken hand next Thursday.



Blaize Talagi and Jack Cole are other options out wide. The Panthers will also have greater clarity on Yeo’s recovery timeframe and chances of playing again this year as swelling continues to reduce in his pec. The prospect of Yeo leading Penrith’s retention drive comes as the club remains comfortable with Cleary holding fire on his future. The game’s best player had planned to address negotiations once his NSW Origin series had wrapped up, but is still yet to confirm, privately or publicly, whether he wants to re-sign before the November 1 free-agency date or test his value on the open market.



Sources close to the champion No.7 have indicated the lack of clarity does not necessarily point to an eventual exit from Penrith, nor that talks will be delayed until the end of the Panthers season. Related Article NRL 2026 Daly Cherry-Evans didn’t want talk of his future to take the gloss off Roosters’ win. So he waited seven hours Coach and father Ivan, who will be replaced by assistant Peter Wallace at the end of 2027, admitted this week that rival NRL clubs, including Penrith, simply cannot compete with the tax-free dollars on offer from expansion outfit PNG Chiefs. The Chiefs have made Cleary their halfback priority after signing teammate and star winger Brian To’o at the start of the week. Veteran prop Moses Leota, back-rower Liam Martin and Talagi are Penrith’s next most notable names coming off-contract in 2027. Leota, who was granted a brief window to test his market value earlier this year, is prepared to re-sign for slightly less than the $900,000 his management believes he can earn elsewhere.

World.title: This unsettling novel will stay with you long after you finish it
World.content:
CultureBooksReview This unsettling novel will stay with you long after you finish it Declan Fry August 14, 2026 — 1:13pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

You sit down to eat breakfast. The sun is shining. The sky is blue. You pick up your spoon. You eat scalpels. Maggots. The maggots squirm upon your tongue. You swallow them down. For years – maybe since the day you were born – life has been like this. Some days less. Some days more. By now you barely even notice. What would you do? Would you care? That is the question Maria Stepanova’s novel asks. Written in Germany after the author was exiled from her native Russia, The Disappearing Act was published in 2024 as Фокус, pronounced “focus” and meaning “trick” or “sleight of hand”. It is about a woman, M, whose sense of self is haunted by the biggest trickster of all, “the beast”. Russian writer Maria Stepanova. Europa Press via Getty Images Waging war upon a less powerful neighbour, “the beast” touches “everyone who had ever lived in the land where she was born”. Like God and death, the beast is inescapable.



Sound like Putin’s Russia? Maybe. But the beast is bigger than that. The beast is life’s violent contour. The force of uncontained power. How it can nestle inside one’s language, one’s voice, one’s being. Photo: Stepanova’s decision to anonymise the novel’s detail feels like defiance. State censors, if not readers themselves, often hunger for names. Wanna see me in M? Stepanova seems to ask. That’s your prerogative. M does not want to be called upon to account for the beast’s whims and dispositions. She calls herself a “Russian novelist” and is hailed as one by certain occasions – like the literary festival she is on her way to attend in an unnamed European town. But she is uncomfortable identifying as a novelist. Stranded before she can arrive at the festival, she imagines herself like the Soviet emigrant in Nabokov’s tale The Visit to the Museum, suddenly transported to Leningrad. She senses that, so long as others are destroyed by the beast, she cannot be saved. Named for the industrial waste caused by lead mining – pollution that accelerated rapidly in Stalin’s Russia – the American noise rock band Chat Pile captures the anguish M feels: “From the time you were born it was over.” Stranded, M leaves her old life behind. She feels her inner self cease “banging itself against the walls in search of an exit”. Discarding nearly everything – her suitcase, phone, copies of the book she is promoting, even her passport and name – she wonders if “the only way to get rid of the beast was to get rid of oneself”.



Her decision to give up her old life could be read as renewal. Or obliteration. Encountering strangers – including a travelling circus – M fantasises about escape from the confusion of her old life. But the collective, the crowd, is not what it appears: among them, people may hold authority and never be made accountable. Think, in Australia, of Nauru. Think of the collective theft of land that gave birth to the nation. Tellingly, M confuses the name of her hotel – Petuh – with Petukh, those Russian prisoners reduced to being “common prey” so that “anyone henceforth could use him as and when they wanted”. She sees their heads plunged deep in the excrement of their fellow prisoners, polluted by shared waste. Like the linguist in Paul Bowles’ 1945 story A Distant Episode – brutalised, his tongue and connection to the world he knew severed by forces beyond his control – M’s desire for innocence, if not something stronger, compels her to seek anonymity among those with whom she shares no linguistic or cultural connection. In this respect, the book recalls authors like Peter Handke writing about the “inspired namelessness” of non-verbal communication. Stepanova even references Wim Wenders’ film Wings of Desire, which Handke helped write. I was also reminded of another German-language author, Yoko Tawada, whose characters, dislocated from linguistic or social attachments, seek freedom in chance encounters and imaginative play. Editor's pick Literature The 3000-year-old poem Australians suddenly can’t get enough of Yet imaginative escape is never entirely innocent. Without vigilance, it can become an act of looking away. Like her masterly In Memory of Memory (2021), Stepanova asks us: if hell is built gradually, little by little, day by day, by the time anyone notices, will you be covered in blood? The beast is part of ordinary life. Yet ordinariness does not guarantee you protection. Ordinary life is always on the verge of violation. We draw apart the curtains, never knowing if a landscape or hellscape might greet us. The Disappearing Act, like its protagonist – a woman with a suitcase but nowhere to go, a phone but no one to call, belongings but no plans to stay – is itinerant, whimsical, disturbing, brutal and, yes, beautiful. It informs us that, sometimes, it is better to destroy yourself than to carry on as if everything were the same. It is better to stop believing the world you live in is the same one you once knew. Hell may be close but the void is even closer – and it’s when the flames burn brightest that we learn what it means to live.



The Disappearing Act by Maria Stepanova, translated by Sasha Dugdale, is published by Fitzcarraldo ($30). The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Accelerate Resources opens second front with rich WA manganese play
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Accelerate Resources opens second front with rich WA manganese play Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Andrew Todd August 14, 2026 — 1:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There are moments in an exploration company’s life that can define its future, where a persistent geological hunch pays off and a project suddenly shifts from being a line item in a portfolio to a potential company-maker. For Accelerate Resources, that moment appears to have arrived at its dual-commodity portfolio in Western Australia. While the company has been consistently revealing shallow gold prospects in the world-class Eastern Goldfields, the sheer scale and grade of the manganese mineralisation it has uncovered at its Woodie Woodie North manganese project in the Pilbara hints at a large-scale system for Accelerate and elevated the junior into the class of both a critical minerals and precious metals player. Outcropping manganese at Accelerate Resources’ Woodie Woodie North project is located just 55km north of Consolidated Minerals’ long-running Woodie Woodie manganese mine in the Pilbara. The Woodie Woodie North project is strategically located in one of Australia’s rarest manganese provinces. It sits just 55 kilometres north of Consolidated Minerals’ operating Woodie Woodie mine - mainland Australia’s only and longest-running producer of high-grade manganese ore. Being on the doorstep of a major, multi-decade mining operation is an enviable position for any explorer but more importantly, the at-surface geology doesn’t respect tenement boundaries. The company says it now appears to be sitting on a significant extension of the same mineralised system that has made its neighbour a globally significant producer. This latest discovery by Accelerate now suggests there is plenty more where that came from.



‘We have now mapped more than 200 manganese outcrops and occurrences defining around 9.7 hectares of mineralised manganese exposure.’ Accelerate Resources chief executive officer Luke Meter The company says its project covers a substantial 432-square-kilometres of highly prospective ground, incorporating seven mapped, large-scale manganese corridors that stretch over a combined 42km of strike. It’s a district-scale footprint and the early-stage work is definitely hinting at district-scale potential. Recent detailed mapping and LiDAR surveys have identified more than 200 individual manganese outcrops across the project’s Gingarrigan-El Largo area, defining a combined mineralised footprint of almost 10 hectares at surface. And the grades are nothing short of spectacular. Rock chip sampling from the newly defined Rancor and Wampa prospects has returned grades as high as 58.4 per cent manganese, with a slew of other impressive hits including 57.6 per cent, 55.6 per cent - for context Australia’s two operating mines run a resource around 40 per cent manganese.



The outcropping grades look bang on for direct-shipping ore (DSO) grades. DSO is the holy grail for bulk commodity miners, as it means the ore is high-grade enough to be dug up and shipped directly to customers with minimal processing, dramatically slashing both capital and operating costs. And with the project nestled just 260km from Port Hedland and 55km north of Consolidated Minerals’ Woodie Woodie infrastructure, there is plenty of promise for a DSO scenario. The company’s Rancor prospect alone is now defined by a one-hectare manganese outcrop with an apparent thickness of up to 10 metres. With heritage surveys now complete, the company is gearing up for a maiden reverse-circulation drilling program to test these exceptional surface targets at depth. Accelerate Resources chief executive officer Luke Meter said: “The scale of the surface manganese at Gingarrigan and El Largo is becoming increasingly clear. We have now mapped more than 200 manganese outcrops and occurrences defining around 9.7 hectares of mineralised manganese exposure, with several of the larger bodies showing a close relationship to the structural architecture highlighted by the gravity survey.” Accelerate says the project already boasts a 1.2 million tonne resource grading 19.1 per cent manganese, with an exploration target of between 5.3 and 10.7 million tonnes at 10 to 19 per cent in the books. Following the definition of 200 plus outcropping discoveries, the exploration target would look to be just tip of the iceberg at Gingarrigan and El Largo, with plenty more upside now on the table for the explorer. While manganese remains a critical and irreplaceable ingredient in steelmaking, its future is also being supercharged by the electric vehicle revolution. It is a key component in nickel-manganese-cobalt batteries and is crucial to the emerging, lower-cost battery chemistries like lithium-manganese-iron-phosphate (LMFP), which are being rapidly being adopted by industry giants like CATL and BYD.



A drill rig on site at Accelerate Resources’ latest Spencers gold discovery outside Kalgoorlie in WA. But while the manganese story has deservedly grabbed the spotlight, Accelerate has not taken its eye off its original precious prize. The company’s flagship Balagundi project continues to turn up high-grade gold discoveries in the prime real estate of WA’s Eastern Goldfields. Just 15km east of Kalgoorlie, the project sits in the heartland of Australian gold mining, putting Accelerate in the shadow of the headframes of the 70-million-ounce Super Pit and neighbouring the 6-million-ounce-plus Kanowna Belle mine. The project’s proximity to a host of hungry, third-party processing mills means even a modest-sized discovery in today’s gold price environment can be highly economic, offering several low-capital pathways to potential production that has served countless goldfields juniors well in recent years. Accelerate recently doubled its footprint at Balagundi insisting a broader gold system is emerging within its gold corridors, following a second shallow gold discovery at its Spencers prospect, where shallow drilling returned a thick 28-metre hit grading 1.01 grams per tonne gold from just 36m. The prospect lies within a granted mining lease at Balagundi and has already been defined over 300m of strike, providing a clear target for fast-tracked production ounces. Spencers sits at just one of a raft of gold prospects along the company’s Paris Gift gold trend, which cuts through its prime Kalgoorlie tenure. Add in its Paris Gift, Mt Bellew, Fluffy and Delta prospects and the company has more than its fair share of long ignored, shallow gold prospects to keep it busy in the goldfields.



Accelerate’s classic Kalgoorlie gold play has a clear, low-cost path to potential production and now sits right alongside a potentially company-making, critical minerals project with jaw-dropping grades in an emerging manganese district. For Accelerate, the exploration journey has led to two distinct destinations. One is paved with the golden promise of the Eastern Goldfields, the other with the industrial muscle of Pilbara manganese. With drilling set to begin on its high-grade manganese targets, the market may not have to wait long to see which path delivers first. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? World.title: Kuniko drilling flags NSW resource growth
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Kuniko drilling flags NSW resource growth Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward August 14, 2026 — 1:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A resource upgrade looks to be on the cards for Kuniko Limited at its Commonwealth-Silica Hill project after a recently completed phase-two drilling campaign hit visible sulphides outside the existing resource block model. Two diamond holes totalling 724m successfully intersected zones of alteration and sulphide-bearing veins providing an encouraging start to the company’s broader exploration program, designed to build on a previous bonanza-grade discovery at the project which sits in the heart of NSW’s prolific Lachlan Fold Belt. Kuniko Limited’s Commonwealth gold-silver project in NSW where it recently uncovered a stunning bonanza-grade discovery. The early results offer compelling validation for the company which recently took the reins of the project after securing a controlling 51 per cent stake from Impact Minerals more than a year ahead of schedule. Now in the driver’s seat, Kuniko is aiming to prove its belief that the project could host a far larger district-scale mineral system than previously thought. The project is situated 100 kilometres north of Orange in what is considered elephant country for mineral explorers with the region populated by world-class operations, including Newmont’s Cadia-Ridgeway mine and Evolution Mining’s Cowal and Northparkes projects. Kuniko’s ground also lies along-trend from Alkane Resources’ massive Boda-Kaiser porphyry copper-gold discovery.



‘The potential for these extensions to add scale and high-grade mineralisation to Silica Hill is an important catalyst for Kuniko.’ Kuniko Limited managing director Maja McGuire Commonwealth contains two distinct deposits located just 200m from each other. The first, Commonwealth Main, is a precious-metals-rich volcanogenic massive sulphide (VMS) system. The second, Silica Hill, is a high-grade epithermal silver-gold system and is the focus of the current drilling. A previous historical JORC-inferred resource outlined by Impact Minerals tallied up 88,800 ounces of gold and 3.3 million ounces of silver with the system remaining open along strike and at depth. Kuniko’s latest drilling was designed to test continuity around a stunning phase-one discovery hole. That initial hole returned a remarkable intercept of 0.5 metres grading an eye-watering 347 grams per tonne gold (g/t) equivalent which included a coffee spitting 20,603g/t silver, or more than 2 per cent. The first of the new holes was drilled 60m down-dip of that discovery while the second was collared about 40m up-dip. Kuniko says both holes hit their targets intersecting alteration and sulphide-bearing stringer and stockwork veining consistent with the mineralisation seen in the original discovery hole. Kuniko Limited managing director Maja McGuire said: “The first two holes of our Phase 2 drilling program have delivered an encouraging start at Silica Hill, with both holes intersecting the targeted zones of alteration, disseminated sulphides and stringer-vein mineralisation. Importantly, drilling has now demonstrated approximately 100m of continuity across CMKNI007, CMKNI004 and CMKNI008, with all three holes located outside the existing mineralised block model. This provides a compelling opportunity to expand the known Silica Hill mineralised footprint.”



Together, the discovery hole and the two new step-out holes demonstrate 100m of up-dip to down-dip continuity in the Silica Hill mineralised system. Notably, all three lie outside the project’s existing mineralised block model highlighting the potential for the company to significantly expand the resource footprint ahead of a planned mineral resource estimate update by December. Visual logging of the core from the down-dip hole identified an initial zone of sulphide-bearing veining from about 205m downhole, followed by a broader 55m-wide zone of stringer and stockwork veining from 260m. The up-dip hole intersected a 45m-wide zone of sulphide-bearing stringer and stockwork veining from about 280m. Kuniko has put the obligatory cautionary note on visual observations however, the presence of sulphides is potentially the first sign that geologists are onto something with promise. Additionally, drilling is ongoing at Main Shaft and Commonwealth South along with further regional work to define more targets. Having gone from being a guest at the party to now running the show, Kuniko is now wasting no time in testing the scale of its flagship asset. With the drill bit confirming the geological model and extending a known high-grade system, all eyes will be on the pending assays to see just how big this discovery, bang in the heart of elephant country, might become.
