World.title: Massive Attack are note perfect in a show where music takes a back seat
World.content:
Key points MUSIC: Massive Attack tour Australia for the first time in 16 years

THEATRE: Break of Day at Malthouse is a remarkable new play

MUSIC: Jaime Martín conducts a five-star performance of Mahler 6

DANCE: Echo Mapping is an intimate solo dance performance that is also a concert

MUSIC

Massive Attack ★★★★★

Rod Laver Arena, August 11 Since forming in 1988, Massive Attack has made a couple of the greatest albums of all time and nudged the top of the pop charts. They also have a decades-long history of anti-war and human rights advocacy, most recently for Palestine. Grant Marshall of Massive Attack performs on stage in Melbourne. Richard Clifford They were recently detained in, and then banned from, Singapore after expressing solidarity and unfurling a Palestinian flag on stage – contravening a ban on displaying foreign flags. This was just prior to arriving in Australia, home of our own cool and normal discourse. Now that we’ve addressed the elephant in the room, we can move past the ugly business of politics and talk about how much fun we had at the Massive Attack show.



Just joking! Of course that’s not what happened! Anyone hoping for an uncomplicated night of nostalgia at the paranoia factory would have walked away disappointed. Likely crawled away, with ears, eyes, and brain bleeding. Music takes a back seat on this tour. The players, including core members Robert “3D” Del Naja and Grant “Daddy G” Marshall, perform mostly in the shadows, ceding the floor to a visual experience that’s equally mesmerising and assaultive. Massive Attack on stage at Rod Laver Arena. Richard Clifford As the first bars land, morbid statistics cascade across the screen: children killed by guns in the US this year, in various wars. It rarely gets more cheerful. AI surveillance, hate speech, influencers (Australian wellness grifters get a shout-out), aspiring fascists, conspiracy theories, tax havens, K-pop dance routines juxtaposed with government massacre. Whenever the audience is threatened with a good time, it’s followed by apparently limitless footage of war crimes committed by some of Australia’s allies.



A nightmarish tour of the internet gives way to a map of Palantir’s chokehold on the planet, then to the Congolese children mining the minerals behind it. Cumulatively an overwhelming panorama of the digital psychosis engulfing the world, soundtracked by Massive Attack. The band itself? Note perfect. Especially when feature artists emerge from the shadows to lend themselves to tracks. Massive Attack is note perfect in their first Melbourne performance in 16 years. Richard Clifford Roots reggae singer Horace Andy laces Hymn of the Big Wheel with gravitas. Deborah Miller sings Shara Nelson’s parts on Safe from Harm with such transcendent beauty and power the crowd roars with every high note. Former Cocteau Twin Elizabeth Fraser’s ethereal, haunting voice is undiminished, both on the Tim Buckley cover Song to The Siren and show closer Teardrop. A panacea of a song at any time, but when the screens finally go dark and politics leaves the room for three minutes, it tips towards the sublime.

Reviewed by Liam Pieper



THEATRE

Break of Day ★★★★

Malthouse Theatre, until August 29 Over the last few decades, much of our most important drama has laid siege to the myth of Australian egalitarianism. That’s true across all domains of social prejudice and marginalisation – gender, race, sexual orientation, and so on. Yet, all of these can intersect with economic disadvantage, and as the Gini coefficient continues to rise, so too does theatre that refuses to look away from the have-nots. Kat Stewart and Sherry-Lee Watson play mother and daughter. Pia Johnson Steve Rodgers joins such internationally lauded playwrights as Patricia Cornelius and Daniel Keene in focusing with great human intensity on a collective blind spot: those living at the wrong end of increasing wealth and income inequality. Break of Day is set in the fictional Burra Creek – an impoverished exurb of a satellite city, where single mum Pam (Kat Stewart) works night shift at an Amazon-style warehouse. We first see her walking home from work, through a monologue that touches on her invisibility, but which also highlights an opposite risk. One doco about Burra Creek was a voyeuristic slide into poverty porn: it smeared the community as all “booze an’ meth an’ KFC” and not much else.



Pam’s daughter Rae (Sherry-Lee Watson) is in year 12 at high school. She’s bright enough for university (and the social mobility that goes with it), and Pam is desperate to ensure that she seizes the opportunity. The deck is stacked against Rae: her obnoxious alcoholic grandfather (Richard Piper) descends on their one-bedroom flat, and her computer packs up while she’s trying to write an essay about Nabokov’s Lolita. Plus, there’s the teenage distraction of first love with charismatic Jed (Theo Clarke), who wants to be an actor. Break of Day is a remarkable new play. Pia Johnson With Rae’s future at stake, Pam will risk everything – including her lifelong friendship with her work supervisor Sanjeeva (Chum Ehelepola) – to help her daughter make the grade. Sarah Goodes’ sensitive direction – and the layered ironies and intimacies of Rodgers’ brilliantly overheard script – underpin some wonderful performances.



Kat Stewart takes a scene or two to descend the social ladder and work herself into potty-mouthed precision, but once she does, it’s a compelling portrayal of a woman so rich in the one thing money can’t buy that she’s willing to collude in her own debasement. (Pam’s desperate love is also an existential evasion: who will she be once her daughter flies the coop?) More debased still is Piper as the abusive grandfather. It’s a piteous, fearlessly awful performance, and a sign of the playwright’s gift for dramatic irony that he allows this character to announce the crux of the issue – Thinks she’s so f---in’ special. She’s got rights! Everyone

now, everyone’s got rights, all these f---in’ rights! -

Except for poor people. Nothin’ people! Poor f---in’ nothin’

people have still got nothin’... – after a despicable misogynist rant aimed at his granddaughter. That said, bleakness doesn’t reign in this play, largely thanks to two younger actors stealing the show. You can’t look away from either of them – not the extraordinary ferocity and tenderness that Watson brings to the precocious Rae, nor Clarke’s magnetism and ease as an Aboriginal boy who’s a born performer.



(One highlight sees Jed practising a Caliban speech from The Tempest to soothe himself as he’s mucking out a toilet. The scene floored me, and there isn’t much I wouldn’t do to see an actor as talented as Clarke perform Shakespeare.) Related Article Stage You probably never wonder who’s packing your parcels. Perhaps you will now Delight isn’t restricted to the young: Ehelepola paints an overlooked character in deft strokes – a mild-mannered and restrained persona, trauma under the mask, and, crucially, a moment of unexpected joy. Anna Cordingley’s set is a revolving monument to Pam’s home and workplace and the liminal spaces between them. It frames the actors well and creates a powerfully circular momentum, though you do wonder about the cost. Will such maximalism push ticket prices up so that the poor won’t be able to afford to attend the show? It’s a troubling to think that they may be excluded from the world premiere season of this remarkable new play.

Reviewed by Cameron Woodhead



MUSIC

Jaime Conducts Mahler 6 ★★★★★

Melbourne Symphony Orchestra, Hamer Hall, August 13 Mahler’s Symphony No. 6 is a work of stunning clairvoyance. Although happy at the time, Mahler conjured up a hero hounded by death who is ultimately felled by three fateful blows. Five years after the premiere, Mahler was dead at the age 50, having indeed suffered three blows: forced resignation from the Vienna Opera, the death of his young daughter, and the diagnosis of fatal heart disease. Jaime Martín conducts the MSO in Mahler 6 Laura Manariti Under chief conductor Jaime Martín, the Melbourne Symphony brought vibrant urgency to the rich musical and psychological textures of this troubled masterpiece. Largely balancing the need for observing Mahler’s minutely detailed writing for huge forces with broader dramatic imperatives, Martín revealed Mahler’s hero to be a deeply complex character.



In driving the opening death march with such implacability, Martín created a sense of suffocating imprisonment that meant the second theme (intended to evoke Mahler’s wife) was not so much a lyrical contrast as a reminder of the shortness of happiness. Moments of yearning for lost innocence were beautifully captured by luxuriant string tone and the distant ringing of cowbells in the Andante (placed as the second movement according to Mahler’s final wishes) only to become torturous in the sinister scherzo, where elements of fear, regret and self-doubt re-emerged. Martín respected Mahler’s superstitious omission of the last of three devastating hammer blows in the finale, even though there is a strong musical case for its reinstatement. Demonstrating huge commitment, the orchestra brought this colossal emotional maelstrom to a devastating close. Cameos by concertmaster Natalie Chee and principal horn Nicolas Fleury were indicative of the orchestra’s superlative playing throughout. Yorta Yorta composer James Henry’s Freshwater Saltwater was a skilfully orchestrated prelude, using the blending of fresh and salt water in the Yarra as an analogy for the co-existence of cultures both here and in Mahler’s Vienna.

Reviewed by Tony Way



DANCE

Echo Mapping ★★★★

The Substation, Newport, until August 15 Echo Mapping, an intimate solo dance performance that is also a concert, has the cool austerity and high-art seriousness of a late-night gallery event. It’s therefore perfectly at home at the Substation, amid the attractively exposed concrete, iron and brickwork. Composer Jack Prest and dancer Azzam Mohamed perform at The Substation. Sarah Walker The space is shared by dancer Azzam Mohamed and composer Jack Prest, with the latter stationed behind a music desk. Both appear in plain T-shirts and nondescript trousers. Staged in the round with the house lights raised, the performance has a refreshing immediacy. It begins in silence, with Mohamed holding a sequence of still poses. Then Prest offers a clean, affirmative three-note trumpet figure. Momentum gathers rapidly: Mohamed whoops and shouts, stamps out a rhythm, then breaks into a compulsively repeated jazz-dance phrase.



When this subsides, Mohamed again draws his extremities inward. He clenches. His hands twist into fantastic shapes around his head. Then loosens himself, more gradually, finding elasticity through a recurring motif in which his hands, arms and shoulders knead the space before him. Related Article Stage Want intimate conversations with strangers in the night? Walk this way Prest builds his score from simple inputs, accumulating layers and effects while also incorporating snatches of tunes supplied by Mohamed. The dancer maps this changing sonic terrain through variations of joy and languor, hips rocking and dipping as he spirals around the room. The show has an improvised sort of energy and yet as it winds down, returning to the sonorous minimalism of its beginnings, the logic of its development becomes apparent. Mohamed seems to replay the performance in reverse, retracing its gestures until, once again, all becomes still. Perhaps the most interesting detail in Echo Mapping is the relationship between the artists: throughout the performance they treat each other with a gentle but undemonstrative masculine regard – inhabiting different worlds but sharing a boundary in the event of their collaboration.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Sydney private school put dog collar and lead on student, inquiry hears
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWEducation Sydney private school put dog collar and lead on student, inquiry hears Emily Kowal August 14, 2026 — 1:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A former member of Redeemer Baptist School and Church has told a parliamentary inquiry her sister was placed in a dog collar and pulled by a lead, while another witness described the school as a “criminal gang who uses religion as camouflage”. Speaking on the second day of hearings into the North Parramatta private school and its church – which has been described as a “cult” during the inquiry – Helen Johnstone said her family joined the community in 1976 when she was a child. Helen Johnstone gives evidence at the inquiry on Friday. Sitthixay Ditthavong “Within months of joining the community, [my sisters] and I can remember feelings of discomfort, fear of adults within the community, and a sharp change in our lives,” she said. “It was a change for the worse.” Johnstone told the inquiry her older sister was viewed as a “rebel” and subjected to regular abuse.



“I witnessed her experience some awful treatment, including a dog collar being placed on her neck and being pulled around by a dog lead,” Johnstone told the inquiry. She told the inquiry she witnessed her sister being held underwater and thrown into a “filthy duck pond”, and “shunned, shamed and humiliated routinely”. Johnstone also detailed the abuse of her foster brother, an Indigenous boy she believes may have been part of the Stolen Generation. She recalled her father belting the boy while he lay curled in the fetal position. “He came into a home where learning consisted of punishment,” she recalled. “He was routinely hit and belted for not eating, getting homework answers wrong, soiling his pants or his bed, etcetera.” Witnesses have told the inquiry corporal punishment was common within the church until as late as 2005.



“Sadly, he’s still in the community today and was subsequently adopted into the family. I’d like the circumstances around his arrival investigated,” said Johnstone. The inquiry also heard sweeping allegations of financial misconduct. Graeme Glossop gives evidence at the parliamentary inquiry on Friday. Sitthixay Ditthavong Accountant Graeme Glossop, who previously took on the school in 2004, accused the institution of operating a “scheme of arrangement designed to avoid taxation.” He told the inquiry the school and church were a “criminal gang who uses religion as a camouflage” and were “stealing government money”.



He said the school and church operate a “scheme of arrangement designed to avoid taxation,” and that the school and church were not paying fringe benefits tax. Glossop said the church and school community “had a disease”. “It’s like a cancer going through that whole community, and people are getting affected by it,” he said. Related Investigation

Private schools Redeemer Baptist School investigation Former member Barney Jones testified the institution enjoyed “a series of beneficial loopholes” used to amass wealth, including at least 40 properties valued at a minimum of $140 million. Because volunteers are paid low stipends, Jones said the institution avoids payroll tax, GST, capital gains tax, fringe benefits tax, stamp duty, and HECS repayments. He highlighted what he called “double-dipping” into government funds, claiming members accessed Centrelink benefits to support their lifestyles due to their artificially low incomes.



Holding up a 102-page dossier documenting alleged legislative breaches and employment practices, Jones said he had raised the alarm with the Board of Studies (now the NSW Education Standards Authority) in 2005, but his warnings “fell on deaf ears”. NESA told the inquiry on Monday it was investigating the school under section 83C of the Education Act, which requires non-government schools to operate on a not-for-profit basis to remain eligible for government funding. Redeemer leader and principal Jonathan Cannon was invited to attend the inquiry, but headmaster and elder Russell Bailey declined, citing concerns over procedural fairness. Related Article Updated

Education ‘Fire and brimstone on acid’: Inside a Sydney private school’s control tactics In a written response, Bailey argued the inquiry was unfairly targeting the school, maintaining the school and church were two separate legal entities. Bailey said the school’s 535 students had now been labelled as “members of a cult, despite not even being members of the Church (which is also not a cult)”.



“The inquiry should be ashamed of itself for that baseless aspersion,” Bailey wrote. Both Jones and Johnstone told the inquiry there was “absolutely no difference between school and church.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Complainant ‘C’ felt ‘uncomfortable’ in bedroom at former 2GB broadcaster’s farm, court told
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day eight of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. My colleagues Clare Sibthorpe and Harriet Alexander will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

The NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court building will hear today from complainant “C”, the second of six men who have accused the former 2GB host of unwanted touching and kissing over a 20-year period.

Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Friday. Peter Rae

Jones denies the claims and is entitled to the presumption of innocence.

In the first week of the trial, the court heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted “J”, a young athlete, starting with unwanted kissing and progressing to touching. On the Crown’s case, “J” was aged between 17 and 21 at the time of the nine alleged indecent assaults.

The defence case is that the alleged incidents didn’t happen.

This week, the older brother of “J” and the complainant’s ex-girlfriend gave evidence about what they said he told them about the alleged assaults, and his mother and his former coach gave evidence yesterday.

His mother testified that “J” initially told her that Jones had not touched him, before telling her the following year that he had lied. She said that she was in shock when “J” made the disclosure, and she told her son she should have protected him.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men without their consent between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him.

Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, said during her opening address to the court that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Young Talent Time legend Johnny Young dies aged 79
World.content:
Updated CultureTV & radioVale Young Talent Time legend Johnny Young dies aged 79 Chris Hook Updated August 14, 2026 — 1:15pm ,first published 11:31am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former Young Talent Time host Johnny Young has died aged 79, his family announced on Friday morning. Young’s family said he had died following a “brief battle with pancreatic cancer”. Musician Johnny Young at his home in Perth, Western Australia, in 2018. Tony McDonough Although he was best known for his work on the children’s talent show Young Talent Time, which spawned the careers of stars such as Dannii Minogue, Tina Arena and Debra Byrne, Young was also a singer-songwriter in his own right, penning hits such as The Real Thing for Russell Morris and Smiley for Ronnie Burns. Born Johnny de Jong in The Netherlands in 1947, the youngest of four children, Young migrated with his family to Australia following World War II and settled in Perth, where he grew up in the suburb of Kalamunda.



Loading After working as a trainee disc jockey in his late teens, Young scored a job as the host of Channel 7 Perth’s pop music show Club Seventeen, where he met various pop stars and began writing and performing himself. After a brief period in London, Young returned to Australia and launched Young Talent Time in 1971. The show would become appointment viewing for families across the country and ran until 1988. Young with Dannii Minogue (left) and Lorena Novoa in 1987. The show featured a core group of performers doing well-known pop songs, as well as hopeful youngsters competing in a talent show, and making household names of Minogue (long before Kylie came to fame) and Arena, among others. Each week, Young would sign off by singing The Beatles’ All My Loving, a version of which he had recorded in 1967.



Related Article Obituaries There was more to Johnny Young than Young Talent Time. He also wrote one of Australia’s biggest hit songs Earlier this month, Arena paid tribute to Young’s guidance in comments to this masthead. “He’s very much like a father figure; he wanted me to be as protected as I possibly could,” she said. “There were times when he said, ‘Be careful, I don’t like that person’ – and he was right. He taught me about discernment as a very little girl. I wasn’t able to intellectualise the term back then, but it became much clearer down the track.” In 1990, Young was inducted into the Logies Hall of Fame. In 2010, Arena returned to Australia from her Paris base to induct Young into the ARIA Hall of Fame.



“I don’t think I would ever have had the beauty and the diversity of career that I’ve had without my apprenticeship on TV,” Arena said at the induction. Arena also performed Young’s Here Comes the Star, which was a hit in 1969 in Australia for Ross D Wylie and in Britain for Herman’s Hermits. Following news of his death, Beven Addinsall, who joined Young Talent Time at the age of 11, paid tribute to Young on Instagram, sharing a photo of himself alongside Young on a red carpet. “Rest in peace, my dear friend,” the caption read.

World.title: Panthers close in on massive re-signing but mystery remains over Cleary
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Panthers close in on massive re-signing but mystery remains over Cleary Dan Walsh August 14, 2026 — 1:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Penrith are closing in on the biggest piece of their multi-million dollar retention puzzle yet, with co-captain Isaah Yeo expected to recommit to the club before the finals. While champion halfback Nathan Cleary is still yet to sit down with Panthers officials or his management to discuss his future, extension talks with Yeo progressed positively this week as he rehabilitates his pectoral injury. Loading Multiple sources speaking on the condition of anonymity due to the confidential nature of negotiations expect Yeo’s future to be finalised over the last few rounds of the regular season. The Australian, NSW Origin and four-time premiership-winning Panthers skipper ranks behind only Cleary in Penrith’s roster priorities, and has long been considered the most likely of their out-and-out stars to stay put.



The terms of Penrith’s latest offer to Yeo, 31, are unclear. But the prospect of being a one-club player with a multi-year deal holds obvious appeal to Yeo, who is on track to pass the fabled 300-game milestone next season. In another piece of good news for the Panthers, fellow back-rower Isaiah Papalii has told the club he will take up a new deal beyond 2027. Injured Panthers captain Isaah Yeo. NRL Imagery As reported by this masthead on Wednesday, centre Paul Alamoti is also set to re-sign as he awaits scan results on a hamstring injury suffered late against the Roosters in Thursday night’s enthralling 12-6 loss. Alamoti has already been scratched for next week’s clash against Melbourne. Left centre Izack Tago is expected to switch to the opposite side in Alamoti’s place against the Storm, with Casey McLean pushing to return from a broken hand next Thursday.



Blaize Talagi and Jack Cole are other options out wide. The Panthers will also have greater clarity on Yeo’s recovery timeframe and chances of playing again this year as swelling continues to reduce in his pec. The prospect of Yeo leading Penrith’s retention drive comes as the club remains comfortable with Cleary holding fire on his future. The game’s best player had planned to address negotiations once his NSW Origin series had wrapped up, but is still yet to confirm, privately or publicly, whether he wants to re-sign before the November 1 free-agency date or test his value on the open market.



Sources close to the champion No.7 have indicated the lack of clarity does not necessarily point to an eventual exit from Penrith, nor that talks will be delayed until the end of the Panthers season. Related Article NRL 2026 Daly Cherry-Evans didn’t want talk of his future to take the gloss off Roosters’ win. So he waited seven hours Coach and father Ivan, who will be replaced by assistant Peter Wallace at the end of 2027, admitted this week that rival NRL clubs, including Penrith, simply cannot compete with the tax-free dollars on offer from expansion outfit PNG Chiefs. The Chiefs have made Cleary their halfback priority after signing teammate and star winger Brian To’o at the start of the week. Veteran prop Moses Leota, back-rower Liam Martin and Talagi are Penrith’s next most notable names coming off-contract in 2027. Leota, who was granted a brief window to test his market value earlier this year, is prepared to re-sign for slightly less than the $900,000 his management believes he can earn elsewhere.

World.title: This unsettling novel will stay with you long after you finish it
World.content:
CultureBooksReview This unsettling novel will stay with you long after you finish it Declan Fry August 14, 2026 — 1:13pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

You sit down to eat breakfast. The sun is shining. The sky is blue. You pick up your spoon. You eat scalpels. Maggots. The maggots squirm upon your tongue. You swallow them down. For years – maybe since the day you were born – life has been like this. Some days less. Some days more. By now you barely even notice. What would you do? Would you care? That is the question Maria Stepanova’s novel asks. Written in Germany after the author was exiled from her native Russia, The Disappearing Act was published in 2024 as Фокус, pronounced “focus” and meaning “trick” or “sleight of hand”. It is about a woman, M, whose sense of self is haunted by the biggest trickster of all, “the beast”. Russian writer Maria Stepanova. Europa Press via Getty Images Waging war upon a less powerful neighbour, “the beast” touches “everyone who had ever lived in the land where she was born”. Like God and death, the beast is inescapable.



Sound like Putin’s Russia? Maybe. But the beast is bigger than that. The beast is life’s violent contour. The force of uncontained power. How it can nestle inside one’s language, one’s voice, one’s being. Photo: Stepanova’s decision to anonymise the novel’s detail feels like defiance. State censors, if not readers themselves, often hunger for names. Wanna see me in M? Stepanova seems to ask. That’s your prerogative. M does not want to be called upon to account for the beast’s whims and dispositions. She calls herself a “Russian novelist” and is hailed as one by certain occasions – like the literary festival she is on her way to attend in an unnamed European town. But she is uncomfortable identifying as a novelist. Stranded before she can arrive at the festival, she imagines herself like the Soviet emigrant in Nabokov’s tale The Visit to the Museum, suddenly transported to Leningrad. She senses that, so long as others are destroyed by the beast, she cannot be saved. Named for the industrial waste caused by lead mining – pollution that accelerated rapidly in Stalin’s Russia – the American noise rock band Chat Pile captures the anguish M feels: “From the time you were born it was over.” Stranded, M leaves her old life behind. She feels her inner self cease “banging itself against the walls in search of an exit”. Discarding nearly everything – her suitcase, phone, copies of the book she is promoting, even her passport and name – she wonders if “the only way to get rid of the beast was to get rid of oneself”.



Her decision to give up her old life could be read as renewal. Or obliteration. Encountering strangers – including a travelling circus – M fantasises about escape from the confusion of her old life. But the collective, the crowd, is not what it appears: among them, people may hold authority and never be made accountable. Think, in Australia, of Nauru. Think of the collective theft of land that gave birth to the nation. Tellingly, M confuses the name of her hotel – Petuh – with Petukh, those Russian prisoners reduced to being “common prey” so that “anyone henceforth could use him as and when they wanted”. She sees their heads plunged deep in the excrement of their fellow prisoners, polluted by shared waste. Like the linguist in Paul Bowles’ 1945 story A Distant Episode – brutalised, his tongue and connection to the world he knew severed by forces beyond his control – M’s desire for innocence, if not something stronger, compels her to seek anonymity among those with whom she shares no linguistic or cultural connection. In this respect, the book recalls authors like Peter Handke writing about the “inspired namelessness” of non-verbal communication. Stepanova even references Wim Wenders’ film Wings of Desire, which Handke helped write. I was also reminded of another German-language author, Yoko Tawada, whose characters, dislocated from linguistic or social attachments, seek freedom in chance encounters and imaginative play. Editor's pick Literature The 3000-year-old poem Australians suddenly can’t get enough of Yet imaginative escape is never entirely innocent. Without vigilance, it can become an act of looking away. Like her masterly In Memory of Memory (2021), Stepanova asks us: if hell is built gradually, little by little, day by day, by the time anyone notices, will you be covered in blood? The beast is part of ordinary life. Yet ordinariness does not guarantee you protection. Ordinary life is always on the verge of violation. We draw apart the curtains, never knowing if a landscape or hellscape might greet us. The Disappearing Act, like its protagonist – a woman with a suitcase but nowhere to go, a phone but no one to call, belongings but no plans to stay – is itinerant, whimsical, disturbing, brutal and, yes, beautiful. It informs us that, sometimes, it is better to destroy yourself than to carry on as if everything were the same. It is better to stop believing the world you live in is the same one you once knew. Hell may be close but the void is even closer – and it’s when the flames burn brightest that we learn what it means to live.



The Disappearing Act by Maria Stepanova, translated by Sasha Dugdale, is published by Fitzcarraldo ($30). The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Accelerate Resources opens second front with rich WA manganese play
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Accelerate Resources opens second front with rich WA manganese play Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Andrew Todd August 14, 2026 — 1:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There are moments in an exploration company’s life that can define its future, where a persistent geological hunch pays off and a project suddenly shifts from being a line item in a portfolio to a potential company-maker. For Accelerate Resources, that moment appears to have arrived at its dual-commodity portfolio in Western Australia. While the company has been consistently revealing shallow gold prospects in the world-class Eastern Goldfields, the sheer scale and grade of the manganese mineralisation it has uncovered at its Woodie Woodie North manganese project in the Pilbara hints at a large-scale system for Accelerate and elevated the junior into the class of both a critical minerals and precious metals player. Outcropping manganese at Accelerate Resources’ Woodie Woodie North project is located just 55km north of Consolidated Minerals’ long-running Woodie Woodie manganese mine in the Pilbara. The Woodie Woodie North project is strategically located in one of Australia’s rarest manganese provinces. It sits just 55 kilometres north of Consolidated Minerals’ operating Woodie Woodie mine - mainland Australia’s only and longest-running producer of high-grade manganese ore. Being on the doorstep of a major, multi-decade mining operation is an enviable position for any explorer but more importantly, the at-surface geology doesn’t respect tenement boundaries. The company says it now appears to be sitting on a significant extension of the same mineralised system that has made its neighbour a globally significant producer. This latest discovery by Accelerate now suggests there is plenty more where that came from.



‘We have now mapped more than 200 manganese outcrops and occurrences defining around 9.7 hectares of mineralised manganese exposure.’ Accelerate Resources chief executive officer Luke Meter The company says its project covers a substantial 432-square-kilometres of highly prospective ground, incorporating seven mapped, large-scale manganese corridors that stretch over a combined 42km of strike. It’s a district-scale footprint and the early-stage work is definitely hinting at district-scale potential. Recent detailed mapping and LiDAR surveys have identified more than 200 individual manganese outcrops across the project’s Gingarrigan-El Largo area, defining a combined mineralised footprint of almost 10 hectares at surface. And the grades are nothing short of spectacular. Rock chip sampling from the newly defined Rancor and Wampa prospects has returned grades as high as 58.4 per cent manganese, with a slew of other impressive hits including 57.6 per cent, 55.6 per cent - for context Australia’s two operating mines run a resource around 40 per cent manganese.



The outcropping grades look bang on for direct-shipping ore (DSO) grades. DSO is the holy grail for bulk commodity miners, as it means the ore is high-grade enough to be dug up and shipped directly to customers with minimal processing, dramatically slashing both capital and operating costs. And with the project nestled just 260km from Port Hedland and 55km north of Consolidated Minerals’ Woodie Woodie infrastructure, there is plenty of promise for a DSO scenario. The company’s Rancor prospect alone is now defined by a one-hectare manganese outcrop with an apparent thickness of up to 10 metres. With heritage surveys now complete, the company is gearing up for a maiden reverse-circulation drilling program to test these exceptional surface targets at depth. Accelerate Resources chief executive officer Luke Meter said: “The scale of the surface manganese at Gingarrigan and El Largo is becoming increasingly clear. We have now mapped more than 200 manganese outcrops and occurrences defining around 9.7 hectares of mineralised manganese exposure, with several of the larger bodies showing a close relationship to the structural architecture highlighted by the gravity survey.” Accelerate says the project already boasts a 1.2 million tonne resource grading 19.1 per cent manganese, with an exploration target of between 5.3 and 10.7 million tonnes at 10 to 19 per cent in the books. Following the definition of 200 plus outcropping discoveries, the exploration target would look to be just tip of the iceberg at Gingarrigan and El Largo, with plenty more upside now on the table for the explorer. While manganese remains a critical and irreplaceable ingredient in steelmaking, its future is also being supercharged by the electric vehicle revolution. It is a key component in nickel-manganese-cobalt batteries and is crucial to the emerging, lower-cost battery chemistries like lithium-manganese-iron-phosphate (LMFP), which are being rapidly being adopted by industry giants like CATL and BYD.



A drill rig on site at Accelerate Resources’ latest Spencers gold discovery outside Kalgoorlie in WA. But while the manganese story has deservedly grabbed the spotlight, Accelerate has not taken its eye off its original precious prize. The company’s flagship Balagundi project continues to turn up high-grade gold discoveries in the prime real estate of WA’s Eastern Goldfields. Just 15km east of Kalgoorlie, the project sits in the heartland of Australian gold mining, putting Accelerate in the shadow of the headframes of the 70-million-ounce Super Pit and neighbouring the 6-million-ounce-plus Kanowna Belle mine. The project’s proximity to a host of hungry, third-party processing mills means even a modest-sized discovery in today’s gold price environment can be highly economic, offering several low-capital pathways to potential production that has served countless goldfields juniors well in recent years. Accelerate recently doubled its footprint at Balagundi insisting a broader gold system is emerging within its gold corridors, following a second shallow gold discovery at its Spencers prospect, where shallow drilling returned a thick 28-metre hit grading 1.01 grams per tonne gold from just 36m. The prospect lies within a granted mining lease at Balagundi and has already been defined over 300m of strike, providing a clear target for fast-tracked production ounces. Spencers sits at just one of a raft of gold prospects along the company’s Paris Gift gold trend, which cuts through its prime Kalgoorlie tenure. Add in its Paris Gift, Mt Bellew, Fluffy and Delta prospects and the company has more than its fair share of long ignored, shallow gold prospects to keep it busy in the goldfields.



Accelerate’s classic Kalgoorlie gold play has a clear, low-cost path to potential production and now sits right alongside a potentially company-making, critical minerals project with jaw-dropping grades in an emerging manganese district. For Accelerate, the exploration journey has led to two distinct destinations. One is paved with the golden promise of the Eastern Goldfields, the other with the industrial muscle of Pilbara manganese. With drilling set to begin on its high-grade manganese targets, the market may not have to wait long to see which path delivers first. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? World.title: Kuniko drilling flags NSW resource growth
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Kuniko drilling flags NSW resource growth Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward August 14, 2026 — 1:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A resource upgrade looks to be on the cards for Kuniko Limited at its Commonwealth-Silica Hill project after a recently completed phase-two drilling campaign hit visible sulphides outside the existing resource block model. Two diamond holes totalling 724m successfully intersected zones of alteration and sulphide-bearing veins providing an encouraging start to the company’s broader exploration program, designed to build on a previous bonanza-grade discovery at the project which sits in the heart of NSW’s prolific Lachlan Fold Belt. Kuniko Limited’s Commonwealth gold-silver project in NSW where it recently uncovered a stunning bonanza-grade discovery. The early results offer compelling validation for the company which recently took the reins of the project after securing a controlling 51 per cent stake from Impact Minerals more than a year ahead of schedule. Now in the driver’s seat, Kuniko is aiming to prove its belief that the project could host a far larger district-scale mineral system than previously thought. The project is situated 100 kilometres north of Orange in what is considered elephant country for mineral explorers with the region populated by world-class operations, including Newmont’s Cadia-Ridgeway mine and Evolution Mining’s Cowal and Northparkes projects. Kuniko’s ground also lies along-trend from Alkane Resources’ massive Boda-Kaiser porphyry copper-gold discovery.



‘The potential for these extensions to add scale and high-grade mineralisation to Silica Hill is an important catalyst for Kuniko.’ Kuniko Limited managing director Maja McGuire Commonwealth contains two distinct deposits located just 200m from each other. The first, Commonwealth Main, is a precious-metals-rich volcanogenic massive sulphide (VMS) system. The second, Silica Hill, is a high-grade epithermal silver-gold system and is the focus of the current drilling. A previous historical JORC-inferred resource outlined by Impact Minerals tallied up 88,800 ounces of gold and 3.3 million ounces of silver with the system remaining open along strike and at depth. Kuniko’s latest drilling was designed to test continuity around a stunning phase-one discovery hole. That initial hole returned a remarkable intercept of 0.5 metres grading an eye-watering 347 grams per tonne gold (g/t) equivalent which included a coffee spitting 20,603g/t silver, or more than 2 per cent. The first of the new holes was drilled 60m down-dip of that discovery while the second was collared about 40m up-dip. Kuniko says both holes hit their targets intersecting alteration and sulphide-bearing stringer and stockwork veining consistent with the mineralisation seen in the original discovery hole. Kuniko Limited managing director Maja McGuire said: “The first two holes of our Phase 2 drilling program have delivered an encouraging start at Silica Hill, with both holes intersecting the targeted zones of alteration, disseminated sulphides and stringer-vein mineralisation. Importantly, drilling has now demonstrated approximately 100m of continuity across CMKNI007, CMKNI004 and CMKNI008, with all three holes located outside the existing mineralised block model. This provides a compelling opportunity to expand the known Silica Hill mineralised footprint.”



Together, the discovery hole and the two new step-out holes demonstrate 100m of up-dip to down-dip continuity in the Silica Hill mineralised system. Notably, all three lie outside the project’s existing mineralised block model highlighting the potential for the company to significantly expand the resource footprint ahead of a planned mineral resource estimate update by December. Visual logging of the core from the down-dip hole identified an initial zone of sulphide-bearing veining from about 205m downhole, followed by a broader 55m-wide zone of stringer and stockwork veining from 260m. The up-dip hole intersected a 45m-wide zone of sulphide-bearing stringer and stockwork veining from about 280m. Kuniko has put the obligatory cautionary note on visual observations however, the presence of sulphides is potentially the first sign that geologists are onto something with promise. Additionally, drilling is ongoing at Main Shaft and Commonwealth South along with further regional work to define more targets. Having gone from being a guest at the party to now running the show, Kuniko is now wasting no time in testing the scale of its flagship asset. With the drill bit confirming the geological model and extending a known high-grade system, all eyes will be on the pending assays to see just how big this discovery, bang in the heart of elephant country, might become.
