World.title: Massive Attack are note perfect in a show where music takes a back seat
World.content:
Key points MUSIC: Massive Attack tour Australia for the first time in 16 years

THEATRE: Break of Day at Malthouse is a remarkable new play

MUSIC: Jaime Martín conducts a five-star performance of Mahler 6

DANCE: Echo Mapping is an intimate solo dance performance that is also a concert

MUSIC

Massive Attack ★★★★★

Rod Laver Arena, August 11 Since forming in 1988, Massive Attack has made a couple of the greatest albums of all time and nudged the top of the pop charts. They also have a decades-long history of anti-war and human rights advocacy, most recently for Palestine. Grant Marshall of Massive Attack performs on stage in Melbourne. Richard Clifford They were recently detained in, and then banned from, Singapore after expressing solidarity and unfurling a Palestinian flag on stage – contravening a ban on displaying foreign flags. This was just prior to arriving in Australia, home of our own cool and normal discourse. Now that we’ve addressed the elephant in the room, we can move past the ugly business of politics and talk about how much fun we had at the Massive Attack show.



Just joking! Of course that’s not what happened! Anyone hoping for an uncomplicated night of nostalgia at the paranoia factory would have walked away disappointed. Likely crawled away, with ears, eyes, and brain bleeding. Music takes a back seat on this tour. The players, including core members Robert “3D” Del Naja and Grant “Daddy G” Marshall, perform mostly in the shadows, ceding the floor to a visual experience that’s equally mesmerising and assaultive. Massive Attack on stage at Rod Laver Arena. Richard Clifford As the first bars land, morbid statistics cascade across the screen: children killed by guns in the US this year, in various wars. It rarely gets more cheerful. AI surveillance, hate speech, influencers (Australian wellness grifters get a shout-out), aspiring fascists, conspiracy theories, tax havens, K-pop dance routines juxtaposed with government massacre. Whenever the audience is threatened with a good time, it’s followed by apparently limitless footage of war crimes committed by some of Australia’s allies.



A nightmarish tour of the internet gives way to a map of Palantir’s chokehold on the planet, then to the Congolese children mining the minerals behind it. Cumulatively an overwhelming panorama of the digital psychosis engulfing the world, soundtracked by Massive Attack. The band itself? Note perfect. Especially when feature artists emerge from the shadows to lend themselves to tracks. Massive Attack is note perfect in their first Melbourne performance in 16 years. Richard Clifford Roots reggae singer Horace Andy laces Hymn of the Big Wheel with gravitas. Deborah Miller sings Shara Nelson’s parts on Safe from Harm with such transcendent beauty and power the crowd roars with every high note. Former Cocteau Twin Elizabeth Fraser’s ethereal, haunting voice is undiminished, both on the Tim Buckley cover Song to The Siren and show closer Teardrop. A panacea of a song at any time, but when the screens finally go dark and politics leaves the room for three minutes, it tips towards the sublime.

Reviewed by Liam Pieper



THEATRE

Break of Day ★★★★

Malthouse Theatre, until August 29 Over the last few decades, much of our most important drama has laid siege to the myth of Australian egalitarianism. That’s true across all domains of social prejudice and marginalisation – gender, race, sexual orientation, and so on. Yet, all of these can intersect with economic disadvantage, and as the Gini coefficient continues to rise, so too does theatre that refuses to look away from the have-nots. Kat Stewart and Sherry-Lee Watson play mother and daughter. Pia Johnson Steve Rodgers joins such internationally lauded playwrights as Patricia Cornelius and Daniel Keene in focusing with great human intensity on a collective blind spot: those living at the wrong end of increasing wealth and income inequality. Break of Day is set in the fictional Burra Creek – an impoverished exurb of a satellite city, where single mum Pam (Kat Stewart) works night shift at an Amazon-style warehouse. We first see her walking home from work, through a monologue that touches on her invisibility, but which also highlights an opposite risk. One doco about Burra Creek was a voyeuristic slide into poverty porn: it smeared the community as all “booze an’ meth an’ KFC” and not much else.



Pam’s daughter Rae (Sherry-Lee Watson) is in year 12 at high school. She’s bright enough for university (and the social mobility that goes with it), and Pam is desperate to ensure that she seizes the opportunity. The deck is stacked against Rae: her obnoxious alcoholic grandfather (Richard Piper) descends on their one-bedroom flat, and her computer packs up while she’s trying to write an essay about Nabokov’s Lolita. Plus, there’s the teenage distraction of first love with charismatic Jed (Theo Clarke), who wants to be an actor. Break of Day is a remarkable new play. Pia Johnson With Rae’s future at stake, Pam will risk everything – including her lifelong friendship with her work supervisor Sanjeeva (Chum Ehelepola) – to help her daughter make the grade. Sarah Goodes’ sensitive direction – and the layered ironies and intimacies of Rodgers’ brilliantly overheard script – underpin some wonderful performances.



Kat Stewart takes a scene or two to descend the social ladder and work herself into potty-mouthed precision, but once she does, it’s a compelling portrayal of a woman so rich in the one thing money can’t buy that she’s willing to collude in her own debasement. (Pam’s desperate love is also an existential evasion: who will she be once her daughter flies the coop?) More debased still is Piper as the abusive grandfather. It’s a piteous, fearlessly awful performance, and a sign of the playwright’s gift for dramatic irony that he allows this character to announce the crux of the issue – Thinks she’s so f---in’ special. She’s got rights! Everyone

now, everyone’s got rights, all these f---in’ rights! -

Except for poor people. Nothin’ people! Poor f---in’ nothin’

people have still got nothin’... – after a despicable misogynist rant aimed at his granddaughter. That said, bleakness doesn’t reign in this play, largely thanks to two younger actors stealing the show. You can’t look away from either of them – not the extraordinary ferocity and tenderness that Watson brings to the precocious Rae, nor Clarke’s magnetism and ease as an Aboriginal boy who’s a born performer.



(One highlight sees Jed practising a Caliban speech from The Tempest to soothe himself as he’s mucking out a toilet. The scene floored me, and there isn’t much I wouldn’t do to see an actor as talented as Clarke perform Shakespeare.) Related Article Stage You probably never wonder who’s packing your parcels. Perhaps you will now Delight isn’t restricted to the young: Ehelepola paints an overlooked character in deft strokes – a mild-mannered and restrained persona, trauma under the mask, and, crucially, a moment of unexpected joy. Anna Cordingley’s set is a revolving monument to Pam’s home and workplace and the liminal spaces between them. It frames the actors well and creates a powerfully circular momentum, though you do wonder about the cost. Will such maximalism push ticket prices up so that the poor won’t be able to afford to attend the show? It’s a troubling to think that they may be excluded from the world premiere season of this remarkable new play.

Reviewed by Cameron Woodhead



MUSIC

Jaime Conducts Mahler 6 ★★★★★

Melbourne Symphony Orchestra, Hamer Hall, August 13 Mahler’s Symphony No. 6 is a work of stunning clairvoyance. Although happy at the time, Mahler conjured up a hero hounded by death who is ultimately felled by three fateful blows. Five years after the premiere, Mahler was dead at the age 50, having indeed suffered three blows: forced resignation from the Vienna Opera, the death of his young daughter, and the diagnosis of fatal heart disease. Jaime Martín conducts the MSO in Mahler 6 Laura Manariti Under chief conductor Jaime Martín, the Melbourne Symphony brought vibrant urgency to the rich musical and psychological textures of this troubled masterpiece. Largely balancing the need for observing Mahler’s minutely detailed writing for huge forces with broader dramatic imperatives, Martín revealed Mahler’s hero to be a deeply complex character.



In driving the opening death march with such implacability, Martín created a sense of suffocating imprisonment that meant the second theme (intended to evoke Mahler’s wife) was not so much a lyrical contrast as a reminder of the shortness of happiness. Moments of yearning for lost innocence were beautifully captured by luxuriant string tone and the distant ringing of cowbells in the Andante (placed as the second movement according to Mahler’s final wishes) only to become torturous in the sinister scherzo, where elements of fear, regret and self-doubt re-emerged. Martín respected Mahler’s superstitious omission of the last of three devastating hammer blows in the finale, even though there is a strong musical case for its reinstatement. Demonstrating huge commitment, the orchestra brought this colossal emotional maelstrom to a devastating close. Cameos by concertmaster Natalie Chee and principal horn Nicolas Fleury were indicative of the orchestra’s superlative playing throughout. Yorta Yorta composer James Henry’s Freshwater Saltwater was a skilfully orchestrated prelude, using the blending of fresh and salt water in the Yarra as an analogy for the co-existence of cultures both here and in Mahler’s Vienna.

Reviewed by Tony Way



DANCE

Echo Mapping ★★★★

The Substation, Newport, until August 15 Echo Mapping, an intimate solo dance performance that is also a concert, has the cool austerity and high-art seriousness of a late-night gallery event. It’s therefore perfectly at home at the Substation, amid the attractively exposed concrete, iron and brickwork. Composer Jack Prest and dancer Azzam Mohamed perform at The Substation. Sarah Walker The space is shared by dancer Azzam Mohamed and composer Jack Prest, with the latter stationed behind a music desk. Both appear in plain T-shirts and nondescript trousers. Staged in the round with the house lights raised, the performance has a refreshing immediacy. It begins in silence, with Mohamed holding a sequence of still poses. Then Prest offers a clean, affirmative three-note trumpet figure. Momentum gathers rapidly: Mohamed whoops and shouts, stamps out a rhythm, then breaks into a compulsively repeated jazz-dance phrase.



When this subsides, Mohamed again draws his extremities inward. He clenches. His hands twist into fantastic shapes around his head. Then loosens himself, more gradually, finding elasticity through a recurring motif in which his hands, arms and shoulders knead the space before him. Related Article Stage Want intimate conversations with strangers in the night? Walk this way Prest builds his score from simple inputs, accumulating layers and effects while also incorporating snatches of tunes supplied by Mohamed. The dancer maps this changing sonic terrain through variations of joy and languor, hips rocking and dipping as he spirals around the room. The show has an improvised sort of energy and yet as it winds down, returning to the sonorous minimalism of its beginnings, the logic of its development becomes apparent. Mohamed seems to replay the performance in reverse, retracing its gestures until, once again, all becomes still. Perhaps the most interesting detail in Echo Mapping is the relationship between the artists: throughout the performance they treat each other with a gentle but undemonstrative masculine regard – inhabiting different worlds but sharing a boundary in the event of their collaboration.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Ex-politician Kiri Allan says public service bloated, slow and overpaid
World.content:
Former Labour cabinet minister Kiri Allan has come out swinging against the public service saying it is bloated, slow, and overpaid.

In her new memoir, Go Hard or Go Home, she is scathing of the sector and doubled-down on her position on Friday, calling for an overhaul on Midday Report.

Kiri Allan on overhauling the public service Midday Report Download MP3 16m

Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche declined to comment.

Allan said there were "exceptional people" throughout the public service and her comments weren't an attack on individuals, but on the system.

She said in the private sector, the incentive to work hard was to "put food on the table" the next day, and maintained the problems she saw with the public sector were particularly acute in upper management.

"What I found with senior bureaucrats is that they're often more political than politicians. They know they're going to out-survive politicians.

"And they just sometimes need to bide their time, say 'Yes minister, absolutely minister.'"

Allan said it was "problematic" for the country's political system, and different from some systems overseas.

She said she also believed in "devolution" and thought taxpayer dollars were overly centralised and wanted to see more money and resources in the hands of communities.

"Because of the policies that our government's provide, there ends up being a lot of gatekeeping in the centre in terms of getting those resources out."

Allan said she ran into this during her time as conservation minister, claiming getting millions of dollars to community groups under the Jobs for Nature programme was a "ridiculous process" that took a couple of years.

She said in another instance, resolving who had cultural rights over whale bones took four years.

The Department of Conservation declined to comment.

Allan said she did not agree with the ACT Party's policy to slash the public sector, but said an overhaul was needed.

World.title: Winston Peters has a choice to make
World.content:
Analysis: With less than three months until the country goes to the polls Winston Peters is at a fork in the road.

The New Zealand First leader needs to quickly choose whether to stay the course with his committed and loyal voter base or potentially put it all on the line seeking new votes on the fringes.

While the spotlight this week was firmly on Christopher Luxon's second confidence vote in four months, the week before it was Peters who was causing headlines for the wrong reasons.

A 1News-Verian poll on Wednesday gives an insight into how the public responded to both.

It had National unchanged on 29 percent and New Zealand First dropping three points to 8 percent - putting it equal with rising minor party, Opportunity.

The poll was conducted between Saturday and Tuesday. 1News pulled out of the field early as a result of Luxon's summoning of his MPs to Wellington, only collecting 847 respondents of a usual 1000 sample size, leaving a margin of error of +/- 3.4 percent.

New Zealand First had been soaring in polls prior to this month - in RNZ's mid-July poll it registered its strongest result in the Reid Research series in nine years reaching 11.5 percent.

Since then Peters gave a speech in Parliament's general debate where he got sidetracked by heckling from Chinese-born Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan, who he told to "go back to your own country", and continued, "that's where they lie like a flatfish".

The comments drew protest from the Chinese Embassy in New Zealand and prompted a response from the office of the Minister of Foreign Affairs, saying he stood by the comments - up until that point Peters had been claiming the comments were made as NZ First leader.

The reaction to the comments has been swift and angry, from the Chinese-Kiwi community, to opposition MPs, and even Peters' very own coalition partners, with Luxon saying it was "racist".

And it's not only non-NZ First voters seemingly fed up with the inflammatory rhetoric.

The comments are clearly impacting its own voter base.

The New Zealand First dilemma

The current iteration of NZ First supporters is two very distinct groups - the pro-industry, mining, exporting, economic growth over environmental concerns types, and a much newer mob of fringe culture war antagonists.

Broadly speaking deputy leader Shane Jones speaks to the first group and Peters the second.

There's crossover for sure with Jones having led the charge on recent anti-immigration rhetoric, warning of a "butter chicken tsunami" from signing an Indian FTA.

But for the most part he steers clear of culture war talking points like Covid vaccination injuries and who should be using which public bathrooms.

Shane Jones RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Increasingly NZ First party stalwarts are tiring of the messaging being focused on appealing to the fringe-newcomers.

With National increasingly a party polling under 30 percent there are votes ripe for the picking, and the latest poll indicates it's Act benefiting from National's stalling and NZ First's drop.

Peters spending his time speaking to a small disillusioned and disenfranchised group of New Zealanders is not going to give him any wins with voters tossing up moving their vote away from the diminishing 'purple vote' of National and Labour.

On top of that NZ First is also at risk of giving Act some of its base, voters who back a return of the coalition but are losing faith in Peters' distractions.

Peters already has a playbook for how badly this could end - it was the 2020 election where he went from being deputy prime minister and foreign minister to being out of Parliament altogether.

Having spent both the 2017 and 2020 election campaign on the road with Peters the difference in strategy between the two was incredibly stark.

In 2017 Peters was firing on all cylinders, admittedly from a position of Opposition which he relishes, but also being very deliberate about targeting National and Labour voters and speaking to middle New Zealand as a kingmaker who could keep Act and the Greens in check.

By 2020 he was campaigning from a coalition with a Labour government in the middle of a pandemic with a hugely popular prime minister.

Just before he went out on the road Peters said he would run a "relentlessly positive" campaign focused on what Labour and New Zealand First had achieved in coalition together.

Then within the first few days of the campaign starting in August then-prime minister Jacinda Ardern announced the election date was postponed from September to October while Auckland dealt with a new community cluster and the rest of the country would remain at Level 2.

The restrictions significantly impacted the way parties could campaign - Peters' usual town hall meetings and public gatherings weren't allowed and very quickly he turned on Ardern and started running a campaign opposing her at a time her personal popularity was skyrocketing.

It was a fatal mistake by Peters, and one many in his party didn't support including senior MPs at the time, Ron Mark and Tracey Martin.

While one camp was telling him to stick to the original strategy there were others encouraging his resentment and hyping him up to go on the attack.

By election night in Russell, he only had Shane Jones at his side, having isolated himself from the rest of his MPs, and the party was ejected from Parliament.

There's a huge lesson in that three-month period of NZ First's history and Peters is now right back there with a decision to make.

Coalition parties fight their own corners

The Herald-Motu Research Poll of Polls has this week shifted the probability of the coalition having enough support to form a government after the election from 61 percent to 51.5 percent.

National has just been through a second confidence vote in four months of its leader and prime minister and has some serious work to do convincing prospective voters it's worried about the country, and not just itself.

Act, however, is running a different race and deliberately trying to keep the coalition together while also looking to make gains from National and NZ First's slip-ups.

The 1News-Verian poll registered the party on 9 percent - up three points.

Act party supporters have been clear they want stability from the coalition, prompting a focus from the leadership on proposing its own policy and not spending too much time criticising its partners' ideas or personal blunders.

Leader David Seymour has the shackles of being deputy prime minister but is also deliberately trying to give an air of being measured and mature while Luxon and Peters have repeatedly scrapped it out publicly.

He also has the benefit of new candidate Paul Henry, who not only draws big crowds to any public meeting, but can also say some of the things Seymour can't.

Henry isn't an MP in government and has the luxury of being able to take a whack at Luxon and Peters and not look like he's trying to take down the coalition.

World.title: Gisborne residents urged to be ready for flooding and slips
World.content:
MetService says about 40 millimetres of rain has already fallen in Gisborne, after a heavy downpour and thunderstorms on Friday morning.

The weather agency says the area west of Hicks Bay on the East Cape has been worst hit.

It said it was monitoring the Poroporo River which had accumulated 55mm in the last 12 hours.

A line of thunderstorms around the Oweka Bridge had weakened and ceased since midday, it said.

Gisborne's Civil Defence said it had not seen any critical risk and had heard of one incident of minor surface flooding.

Tairāwhiti Civil Defence is urging residents to be ready for potential surface flooding, slips and more as heavy rain moves in.

An orange heavy rain warning is in effect for Gisborne/Tai Rāwhiti, north of Tolaga Bay, until 8pm on Friday night.

"That's in place this morning and 25 millimetres per hour rain rate can cause that rapid flooding. Some places are already seeing quite high rain rate," meteorologist Paris Mitchell said.

Between 90 and 120mm of rain is expected.

The public are being told to clear gutters and drains, steer clear of low-lying areas while the heaviest rain comes through, and drive to the conditions.

MetService said there was only a minimal chance of upgrading its warning to red.

The worst of the weather is forecast for the morning and afternoon - with a thunderstorm warning in place for then.

Gisborne mayor Rehette Stolz asked the public to report any flooding or slips amid heavy downpours.

She said it was very wet but Gisborne was prepared for anything, and civil defence teams were monitoring water levels and flooding.

She reminded people to be cautious and drive to conditions.

MetService said it has recorded up to 10mm of rain per hour already this morning in the northern ranges and 8mm around East Cape.

Earlier, MetService issued a severe thunderstorm warning for the Far North.

World.title: Manufacturing sector expanding at a slower pace as firms take cautionary approach
World.content:
The manufacturing sector remains in expansion mode, albeit at a slower pace, as firms took a more cautionary tone in July.

The BNZ-Business New Zealand Performance of Manufacturing Index fell 5.8 points last month to 54.3 - a reading above 50 indicated the sector was expanding.

"We acknowledge 54.3 is softer than June's staggering result, however, some month-on-month volatility in the PMI is common and not an immediate cause for concern," BNZ senior economist Doug Steel said.

Production was the strongest at 57.3, followed by deliveries at 55.8 and new orders at 53.3.

Employment was the weakest sub index, but remained in expansion at 52.8 - indicating some level of job creation in the manufacturing sector.

Steel said despite the overall expansive theme, there were some "cautionary tales".

"Businesses that returned negative commentary cited geopolitical tensions and fuel price volatility as key concerns, while higher raw material costs, inconsistent forward orders, and softer consumer spending serve a reminder of the headwinds facing an otherwise resilient industry," he said.

BusinessNZ head of advocacy Catherine Beard said after June's "exceptional result" it was not a surprise to see momentum ease but conditions were solid.

"What's more concerning is the shift in sentiment, with 57 percent of comments being negative," Beard said.

"Respondents continue to point to the conflict in the Middle East, high fuel and raw material costs, and a general reluctance from customers to spend, with a number also citing uncertainty ahead of the election."

World.title: Philip Polkinghorne denies direct accusations he killed wife Pauline Hanna during inquest
World.content:
Philip Polkinghorne has denied killing his wife as the accusation was put directly to him at her inquest.

Polkinghorne was cleared of Pauline Hanna's 2021 murder at a trial two years ago but chose not to give evidence there.

On Friday, he got into the witness box at the Coronial inquest into Pauline Hanna's death where police lawyer Alysha McClintock accused him directly.

"You laid her out and you go about making it look like she killed herself," she said.

Polkinghorne answered with an emphatic "no."

McClintock accused Polkinghorne of attacking Hanna after an argument, incapacitating her so she could not fight back, killing her, and making it look like a suicide.

At each step Polkinghorne said "no" or "wrong"

Earlier in the hearing, he admitted he had lied several times since Hanna's death about some of the circumstances surrounding it, but denied it was to cover-up killing Hanna.

McClintock said there would be no other reason to lie.

"If Pauline had killed herself and all you had to do is explain how you found her, we shouldn't have all these lies," McClintock said.

McClintock asked Polkinghorne about a statement from sex worker Madison Ashton, who he'd been in a relationship with.

In it, Ashton said Polkinghorne told her Hanna had broken into their house and killed herself.

Polkinghorne denied saying that, and denied messaging Ashton the day his wife died.

He was grilled about his wife's use of the sleeping pill zopiclone, some of which were his.

Coroner Tania Tetitaha asked him if he had ever been in trouble with the Medical Council for prescribing medicines for himself.

He denied that until McClintock produced a 2018 letter from the council that warned him about self prescribing, including for zopliclone.

"I apologise, I had forgotten about that," he said.

A message from Ashton showed he had spoken to her about the council's letter.

"No biggie, I'll use a false name in the future," he said in the message.

Today, he said the message was "very flippant and inappropriate."

Pauline Hanna's family were able to put questions to Polkinghorne for the first time under oath

Her brother Bruce Hanna spent the time asking about the position of Pauline's arms when she was found.

Through a lawyer, her sister Tracey asked about why Polkinghorne had been searching for information about her injuries in the days after her death.

The purpose of the inquest is to establish the circumstances surrounding Pauline Hanna's death, including whether it was self inflicted.

Several details are suppressed.

World.title: AI accounting startup Sterling raises $3.8m seed round
World.content:
A Wellington-based artificial intelligence startup has raised $3.8 million in one of the larger seed funding rounds seen recently in New Zealand's technology sector.

Sterling, which was founded just 10 months ago, develops software designed to automate routine finance and accounting work. It says the funding will help it expand in New Zealand, Australia and the United States.

The round was led by trans-Tasman venture capital firm Blackbird and included alumni from companies such as Xero, Vend, Pushpay and Trade Me.

Chief executive and co-founder Nik Wakelin said Sterling was designed to act as an "autopilot" for finance teams rather than just another AI chatbot.

"It sits in your finance team, in your inbox and all your systems, picks up things as they arrive and works out where everything goes and files it for you," he told RNZ.

"The idea is by the time your finance team turns up in the morning and has their coffee, everything's done and prepped for them, ready to review and tick off."

The company was founded in October last year by Wakelin, formerly of Deliveroo, MinuteDock and Gelato.io, and Ludgwig Wendzich, whose background includes Apple, Vend and Lightspeed.

Wakelin said the idea emerged from conversations with their wives, who are both accountants.

He said advances in generative AI had made it possible to automate tasks that previously required human judgement, such as reviewing expenses, matching transactions and investigating accounting discrepancies.

Finance teams often employed highly qualified accountants to perform repetitive tasks that consumed large amounts of time, he said.

"We kind of call them 70-IQ jobs. You've got these qualified chartered accountants, 170-IQ people, doing the 70-IQ jobs and we want to take that away from them."

Despite being only 10 months old, Sterling said it has been rolled out to users since March, and has already completed about 1200 hours of finance work for customers.

Clients include honey exporter Manukora, early childhood software company Storypark and insurance broker Echelon.

Wakelin said securing backing from Blackbird and well-known figures from New Zealand's technology sector would help accelerate the company's growth.

"We really want to build the next generational technology company," he said.

World.title: Another person found wounded at Gun City shop where man fatally shot by police took gun
World.content:
A wounded person has been found at the same Gun City shop where a man who was later shot dead by police stole an air-rifle.

A retail worker across the road, who did not wish to be named, said three police cars and three ambulances were at the scene.

Hato Hone St John confirmed they were at the scene and had taken a person to Auckland City Hospital in a serious condition.

RNZ/Marika Khabazi

It comes just one day after a 33-year-old man was fatally shot by police as he approached Auckland's Sylvia Park Shopping Centre while carrying a stolen air rifle from Gun City.

RNZ understands the man is Hapai Ropata Clyde Otene.

Police were carrying out a critical incident investigation and had confirmed the IPCA had been notified and would be carrying out its own investigation.

RNZ/Marika Khabazi

RNZ/Marika Khabazi

World.title: Murder sentencing: Family desperate to recover remains of Canterbury father Richard Leman
World.content:
The family of a Canterbury father-of-three murdered and dismembered by Michael Scott Rodger are desperate to find the rest of his body to say goodbye and bury him with dignity.

Rodger shot Richard Leman in April 2023 before dismembering him and stuffing his torso into the boot of his own car and leaving it at an abandoned Rangiora house.

Only Leman's torso has been recovered.

On Friday Rodger was jailed for life with a non-parole period of 17 years for the 41-year-old's murder.

He fixated on the front of the courtroom, never meeting the eyes of Leman's sister as she tearfully told the High Court at Christchurch of the pain Rodger had caused her family.

"He shot him. He then took his head and his limbs, which are still missing," Kim Leman said.

"What did he do with them? Why can't he let Richard come home?

"I'm still searching for Richard. Part of my mind is always looking, always wondering if today will be the day."

Richard Leman who died in April 2023. Supplied / NZ Police

The three years since Leman's death had been exhausting, she said.

"There is no closure, no final goodbye. The loss is not something that happened in the past, it continues every day.

"What was done to Richard's body deprived us of the opportunity to hold him one last time and say goodbye."

She called Rodger evil and a coward.

'I will never forget my mother's screams'

KIm Leman would never forget the day she learned her brother was dead.

"I will never forget my mother's screams," she said.

"The air left my lungs and a crushing weight of grief consumed everything around me.

"There are not enough words in any language to describe the depths of our sorrow."

Other victim impact statements were read by prosecutors Barnaby Hawes and Sean Mallett.

"I cannot comprehend how anyone can be so cruel to take Richard from us," his mother Vanessa's statement said.

"He was a kind and loving man, a devoted father.

"I feel like I have lost Richard twice. The first is when his life was violently taken from him, the second is because I have never had the chance to say goodbye."

"How do you say goodbye when half of the person you love is still missing?" one of his nieces asked in her statement.

"You took away his dignity, you took away our chance to say goodbye," another niece said.

Leman's 11-year-old son, who was aged eight when his father died, said the loss of his father was unfair and had left him angry.

"I have been texting him for three years hoping he will text back," his statement said.

"My heart is broken. I will never see my dad again. I miss my dad so much."

Justice Eaton presided over the trial in the High Court in Christchurch. STUFF / ALDEN WILLIAMS

'Grief never leaves me'

Leman's 82-year-old father Norman said he never imagined he would spend the last years of his life mourning his youngest child.

"Knowing my son died alone, terrified and begging for his life is something that will never leave me until the day I die," his statement said.

"The grief never leaves me. It is there when I wake up in the morning and it is there when I go to sleep at night. No father should ever have to know his son's body was cut in half.

"We cremated Richard without knowing that parts of his body had not been recovered. We have never truly been able to say goodbye."

In a statement released by police after the sentence was handed down, the Leman family said there were no words to truly describe the pain they had lived with since his death.

"Over the years, we have tried to come to terms with an unimaginable loss, but one of the hardest realities is that Richard is still not fully home. We are still missing parts of him. How do you say goodbye when you are still waiting for your loved one to be returned to you? How do you find peace knowing part of the person you love is still missing? That is a burden our family will carry forever," the family said.

"Until every part of Richard that can be recovered is brought home to his family, we do not believe the person convicted of murdering him should ever be granted parole."

While the court process had come to an end, the Leman family said their grief endured.

"He was far more than a court case or a headline. He was a father, a son, a brother, an uncle, a family member and a friend. He was loved, he mattered and he deserved so much more."

The family said they were frustrated and hurt by Rodger being granted name suppression and legal protections around his criminal history during the court process.

"We understand that the justice system has rules designed to protect the fairness of a trial. But from the perspective of Richard's family, it was incredibly difficult to watch so much care being taken to protect the rights of the man accused of taking Richard's life," they said.

"At times, it felt as though the person accused of Richard's murder was being protected while Richard and our family were left to carry the consequences."

Michael Rodger during the trial. RNZ / Nathan Mckinnon

Rodger denied the killing

A High Court jury took two days of deliberations to reach a unanimous guilty verdict in March following a four-week trial.

The Crown's case was that Rodger shot Leman once in the thigh and then fatally in the chest at a property in Andrew Street in Rangiora.

Rodger denied shooting or killing Leman, instead blaming "Mr X" who he refused to identify after previously suffering a beating in prison.

The prosecution said Leman smoked methamphetamine with his friend Sara Plimmer before the pair went to the home of another woman, Morgan Grant, to bring her food.

Leman went to look for a way to smoke more methamphetamine while the two women sat in a bedroom and ate Burger King.

Rodger, who had been invited to the address by Grant, got into an argument with Leman.

The two women found Leman and Rodger facing off in the lounge and Rodger was holding a gun.

No-one gave Leman first-aid or called emergency services after the two shots were fired and Leman died within minutes.

Rodger's DNA was found on the cap of a petrol container at the home where Leman's torso was found as well as on the inside of a door handle of the car where his torso was hidden.

The women told the jury Rodger had threatened to kill them, took Leman's drugs and cash and dragged his body to another room.

The prosecution pointed to CCTV footage, telecommunication data and forensic evidence pointing to Rodger's guilt.

Grant pleaded guilty to being an accessory to Leman's murder in 2024.

Rodger claimed Leman was already dead when he arrived at Grant's property but he admitted concealing and dismembering his body.

Defence lawyer Ethan Huda told the jury there were questions about Rodger's involvement in Leman's death.

A pathologist told the jury Leman could have been stabbed before being shot, a point the prosecution omitted from its closing argument.

Huda said neither Grant nor Plimmer mentioned any stabbing during their evidence and that raised significant doubts over the killing.

The defence also questioned the reliability of some CCTV evidence.

A text message exchange between Grant and another person in the days after Leman's murder had referenced the involvement of multiple "fugitives" in the killing.

Police issued a statement on behalf of Leman's family after Rodger was found guilty.

"Nothing will ever undo what was done to him and nothing will ever bring him back to the people who loved him. Richard was not just a name in a courtroom or a case in a trial," the statement said.

"He was a son, a father, a brother, an uncle and a man who was deeply loved by those closest to him.

World.content:

World.title: EPL side walks off as Spanish club kicks penalty into open net
World.content:
Fulham's preseason match against Málaga turned out to be not too friendly after the English club walked off and coach Álvaro Arbeloa was shown a red card for complaining to the referees.

The match had finished 2-2, after the La Liga side Málaga FC equalised in the 90th minute.

At full-time, the Premier League outfit walked off the pitch while Málaga stayed on, believing a penalty shootout should decide the winner.

Malaga striker Jauregi then kicked a penalty into an open net before celebrating in front of the home fans.

In a post on X, Fulham said both teams had agreed before the match that no penalty shootout would follow a draw.

"We can confirm that prior to the match, both teams agreed that there would not be a penalty shootout in the event of a draw," Fulham wrote on X.

On their club website, Malaga said it believed a shootout was on the cards.

"Although a penalty shootout had been scheduled, Fulham left the pitch, claiming that a shootout had not been included in the contract," the La Liga club said.

World.title: Payne's fame began as a joke. Now his shirt has sparked a bidding war
World.content:
Just a few months ago, few soccer fans outside New Zealand and Australia knew Tim Payne's name. Now they are bidding thousands of dollars for the jersey off his back.

The shirt Payne wore in his debut for Club Olimpia, a Paraguayan soccer powerhouse, has become a coveted piece of match-worn memorabilia since the club put it up for auction online five days ago.

With bidding set to close, the leading offer has climbed above 21 million in Paraguay's currency, the guarani, equivalent to around $5,000.

Viral Kiwi star meets Argentine influencer who boosted following to 5M New Zealand soccer player Tim Payne has met social media influencer Valen Scarsini after the Argentine encouraged his fans to follow the unheralded All Whites player.

It is the latest development in the unlikely rise of the 32-year-old defender, who entered the World Cup with just over 4,000 followers on Instagram and emerged as one of the tournament's biggest social media sensations.

Before representing New Zealand at the World Cup, Payne spent most of his career out of the limelight, playing for low-profile clubs in New Zealand before playing 143 A-League matches for Wellington. He also spent two years with England's Blackburn Rovers but never made a major appearance because of work-permit problems.

Then Argentine soccer influencer Valen Scarsini, known online as El Scarso, went searching for what he called the World Cup's "least-known soccer player".

Scarsini settled on Payne, whose Instagram account had 4,715 followers at the time, and encouraged his more than 2 million followers across Instagram, TikTok and YouTube to follow Payne, flood his posts with supportive comments and mention his name everywhere.

Loading Instagram content

Within days, Payne's following skyrocketed, eventually topping 5.4 million — more than the entire population of his native New Zealand. The surge in online fame helped carry Payne to Paraguay, where he signed with national club champion Olimpia on a one-year deal in June, ending a seven-year stint with Wellington Phoenix.

Payne gave legions of new fans another reason to cheer him during his August 2 debut against Asunción club Rubio Ñu, scoring minutes after coming off the bench to help Olimpia win 5-0.

Now the signed jersey from that match is drawing the sort of interest usually reserved for far more established names — though the leading offer remains a far cry from the millions of dollars paid for jerseys worn by Argentine superstar Lionel Messi and other soccer greats.

"I know exactly what it means to wear these stripes and play in this shirt, and that's why I want to give it to a true Olimpista (Olimpia fan)," Payne said in a video launching the auction.

AP

World.title: Brian To'o is still just the beginning for the PNG Chiefs
World.content:
After a week in the spotlight following the biggest decision of his career, Brian To'o went back to work.

His showing in the Panthers' 12-6 loss to the Roosters was typical of the To'o we've come to know.

The future Papua New Guinea Chief did not bring up his 100th try for the Panthers but did churn through 17 runs for 162 metres to go with five tackle busts and two line breaks. For some wingers that's a big night but for To'o it's the standard.

'Can't compete': Super coaches weigh into PNG Chiefs debate Two of the NRL's most successful modern coaches weigh into the debate about the concessions afforded to the league's forthcoming PNG franchise.

The performance came in the days following confirmation of To'o's move to the Papua New Guinea Chiefs and it shouldn't have been a surprise.

There are good reasons To'o has become the premier winger of his time, and having such a high baseline is one of them.

Continued excellence on his part, for both the rest of this season and his final year with Penrith in 2027, is as close to a given as you'll find anywhere in rugby league.

He is the best player the Chiefs have signed but that may not remain so. Not since the Broncos filled their boots with Queensland-based stars for their inaugural season in 1988 has an expansion team signed so much established talent.

Zac Lomax will return to rugby league with the Chiefs. (Getty Images: Brendon THorne)

Of the six players to commit to the Chiefs, four have played State of Origin in the past two years. Some clubs go decades without signing one or two players who fit such a criteria.

The other two are the greatest try-scorer the Australian game has ever known and one of England's top front-rowers.

Unless Joseph Manu was just in Port Moresby on holiday, it seems likely they'll add the Golden Boot winner from the most recent World Cup to the list before long.

They have achieved all this without really entering the cut and thrust of the transfer market in earnest. Officially, the Chiefs cannot talk to any NRL free agents for the 2028 season until November 1 this year.

Manu has been linked with an NRL return with the Chiefs. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

Each of the signings they've made within the NRL have come because a club granted permission for the player in question to negotiate early or because the player activated something in their contract that allowed them to do so.

They've done all this while the luxury compound they're building is still a hole in the ground and before they have a logo or a jersey. To'o himself hasn't even been to Papua New Guinea before.

They're yet to land any young legs but if these are the players they can sign through the activation of obscure clauses and arcane options and the like, imagine what they can do in the jungle of true free agency when they have the biggest and sharpest teeth via their mountain of government funding?

With local products like Gairo Voro, Morea Morea and Finlay Glare, all of whom are enjoying standout seasons with London Broncos and will eventually take up development contracts with the club, to fill out the other end of the roster, the Cheifs can keep aiming high.

The floodgates have yet to truly open but already the ripples of the league's new money-monster are clear to see.

Hudson Young, fresh off a career-changing State of Origin series, is in the Chiefs' sights and despite the Raiders offering just about everything they've got to a player who has found a home in Canberra, fans there are turning as green as their jerseys because they know there's a chance they'll be money-whipped.

Young is the latest player to come into PNG's sights. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The spectre of similar moves loom over a sport addicted to transfer gossip and sank into Thursday's top-of-the-table clash because after the start they've made, no player seems out of reach for the Chiefs.

Not Sam Walker, who turned down the Roosters first contract offer midweek and has the chance to secure untold riches over the final stages of this season, a chance he has surely enhanced after a mature performance that helped put the Tricolours on top of the ladder.

Not Liam Martin, who rattled Cody Ramsey with the best shot of the night or Spencer Leniu, who struggled to find the fire against his former club and looks like he'd benefit from a change of scenery.

Not even Nathan Cleary, who tried every trick he knew but could not break down a resolute Roosters defensive line.

As impossible as it seems to picture him playing rugby league in anything but a Penrith jersey, even he is in play.

Through their tax-free contracts and the legitimacy that comes with signing established stars, the Chiefs have the capability to tip the entire league on its head.

They can pay a battler like a prince, a prince like a king and a king like a god and given they've already shown a taste for the finer things in assembling their roster, there's little reason to expect it won't continue.

Their advantages warp the salary cap beyond recognition and each signing they make is further proof of concept that the gold rush is real.

General manager of football Michael Chammas says he wears it as a badge of honour that clubs are beginning to gripe at the advantages PNG have been given and well may he, given how those clubs, blinded by the glittering of gold, let a Chief into the henhouse.

Why Luai's move to PNG has changed everything Jarome Luai's decision to sign with Papua New Guinea is a showcase of the economic power behind the Chiefs and marks the start of the greatest rugby league gold rush since Super League.

It is hard to begrudge any player for taking what's on offer, like it's hard to begrudge the way Chammas and the Chiefs are going about it. They're playing by the rules they've been given and they're playing by them well.

Ever since Jarome Luai was announced as their first signing, their power has become more and more real and it continues to solidify with every signing they make. Now, they are securing a firm foothold on the high side of an uneven surface.

To'o is the latest, but not the last and rugby league is only just beginning to reckon with the power of what the NRL has created with its concessions to the Chiefs and how it alters the competitive balance of the league.

They have turned the dial as far as it will go and are now waiting to see what happens next, as is their way, and it is happening hard and fast all around us.

The downpour of money is a monsoon that shows no sign of breaking, even as rival clubs get swamped.

And stars like To'o who have been swept along are still just the start. Expect plenty more to dive in.

World.title: Teen Italian star breaks world record for second time this week
World.content:
Italian teenage swimming sensation Sara Curtis has broken the world 50m backstroke world record again, just a day after eclipsing the global mark of Australian great Kaylee McKeown.

The 19-year-old Curtis ‌won gold in 26.56 seconds in the final of the European Championships in Paris on Thursday, local time, clipping another 0.07 seconds off the time of 26.63 she had set in Wednesday's semifinals.

That time had obliterated the three-year-old mark of five-time Olympic champion McKeown, who had clocked 26.86 when winning a World Cup race in Budapest in 2023.

Teenager breaks Kaylee McKeown backstroke world record Italian teenager Sara Curtis has set a new world record in the women's 50m backstroke, beating the mark previously held by Australian great Kaylee McKeown.

It continued the historic week for the Savigliano-born Curtis, who has a Nigerian mother and Italian father, as she becomes the first Black swimmer to hold an individual long-course world record.

Mary-Ambre Moluh, from ​France, finished ‌half a second behind Curtis ​to take the silver, while Britain's Lauren Cox took ​bronze.

"I'm happy I managed it again. It's absurd, another crazy feat," Curtis told Italian TV station Rai 2.

It ​was the ​third medal in Paris for ‌the University of Virginia star, who also took bronze in 100m freestyle and silver in ​the 4x100m freestyle relay.

The teenager had been inching towards the ​world ​record all year, having ​broken the Italian and ‌European records earlier in the season.

"From the moment I set off for Virginia, that's all I thought about, the record. A dream and ​an immense goal," she admitted.

But it has been a tough spell for McKeown, who had to pull out of both the recent Commonwealth Games and the current Pan Pacific Championships because of glandular fever.

The 25-year-old is determined to get back into top shape for the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, where Curtis shapes to be one of the pool stars.

Great Britain's Filip Nowacki claimed the European 200m breaststroke gold, continuing his terrific rise.

The 18-year-old was fresh from winning gold for Jersey at the Commonwealth Games, only the second ever for his little Channel Island home.

AAP

World.title: Four-goal Austin gives Dees perfect start to new AFLW era
World.content:
Melbourne's new dawn in the AFLW has begun with a win, with recruit Mia Austin kicking four goals to give Demons coach Tom Wilson victory in his first match in charge.

Hawthorn tested last year's preliminary finalists at Princes Park on Thursday night, and went into the final quarter level.

But the Dees kept the Hawks scoreless in the final term to secure a 19-point round one triumph.

AFLW double-header season opener left fans with 'lots of mixed feelings' The AFLW opened its 2026 season with a double-header at Docklands Stadium.

The contest was the first time Melbourne's women have not been coached by Mick Stinear, who is now in charge at Geelong, with Wilson taking over to start his AFLW coaching career.

Liv Purcell returned from the knee reconstruction that kept her to only two games last season and she was best afield, racking up 32 possessions and nine tackles.

Recruited from Carlton, Austin was outstanding and looks the ideal replacement for Eden Zanker, now at Fremantle.

Melbourne captain Kate Hore also starred, but goal kicking let her down and she finished with a wasteful 1.4.

The Hawks rallied after a slow start as they unveiled their key-forward double act, with former Gold Coast player Jacqueline Dupuy joining All-Australian Aine McDonagh.

Dupuy took nine marks and kicked a goal, while McDonagh made a strong start with three majors.

Hawthorn defender Jenna Richardson, who took 11 marks, and ruck Lucy Wales impressed.

With Hore, Tayla Harris and Purcell firing, the Dees threatened to kill off the game early.

Melbourne kicked the first three goals of the game and were up by 23 late in the opening term.

But Dupuy kicked her first for the Hawks to keep them within 17 points at the first change.

The game flipped in the second, as Dupuy and McDonagh fired in attack. Hawthorn kicked three goals to one and only trailed by seven points at the main break.

Jacinta Hose's long-overdue AFLW debut ended in more pain for the Demons' ruck when she was forced out of the game in the second quarter with an ankle injury.

Hose was drafted in 2023, but two knee reconstructions have stalled her career.

When McDonagh kicked the only goal of the third quarter, the Hawks led for the first time in the game and scores were tied at the final change.

But Austin kicked her fourth goal at the start of the last quarter and Elizabeth McNamara added another a couple of minutes later to steady for Melbourne.

While Shelley Heath goaled 11 minutes into the term, the Demons had a three-goal break and the game was over.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Cherry-Evans confirms NRL exit in shock call after Roosters win
World.content:
Daly Cherry-Evans has given himself every chance to book-end his NRL career with a second premiership after confirming 2026 will be his last season in Australia.

The Sydney Roosters star announced today he would finish in the NRL at season's end, before moving to the English Super League for a one-year swan song at Hull FC.

His exit will bring the curtain down on one of the NRL's most storied careers, after debuting at Manly in 2011 before his shock Sea Eagles exit at the end of last season.

At the age of 37, Cherry-Evans is the second-most-capped player in NRL history and has a string of records, including the most 40-20s ever kicked, most golden-point winners and most field goals in the NRL era.

He also captained both Queensland and Australia, helping lead the Maroons to three series wins and claiming a Clive Churchill Medal in 2013.

Cherry-Evans led the Maroons to three series victories as captain. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

His announcement comes despite him showing last night he is still playing as well as ever, scoring both of the Roosters' tries in a 12-6 win over Penrith.

After beginning his career with a premiership as a rookie halfback at Manly in 2011, Cherry-Evans now has the Roosters in first with a second title looking a real possibility.

"I still have a real desire to play and compete, so the opportunity to join Hull FC and experience the Super League is something I'm genuinely excited about," Cherry-Evans said.

"But there's still plenty of football to be played this season, and that's where my focus is.

"We've got a lot we still want to achieve as a team here at the Roosters, and I'm determined to give my all and play my part in that."

Rumours of Cherry-Evans' Super League move had come as something of a shock earlier this week.

Hull will be coached next season by Steve McNamara, who is a long-time friend and former assistant of Roosters' coach Trent Robinson.

The former Queensland halfback shocked Manly last March when he announced he would leave the club after 15 seasons there.

He insisted today he had no ill feelings towards the Sea Eagles, where he remains the most-capped player in the club's history.

"Manly will always hold a special place for me and my family," he said.

Roosters force first NRL lead change in five months There's a new name at the top of the NRL ladder for the first time since March after the Roosters outlasted Penrith in a possible grand final preview.

"I spent more than 15 years there, made lifelong friendships and was fortunate to experience so much throughout my time at the club.

"Coming to the Roosters this year gave me the opportunity to challenge myself in a completely new environment, and I've loved being part of this club."

Cherry-Evans' Roosters arrival has prompted the Tri-colours to deploy promising playmaker Hugo Savala in the centres this season.

Robinson described coaching Cherry-Evans as a "gift" after his side climbed to first and moved to within touching distance of the minor premiership.

"You talk about external motivation, but to watch someone care about the way that he plays the game and goes about it," Robinson said.

"Maybe two or three years ago at a charity function, I almost bought his boot for a couple of thousand dollars, but one of my mates got it before me.

"I feel like a guy plays with a spirit… I really enjoy watching him play, and I've said that, but I've enjoyed watching him come and want to improve his game."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: King could beat Longmuir to AFL's coach of the year gong
World.content:
Melbourne's stunning win over Fremantle was more than a statement.

It was the destruction of any sentiment that the Demons have been punching above their weight, and a warning that they are a true contender.

For first-year coach Steven King, it was also confirmation that he is the main threat to Justin Longmuir's status as the AFL's coach of the year.

Considering the latter's success so far in 2026, that is quite an achievement.

Christian Petracca left Melbourne at the end of 2025. (Getty images: Morgan Hancock)

When Melbourne sacked premiership coach Simon Goodwin four years after a drought-breaking flag, and then lost Norm Smith medallist Christian Petracca and four-time best and fairest winner Clayton Oliver to rival clubs, nobody thought the Demons would bounce back this emphatically.

Now they are fighting for a top-four finish and have scored more than 100 points in four of their past six games, despite losing star forward Brody Mihocek to a season-ending neck injury.

New structure on old foundation

The belief at Melbourne is palpable.

"If we play our brand of footy we can beat anyone. That's the belief Kingy's driving in us," Harrison Petty told ABC Sport after the Demons' win over Fremantle.

"We play a brutal game of footy and we try to play with a bit of flair. In previous years we haven't done that, and this year it's changed. It's an exciting brand."

After the victory, King credited Goodwin for paving the way to the side's success.

Simon Goodwin was sacked last August. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

"I think you missed the foundations of what was already here," he said.

"They won a premiership five years ago.

" Simon Goodwin was a great coach of this footy club. So I've walked into a group that knows how to compete around the footy and defend. "

His sentiments are reflected in the Demons' statistics.

Have the AFL's rule changes worked? Not exactly A raft of AFL rule changes for the 2026 season have either excited or horrified a range of fans — Cody Atkinson and Sean Lawson examine the changes and whether they have had the desired impact.

Melbourne already boasted a competitive midfield that was fourth for clearance differential and first for contested possession differential last season, but it fell down in its ball movement.

In 2026, Steven King has overcome the loss of the club's two best midfielders and still improved to third for transition, first for clearance differential and sixth for inside-50 differential.

Their only weakness is in defence, sitting 14th for points against.

Does King beat Longmuir?

So what makes a coach of the year? Is it surmounting numerous obstacles to rise up the ladder? Or should it be the leader of the best side of the season?

Longmuir has put the Dockers in the box seat for their second-ever minor premiership, lifting the side from sixth to first in his seventh season.

Justin Longmuir makes a strong case to be the AFL's coach of the year. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

The football gods have smiled on him with a league-high 11 players featuring in every game this season and the likelihood of at least five players in the All-Australian squad.

But how can you argue against the figurehead of a side that has had three losses, a club-record 14-game win streak and is two games clear at the top of the table, being crowned the game's best coach?

Of the 23 winners of coach of the year, 39 per cent have won the premiership, 56 per cent have made the grand final and 78 per cent have made the top four — supporting the argument ladder position is a key factor.

How the Hawks are making their two-ruck strategy work Once thought to be dead and buried, the era of the dual ruck has been resuscitated by a handful of clubs in finals contention, including Hawthorn.

More than 80 per cent of winners rose up the ladder, but the four first-year winners did not make a grand final that same season.

Winning the accolade is a massive sign of future success, with 11 of the 16 winners delivering a flag after receiving the gong.

It is a debate that will divide the footy community across the next fortnight, but neither coach will be anxious about the winner.

Longmuir's Dockers are the premiership favourite but are now batting away doubters following their loss at the MCG.

King's Dees, meanwhile, feel like the dark horse who could not only shape September but might just finish the month with the grandest prize of all.

Tech.title: Trump declares 100 percent tariffs on many drones and all aircraft parts
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

DJI ban: how the world’s biggest dronemaker is getting shoved out of the US

The United States has already banned future foreign drones from entering the United States unless their companies kiss the ring — as well as routers, robots, and Roombas. Now, President Donald Trump is targeting existing drone imports and parts, too. He’s going to try to make them cost a lot more.

In a presidential action, he’s declared a whopping 100 percent tariff on imports of drones with thermal cameras, drones weighing over 25kg (57 pounds), and any kind of part for any kind of unmanned aircraft weighing over 25kg — you can read the full list here. For all other drones, including tiny sub-250-gram “Mini” consumer drones, he’s declared a 25 percent tariff.

In Trump fashion, these tariffs have a huge loophole: if a company commits to making some of their drones or aircraft parts in the United States, they don’t have to pay tariffs. Trump suggested he’d make similar deals when he threatened a 100 percent tariff on computer chips last year.

And Trump is giving the EU, Japan, Liechtenstein, South Korea, Switzerland, and Taiwan a lower rate of 15 percent, and a rate of 10 percent for the UK, “provided that substantially all hardware, software, and technology originates from within these countries and the United States.”

Stated reasons for the new tariffs include:

“many U.S. commercial manufacturers that produce UAS domestically are highly dependent on foreign sources for critical UAS components, such as motors, electronic speed controllers, lithium-ion batteries, and docking stations, which creates unacceptable national security vulnerabilities.”

“products pose an information technology security risk because their software allows data to be sent back to the manufacturer in a foreign country.”

“there are concerns as to whether the U.S. industry can produce UAS and UAS components at the required speed and scale to adequately support national security operations and activities, including during a surge for wartime or armed conflict, or in a manner to sustain long-term economic competitiveness.”

Trump is also dangling a carrot, not just wielding a stick. The proclamation states that he’s authorizing the Secretary of Commerce to create a new program “to incentivize new investment in U.S. production facilities to produce UAS and UAS components.” That could be interesting, but last we checked, the government’s drone incentives were aimed towards drones for war.

The Supreme Court already ruled earlier this year that Trump’s global tariffs were illegal; the US Court of International Trade ruled against them too, though Trump continues to announce more.

As of today, it appears that Trump’s tariffs are enriching corporate America at the expense of everyday citizens. First, companies raise their prices so that you pay the cost of tariffs instead of them. Then, those companies get gigantic refunds from the government when the tariffs are declared illegal. Finally, they profit. Companies do not pass those refunds along to you, even though you paid for them, and they do not lower their prices either.

The tariffs aren’t the US government’s only attempt to target larger foreign drones in the US. The FCC recently threatened to retroactively ban “military-grade” drones using definitions that would also catch drones for farmers, first responders, and light shows in the same net.

Tech.title: Apple and Epic argue over how much Apple should get from purchases made outside the App Store
Tech.content:
Apple’s filing is in, and Apple admitted that under the Ninth Circuit’s definition of “necessary costs” they would charge 0% for purchases made via linkouts to the web.

Apple proposed linkout fees of 15% for standard apps and 5% for Small Business Program apps. Epic believes these fees are far outside of the bounds of the Ninth Circuit’s guidance on permissible fees, and we have roughly 60 days to file our opposition supported by expert witnesses.

Tech.title: ‘That is not acceptable’: Judge orders Google to make rival app store installs easier
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

One month after Epic Games and Google seemingly stopped fighting over the future of Android app distribution, they were back in a San Francisco courtroom today — where Judge James Donato just ordered Google to make it easier to install rival app stores on Android.

It’s been nearly three years since a jury unanimously decided that Google had an illegal monopoly over Android apps, and almost two years since Judge Donato decided the best way of undoing that monopoly would be to crack open Android app distribution. Donato ordered Google to carry rival Android app stores inside its own Google Play Store, and to provide rivals with complecte access to Google’s full catalog of apps, for several years.

But Epic argued that Google is still making it too difficult to install rival app stores, showing the entire courtroom a live demo of how many steps it currently takes — and Judge Donato agreed that some of those steps were unnecessary “anticompetitive friction” and ordered Google to remove them.

First, Epic’s lawyer Yonatan Even showed that if you search Google’s Play Store for the term “store for apps,” no third-party app stores appear, only physical stores. “Wait, why did Walmart come up?” Judge Donato asked. “That’s not good,” he exclaimed.

These are my own screenshots, not the live demo shown in court, as no photography is allowed there. Images: Google

“That is not acceptable, that has to be fixed. I want every possible variation that’s even only 70 percent properly phrased,” Donato ordered. Google’s counsel agreed to make it happen.

Similarly, Judge Donato bristled when he saw that users have to press a “view” button before they can press an “install” button when choosing to install a third-party app store, and so that will change too. “You don’t get that when you’re looking at Apple Music,” he noted.

“Make that install, not view,” Donato ordered, and Google agreed to do so.

Later, Epic showed that when you search for “app store,” or even if you search directly for Aptoide, the first rival store to make it into the Google Play Store, Google doesn’t surface a normal list of apps — it shows you a new banner you have to click through to a dedicated third-party app store page.

That’s not just a problem for brand-new app stores, argued Even. Big, established companies like Amazon might decide not to launch app stores because they’d be losing the ability to appear in normal appstore search results.

Judge Donato ordered Google to fix that one, too, telling the company that it didn’t make any sense. “Why doesn’t it say ‘are you looking for music’ when you type in ‘music store’?” he asked.

Google’s attorney replied that Epic and Google had already agreed that app stores are a special category of apps that have advanced permissions. But Donato said the warning on the third-party app store page itself was sufficient to address that — there’s no need to ask a user whether they really want the thing they searched for, whether it’s a game store or a glass of water.

“We all know that when you go to a Google store or an Apple store and you type in the name of your app, you’re going to get one thing you were looking for and ten things you don’t want,” said the judge, explaining that he doesn’t think average users will be confused when they get what they’re asking for.

“Take off the ‘are you looking for’ screen, there’s no purpose for that. There’s a friction there that has no purpose whatsoever,” Donato said.

The judge wants these changes fast. “Have it done by a week from today,” he told Google. “If there’s some problem with that, let me know.‘

Tech.title: The fight over Flock and other ALPRs
Tech.content:
There are over 120,000 of Flock’s automatic license plate reader (ALPR) cameras installed all over the US. Flock’s cameras, and others like them, use AI to identify and track vehicles based on their license plate number, make, model, color, and other info, networked together to track vehicles and people’s movements throughout the day and across the country.

Dozens of communities have canceled contracts for the cameras or turned them off, including Los Angeles, as officials have pushed for more limits on the data they collect, who has access to it, and how it can be used in the future. Earlier this year, Amazon-owned Ring canceled a partnership with Flock after online backlash.

Tech.title: Microsoft’s Clippy-like Mico character is no longer the face of Copilot
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Microsoft Copilot will no longer show its emotive yellow blob, Mico, when you use the chatbot’s voice mode. In a support page, Microsoft says it’s going to move Mico to its Learn Live platform, where the avatar will have “more to react to,” as reported earlier by GeekWire.

Mico launched in Copilot’s voice mode last October, with Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman pitching the avatar as a way to give the chatbot an “identity.” The blob would react to what you say in real-time, complete with facial expressions and animations.

Mico joins the long list of virtual helpers that Microsoft has retired over the years, like Clippy, Cortana, and Rover. “Mico helped us learn about warmth, expressiveness, and how people want to talk with AI,” Microsoft’s support page says. “Those learnings are shaping Copilot going forward.” Microsoft is removing Mico from Copilot “in waves.”

The change is part of Microsoft’s plans to merge its Copilot and Microsoft 365 Copilot apps. It also comes just months after an AI reshuffling that put Jacob Andreou in charge of Copilot, while Suleyman turned his attention to developing new AI models.

Tech.title: Netflix is closing two game studios
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Netflix plans to shut down two of its gaming studios, as reported by Game File and Variety, as it makes a bigger shift toward party games and titles streamed to TVs.

One of the studios being shut down is Night School Studio, creators of the Oxenfree series. Netflix bought Night School in 2021, and it just released a horror experience called Unhinged for TVs and launched a mobile game in 2025 tied to Black Mirror. The other studio that’s set to close is Helsinki-based Moonloot Games, which was created in 2022.

Netflix’s big push into TV-based games kicked off late last year and was a pivot from a mobile-focused approach that featured prestige indie titles. But Netflix has let many of those indie hits leave its mobile lineup as it focuses instead on four pillars of kids, party, narrative, and “mainstream” games.

“As we continue to prioritize these areas, we see an opportunity to be more focused in our execution, so we are making organizational changes to the business to match those priorities,” Netflix spokesperson Chrissy Kelleher tells The Verge. Netflix is also eliminating “some” additional roles in its games business, according to Kelleher. The cuts include Tara Voelker, who says she was the “single accessibility person” on the gaming team.

Tech.title: This school-friendly laptop from HP is $300 off
Tech.content:
Brad Bourque is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

With memory prices still high and showing no signs of dropping, we’re always happy to find a good deal on a budget-friendly system with an adequate amount of RAM. Best Buy has the HP OmniBook X Flip discounted by $300, bringing the cost down to $699.99. This model is equipped with an Intel Core Ultra 5 and 16GB of LPDDR5X memory, which should be great for both web browsing and homework, and a 512GB SSD for storage. The screen is a 1920 x 1200 LED touchscreen, with a fully rotating hinge for tented or tablet mode.

While the Intel Core 5 Ultra may not be the most powerful chip for heavy workloads or gaming, the OmniBook makes up for it with strong battery life and connectivity. HP claims the system can run for over 22 hours of video playback on a single charge, and fast charging can take the battery to 50 percent in just 30 minutes.
